The couplet's variation is the sūrah's way of refusing monotony inside paradise: even in a place without want, the soul still selects and still longs, and the text dignifies both verbs. Later verses will repeat the structure for the right-hand people — fruit "in season, not forbidden" — and the contrast confirms the design: the near-rank's desire is its logistics. Nothing is asked of them, and the sūrah's restraint about how anything arrives — no kitchen, no spring, no storehouse named in this couplet — makes the verbs of want the only machinery the scene permits.

**Why Meat Belongs to This Verse and Not to the Argument**

It is easy to skim 56:20–21 as decoration after 18–19's cups, and the placement argues otherwise. The sūrah's next movement (25–26) will define the Garden by its soundscape — no vanity, no sin's instigation, only "peace, peace" — and the birds' verse, immediately before it, is the last word of the body's catalog. Flesh, fruit, drink: the animal functions are complete before the sūrah moves, in 25–37, to speech, plants, water, shade, spouses, and numbers, which is the sequence of a human being restored, sense by sense, to a world with none of its costs. Verse 21, at the hinge, does the dirty work the others avoid — meat, the one food that in this world means death — and does it in three words that mention neither animal nor knife. The resurrection of the body, which the whole chapter exists to defend, is stated here in its least defensible detail, and the sūrah lets the wish-verb carry the burden the audience might ask to see.

**Ṭayr in the Qur'an's Wider Sky**

These birds are the last stop on a journey the Book makes them take. In the dominion chapter, birds are the resurrection's public sign — "Do they not see the birds above them, spreading their wings and folding them in?" (67:19), creatures whose flight is itself an argument about God's hold on what flies. In the table chapter, God commands Abraham to slaughter four birds and lay their parts on hills, and when he calls them they come running (2:260) — the first resurrection demonstration in the Qur'an's sequence, performed with poultry. The sūrah of Jesus gives him clay birds that breathe when he breathes on them. Al-Wāqiʿah's dinner of birds belongs to this same argument's end: the birds that demonstrated resurrection in the signs chapters are, for the near-rank, served at table, the demonstrated raised and eaten, and the chapter by this completes a circle its audience could feel without being told: the thing God raises, God also provides, and the miracle the deniers mocked is, in the Garden, merely the menu.
verses.22:
> And ˹they will have˺ maidens with gorgeous eyes

**Qāṣirāt: The Gaze That Has Arrived**

In its companion chapters the Book completes the image with the detail that carries the sūrah's whole psychology of desire: these are "restraining their glances" — qāṣirāt aṭṭarf (37:48; 38:52) — eyes that have stopped reaching, companions whose gaze is fixed on their own and who themselves look at no one else. The two directions matter together: desire in the Garden is not an intensified appetite but an appetite that has come to rest, and the "wide-eyed" of verse 22 in this sūrah and the "restrained" in its neighbors describe one condition from each side — the eye open and the eye contented. The phrase is the answer to the restlessness every husband and wife of the world knows; the sūrah promises not the addition of beauty to an envious, ranging heart but the removal of ranging itself, which is the chapter's consistent technique: cups with no headache (19), fruit with no season (20), and companions with no wander.

**Served or Serving: The Syntax in Two Hands**

Verse 22 has a famous grammatical fork. The maidens can be read as another item in the gift-list — "and maidens" hanging on the understood "We will have given them" back in the scene's verbs — or as a second subject of the youths' verb of circling service, so that they too wait upon the near-rank. The commentators record both, and each has real support: the gift-reading matches 20–21, where fruit and birds arrive as objects of choosing, and the serving-reading matches 17, where the chapter has already introduced a class of attendants and might be doubling its staff. Nothing in the Arabic decides, and the undecidability may be a grace: the same beings occupy, in the audience's imagination, the place of the given and the place of the giver, and the sūrah lets "maidens with gorgeous eyes" stand between the two grammars without embarrassment, in the one scene where no honor is compromised by serving because nobody is diminished by it.

**The Pearl, the Maiden, and the Sūrah's Swapped Economy**

Verse 23 will dress the maidens in a simile — "like pristine pearls" — but readers should count, from 22, what the chapter has been doing with the audience's luxury goods since verse 15. Jewels belong on furniture, pearls on bodies, gold on couch-cushions; the things Makkah traded and hoarded have been redistributed as surfaces and persons of the Garden, never as possessions of the self. In the near-rank nobody owns a pearl — a pearl is what a companion of the near-rank is like. The chapter's economy of precious objects, read from verse 22, is a complete inversion of the hoarder's logic the sūrah's Iron neighbor legislated: wealth is demoted to décor, and persons are promoted to the worth that wealth used to claim. The "gorgeous eyes" are therefore, in the chapter's arithmetic, more precious than the jewelry they outshine, and that is the verse's contribution to the sūrah's long argument about what solid things are for.

**What the Sūrah Refuses to Say About Them**

The reticence of 22 deserves one final clause of notice: the sūrah gives these companions no portrait — no faces, no hair, no bodies beyond the eye. The chapter that named ewers and couches in detail stops at the eyes of its most intimate promise, and the restraint is its own instruction about the audience's projections: the text will say "maidens" and "gorgeous eyes" and nothing else, leaving the rest to the pearl's simile (23) and to the reader's own history of beauty. In the chapter of the Event, everything solid becomes dust; what remains to the near-rank is what can look back, and verse 22 says exactly that, and stops.
verses.23:
> like pristine pearls

**Maknūn: The Beauty Nobody Has Touched**

The simile's adjective is maknūn, passive of kanana — to store, to hide away — and the image it carries is the pearl still in its shell, still in its bed on the sea-floor: a thing of value that has not been handled, aired, priced, or worn. The sūrah's neighbors use the same figure twice more, — the identical adjective that the Mount sūrah lends its youthful servants ("like spotless pearls," 52:24), while the Insān sūrah likens its eternal pages to scattered pearls (76:19) — but here the effect on the verse's grammar is the whole theology: "maidens… like pearls with hidden treasure in them" says that in the near-rank the most precious beings are the untouched ones, and untouchedness — not the shine — is the property being compared. Every other pearl image in the audience's world was about extraction: diving, trading, drilling, stringing. The sūrah borrows the gem and returns it to the seabed, so that its companions' value is defined by what has never happened to them. In a chapter whose first verses strip the world of all its handled things, the hidden pearl is the one object that cannot be seized, lost, or hoarded, because it was never exposed.

**Dust and Pearl: The Chapter's Opposing Similes**

Place verse 23 back against verse 6 and the sūrah's architecture appears in two images. The first verse-group of the Event ended with the mountains crushed until they are "scattered dust" — the most exposed, trampled, unvalued of substances — and the reward-section now ends its human catalog with the most hidden, courted, and guarded of substances. Al-Wāqiʿah's Day divides people by their relationship to visibility: the deniers are what the wind makes of everything it can see, and the near ones are surrounded by what no eye was made to reach. Between the two similes sit the censuses and the cups, but the chapter's physics is already stated in the pair: to be unmade is to be scattered, to be honored is to be kept. The pearl is also, anatomically, an answer to the dust — a grain of irritation sealed, layer by layer, into luster, the one substance that is a stored-up hurt made beautiful, and the sūrah's audience, who had watched their mountains lose their surfaces, are being told what happens to pain that God chooses to close over instead of scattering.
verses.24:
> ˹all˺ as a reward for what they used to do

**Jazaʾ: The Root That Means Matching**

The noun is jazaʾ, from the root of going-between and equivalence — to repay a debt with its like, to settle — and the sūrah uses it here as a bare accusative, a hanging verbal noun that reads as a verdict appended to the whole preceding scene: ˹all this˺ ˹is˺ a recompense. The verse does not say the reward "exceeds" the deeds, nor that it "pays" them like a wage; the root's semantics is fittingness, the scale that matches. The classical reading of the sūrah's Paradise is built on this double awareness: what the near-rank receives is proportionate — the scene from 15 to 23 is not a fairy-tale surfeit but the exact correlate of lives spent in faith and its practices — and yet the proportionality is not arithmetic, because the matching is of kinds, not quanta: those who were brought near are near, those who chose God over the market choose fruit and birds, those who served guests recline as guests.

**Hospitality and Wages: Reading 24 Against 15**

The tension in the room is worth naming plainly. Verses 15–23 describe passive enjoyment — reclining, being circled, having cups pressed on them, choosing fruit — and 24 says all of it is "a recompense for what they used to do," and the reader is entitled to ask whether a guest is paid. The sūrah's answer is embedded in the sequence: the recompense clause is appended after the scene as its explanation, not staged inside it as its transaction; nobody in the near-rank is shown settling accounts, and the only agent the verse names acting at all is, again, God. The same appositional construction — "a reward from your Lord, for what he used to do" — closes the sūrah of the Prostration's description of the hidden goods its blessed expect, and the classical readers said the obvious: this book's economy of Paradise is one in which gift and wage are not alternatives, because the Host is also the Judge, and hospitality is what His justice looks like from the guest's side. Verse 24 is that sentence, in three words.

**What the Verse Owes the Deniers**

There is a second edge in 24, aimed back at the beginning of the sūrah. Its opening charged that "man denies Our signs" and that the deniers "used to indulge in sinful conduct" — the same habitual grammar — and the whole chapter will keep the two tracks in one register, "recompense for what they used to do" for the near-rank and the identical logic for the left-hand people's fire: each class's eternity is the fitting shape of what it used to do. The verse is therefore the sūrah's refutation of the accusation that this reward is arbitrary: it is exactly what was done, extended and unmasked — and the reader cannot say the scene is favoritism, because the text has already, in its own vocabulary of habit, made the near-rank's lives the content of their couch. The Day that debases and elevates (3) does not invent verdicts; it installs them, and verse 24 states the installation as the whole reward-section's legal basis before the chapter moves, at 27–44, to do the same for the other two classes.
verses.25:
> There they will never hear any idle or sinful talk—

**Laghv: The Word for Everything Spoken for Nothing**

Laghv is not sin's big brother in the Qur'an's usage; it is the class of the useless and the foul — idle, hurtful, pointless speech, the chatter that occupies the gatherings of the proud. The Qur'an's portrait of the believers opens with "those who avoid idle talk" (23:3), and the Stories chapter has them answer slander by turning away (28:55); the verse following this ban states what replaces laghv — "only good and virtuous speech" (26), which in Arabic is the greeting of peace said twice. The near-rank's estate, then, is delimited at its edge by a noise-policy, and this is not decoration: the first thing al-Wāqiʿah says about the companions of the right, once the exclamations are done, is what their ears will never again have to endure. A hearer of 620 CE lived inside laghv — the market's slander, the poet's lampoon, the tribe's taunt — and the sūrah promises, before food or spouses, silence's opposite: a place where no one has to talk back, because no one talks at all except in greeting.

**"There": Whose Garden Is Being Quiet?**

The pronoun in the verse's Arabic — fīhā — has an antecedent the commentators debated: the gardens of verse 12, the scene of 15–24, or even the cups of 18 whose drinkers were just promised no headache (19's "in them" was the cups or the drinkers, and the earlier chapters' parallels attach "lā rafath" — no obscene speech — to the Garden itself, as the Heifer verse legislates for the nights of Ramaḍān (2:187) and the Ranks sūrah for its guests' cups (37:47)). The debates are minute and the answer is not: whichever antecedent wins, the verse keeps the chapter's method of pairing body and word — the head that will not ache (19) and the room in which no word will wound (25) belong to one estate, and its silence is a physical good, like water and shade, distributed to the class that is described at greater length than any other. The near-rank was granted furniture; the right are granted, first of all, a protected ear.

**The Sin of Idle Talk in a Chapter about Denial**

Set the verse against the sūrah's opening: its verdict on the deniers is a speech-crime from the opening line — the Event before which "no one can deny it has come" (2) — and its transcript of their mockery comes in the middle of the chapter: "When we are dead and reduced to dust and bones, will we really be resurrected?" (56:47), which is laghv in the strongest sense: the joke about resurrection, the heckle at the sermon, the word about the unseen spoken for a laugh. Al-Wāqiʿah's anatomy of hell, when it comes at 41–46, will say nothing about their punishment being noisy; it says instead that they were "luxurious" and persisted in the "great sin" (45–46). Verse 25 stands between these two portraits of talk and is the hinge: the saved are defined as those whose speech got nothing out of them and whom nothing got out of, and the lost as those whose conversation about the biggest fact was a sneer. The Garden's quiet is not aesthetic; it is the final shape of a habit the verse's audience could still break.

**Nothing to Overhear**

One consequence of the ban deserves its plain word: in the Garden there is nothing worth eavesdropping on. The Qur'an elsewhere insists that every word is already recorded — "he does not utter a word but there is a watcher, ready" (50:18) — and the sūrah's verse 25 turns that cosmic surveillance into relief rather than dread: the record of the saved will contain no idle passage to be read back to them, no foul hour of talk to be weighed, because the Garden itself legislates the material out of existence.
verses.26:
> only good and virtuous speech

**Salām: The Greeting That Is the Doctrine**

Peace is the word the Qur'an gives its God as a name, the word the angels use at every gate of Paradise in the chapter of thunder (13:23–24), the greeting of Abraham's guests when they came to him in the form of men, and — in the Jonah chapter's line about the believers — God's own salutation: "their greeting will be, “Peace!”" (10:10). Al-Wāqiʿah's verse stands in the middle of that family without quoting any of it: "peace, peace" is all the chapter needs to make the Garden's speech identical with its theology, because the sūrah's whole argument has been that the Event brings safety to the people of nearness and danger to no one in this room. To hear salām repeated is to have the day's verdict spoken back to you as wish rather than sentence, and the exception clause of verse 26 is thus the only place in the chapter where God lets the saved speak — and what He lets them say is the greeting that asks for what they have already got.

**Two Words against a Loud World**

Consider the argument the verse contains, because it is a argument against noise — the real noise of Makkah's sacred precinct, where the poets competed in the sanctuary's markets, the tribes traded lampoons under the Kaʿba's shadow, and the mushrikāʾ, in the Book's own charge, "made their prayer around the House nothing but whistling and clapping" (the idiom of 8:35, whose two rare nouns the classical readers glossed exactly as avocations of the tongue). A chapter that bans laghv and then permits only salām twice is issuing, at the center of a Paradise description, a critique of the sanctuary's acoustics, and its hearers knew which rooms they were being offered instead. The near-rank's ear is the last possession the sūrah protects before it furnishes the rest, and the protection is total: no vanity, no incitement to sin (25), no satire, no slogan, no claim, no rebuttal — a list of absences that describes, from the inside, what every Makkān gathering was and what the Garden will not be.

**The Bedside Verse**

This clause has a further history worth a sentence. In the same devotional stream that commended reciting al-Wāqiʿah nightly — a practice whose supporting report is judged weak, and the caution belongs wherever the chapter's papyri are quoted — verse 26's doubled salām, which the present translation compresses into "only good and virtuous speech," was what dying people were given to hear, the sūrah's peace said to them in the voice of the chapter, and the comfort literature treated "peace, peace" as the verse's point for exactly this reason: it describes what the dying will hear on the other side of the Event the sūrah's first verses keep sounding. Whatever weight a later age assigns to those reports, the reception shows the verse's double structure plainly — an Last-Day soundscape written for ears at their most frightened — and that is how verse 26 should be read here: not as an ornament of the Garden's inventory, but as the chapter's one direct address to its real audience, a promise that the last sentences on the other side of the thunder are wishes, and nothing else.
verses.27:
> And the people of the right—how ˹blessed˺ will they be

**The Exclamation, Third Time**

The device returns exactly as it broke out at verses 8–9 — "the people of the right, how ˹blessed˺ will they be; the people of the left, how ˹miserable˺ will they be" (56:8–9) — a phrase named and then answered about, and the sūrah has taught its audience the idiom, so that this third occurrence needs no gloss to be felt. The earlier pair of exclamations stood before any description existed; this one stands at the threshold of thirteen verses of description (28–40), which changes its meaning. The question is no longer "what will become of them?" but "what are they, now that they are what they are?" — the wonder raised at the saved person not as hope but as completed fact, the same astonishment the near-rank's verses earned from a census instead of couches. The repetition tells the audience that the Day's classes are not only three tiers on a list; each is a surprise, and even a fully described class, viewed from the inside, still defeats the sentence that began its description.

**Where the Right Hand Comes From**

The idiom aṣḥāb al-maymana, the people of the right side, is older than this sūrah, and the present translation's "people of the right" hides from English readers that the Arabic noun is aṣḥāb, owners and companions at once and is not an Arab invention; the Book's own neighbors speak of the day when the scrolls are handed — 84:7 promises the recipient of the book in the right hand a reckoning "easy," a near-relative of this verse's joy — and the older scriptures, as the chapter on the Sheep notes, knew a placing of the blessed at the right and the accursed at the left (56's own idiom at 8–9 was shown there to be borrowed currency). But "aṣḥāb" deserves attention: aṣḥāb are owners and companions at once — the people who own the right hand, the fellowship that is right-handedness — and the same noun governs the "companions of the Garden" in the Pen chapter's parable (68:17–32, whose owners promised to harvest at dawn and lost the crop). Al-Wāqiʿah's companions of the right are, in their very title, the counter-parable to those hoarding farmers: ownership in this sūrah names a side, not an estate.

**Still a Question After the Answer**

One more effect of the repeated name deserves a sentence of its own, because it is the verse's quietest teaching: the chapter never lets the description close over the wonder. By the time the audience passes the elevated furnishings (34), the newly made companions (35–37), and the closing twin multitudes (39–40), every item the question at verse 27 withheld has been supplied and more, and yet the answer was not that the right-hand people are rich — it is that the question itself, "what are they?", remains the appropriate sentence about any saved person. The sūrah's audience heard the answer in orchard and furniture; the sūrah hears, in its own repeated question, the fact that a human being's rescue from the Event is a marvel that outruns its inventory. That is why the verse's Arabic stops short of predication: the sentence refuses to say "the companions of the right are such-and-such," because the sūrah's God has, in this chapter, already made the question itself the praise.

No one in the room, the verse's syntax implies, owns the title "people of the right" before the Day does; it can only be hoped for, and the chapter's loudest question mark is pitched at exactly that hope.
verses.28:
> ˹They will be˺ amid thornless lote trees

**Sidr: The Tree at the Edge of Everything**

The lote tree carries, in the audience's own scripture-memory, the weight of a boundary. The Star chapter sets at the far end of the Prophet's ascent the lote tree of the ultimate boundary (53:14), beside which — in the reports the collections preserve of that night — the Garden of the Refuge is described; and the Saba chapter tells of a lote-lined garden of the most famous hydraulic miracle in Arabia, the Marib gardens of the two right-hand and left-hand plots, which the people of Sheba lost when the dam broke and whose replacement, the verse says, was bitter fruit, fruitless bushes, and a few sparse thorny trees (34:16) — tamarisk in place of lote. Al-Wāqiʿah's companions of the right stand, verse 28 says, among lote trees that have no thorns — the boundary-tree restored to them as plain garden stock. The resonance is double: the tree no human ascent may pass is, for the saved majority, a hedge in an orchard, and the tree that the ruined South Arabian paradise lost is returned in a form that cannot be dammed, flooded, or forfeited.

**Khāw: The Word That Removes the Weapon**

The adjective, khāw, is the negation of thorniness itself — the classical glosses say it without a hedge of detail: no shawk, no thorn, no prickle — and the sheer plainness of the word is the verse's method: the Garden's flora are defined at the start by subtraction, exactly as its drink was (19) and its speech (25). Thorns in the audience's horticulture were the price of fruit's defense: the acacia arms itself, the jujube bribes with small sweet fruit and pays for it in spines, and every hedge that protected a crop from a hungry camel also made the crop impossible to pick freely. Verse 28's thornless lote is thus a single-image answer to the whole economics of defense — in the near-rank nobody needs protection and nobody needs guarding against, and the plant world, the first thing the class is placed among, has surrendered its knives. The Torah's curse on the tilled ground brought forth "thorns and thistles" as the mark of the fall; the sūrah's counter-ground grows its fruit bare-armed, and the audience who farmed terraces with stones in them knew exactly what had been undone.

**The Left's Menu, Read Backward**

Set the lote tree against the only other tree the chapter names and verse 28 becomes argument, not botany. The people of the left "will certainly eat from ˹the fruit of˺ the trees of Zaqqûm, filling up ˹their˺ bellies with it" (56:52–53), then drink boiling water on top of it (56:54), and the Ranks sūrah asks which lodging is better, the blessed's or "the tree of Zaqqûm" (37:62) — and the right-hand's lote, thornless and honeyed, is the direct negation of that menu's every property: fruit with no defense versus a fruit that is the defense, food that nourishes versus food that scalds. The sūrah's plants, like its water and shade, are distributed in pairs, and the pairing is its most patient form of preaching: it tells the audience that nature is not innocent, that the same earth grows a lote and a zaqqūm, and that what each plant will be on the Day — provision or punishment — is decided, in this chapter's physics, by which class you are standing in.
verses.29:
> clusters of bananas

**Bananas in the Qur'an: The Translation's Decision**

The Arabic says ṭalʿ, the fruit-spadix of the acacia, and the English here says "clusters of bananas" — a decision with a long pedigree rather than an eccentricity, for the classical collections transmit from ʿAbd al-Razzāq's circle and others a report from Ibn ʿAbbās, through Mujāhid, that the ṭalʿ of the Garden is the banana tree of India (mawz), and al-Ṭabarī records the same identification alongside the plain-botanical reading. The translator brackets nothing, which means the rendering leans toward the exotic gloss, and the reader should register both: acacia pods stacked like beads on the thornless desert tree, or bananas piled one above another in their hands, either image saying the same thing about the fruit of Paradise — it comes already clustered, countable, and made for gathering. The verse is two words in Arabic and this is how briefly the chapter builds its orchard.

**Makhṭūf: The Fruit Nobody Climbs For**

The adjective is makhṭūf, from kh-ṭ-f, to snatch — and the sūrahs gloss it as fruit hung low so that whoever wants it takes it without a ladder, without a tool, the bunches bent down within reach of the shortest hand. The same root gives Arabic's word for a robber taken red-handed (mukhtaṭaf), and the verse keeps the snatching image intact: in the Garden the thing you snatch is free, hanging, and nobody's property — fruit that cannot be stolen because it cannot be owned. Together with verse 28's thornlessness, the two adjectives remove the two costs of harvest in the Ḥijāz: pain and labor. The date-palm of the plain was climbed, beaten, netted, and guarded, and every one of those verbs belongs to the world the Event is unmaking; here the orchard has been pre-harvested by its own physics, and "clusters" (the present translation's word) says the stacks are already gathered for the guest's hand. No verse in the chapter argues harder against ownership in fewer syllables: what you can snatch belongs to everyone, and what belongs to everyone cannot be a hoard.

**Clusters and the Chapter's Economics of Enough**

One arithmetic point closes the verse. The right-hand list (28–34) counts: two trees, a shade, a water, a fruit that is "abundant" (32), beds (34) — seven items, and not one of them owned. Verse 29's stacked clusters are the smallest unit of the chapter's anti-economy: fruit gathered is fruit spent, and fruit stacking means the supply outruns the picking. The sūrah that will soon reproach the traders of Makkah for a life spent in "rivalry in increase" (102:1) sets before them, for the right, fruit that increases without rivalry, hanging in ropes that no one cut, in a grove no one fenced. Clusters are abundance the hand can see, and verse 29 gives the audience the quantity of the Garden measured in what their own eyes could count: not gardens, but bananas, stacked, for the taking, forever on schedule.

**What the Two Readings Preach**

The acacia reading and the banana reading do different pastoral work, and the sūra preserved both because each said something the audience needed. Read as ṭalʿ, the verse restores the nomad's own landscape with its harm removed — the tree that pricked the camels and fed the hungry, disarmed, a paradise of home: what the desert owed you in pain it owes you back in clusters. Read as the Indian mawz, the verse promises the thing the desert never had at all — a fruit of the warm lands, brought down by trade, stacked by nature — a paradise of arrival, the caravan's cargo grown on the spot for the very people whose caravans carried it elsewhere. Al-Wāqiʿah, which has already dissolved the distance between horizon and couch, does not adjudicate; it hangs the adjective "stacked" over either tree, and lets both sermons ripen.
verses.30:
> extended shade

**The Only Luxury the Desert Could Not Refuse**

Shade, in the sūrah's world, was not comfort; it was infrastructure — the date-palm was grown for it as much as for fruit, the tent was engineered for it, and the midday rest (qaylūlah, the sun's ceasefire woven into the day's prayer-rhythm) was a survival tactic. To promise "extended shade" to the people of the right is therefore to promise the middle class of the saved their own highest good, stretched. The sūrah's next line about the left will prove how load-bearing the gift is: "in the shade of black smoke, neither cool nor refreshing" (43–44) — the lost get a shade too, in the chapter's grim parallel, and the comparison shows that what makes Paradise paradise, in al-Wāqiʿah's register, is not the presence of the exotic but the absence of the noon.

**Mamdūd: A Passive Verb Doing the Work of a Roof**

Watch the grammar of the four-word block that verses 29–31 form: "clusters of bananas, extended shade, flowing water" (29–31) — three nouns, three passives, and no agent. Nothing sets up the shade, no one dug the stream, no hand stacked the fruit; the participles' voice does in three words what the chapter argued at length against the makers of things: that these goods arrive from a will the guests never met. The same three-word pattern governs the sūrah's argument-half — the water that "comes down from the clouds" (69) and the fire "you kindle" (71) — and verse 30 sits on the Garden side of that seam: the world's shade is a contest of builders, the Garden's is a given. The passives are therefore small theological statements, planted in landscape diction, and any reader tempted to see 30 as pretty description should notice that its syntax refuses the reader a single human verb.

**Shade Against the Sun of That Day**

The Qur'an's the doctrine of the Last Day runs on one meteorological fact: the sun of the Standing is close. "When the sun is wrapped up" (81:1) and humanity sweats toward its chin in the gatherings — this sūrah itself quotes no such line, but its audience needed no quote, and "extended shade" enters the inventory of the saved where the heat is the chapter's unspoken adversary (the left's "scorching heat," 42, names it at last). The shade is thus Last-Day furniture: what the Day's weather makes of you depends on whose shade you are under, and the Book's most consoling image of God's own protection — the seven sheltered in His shade on the Day with no other shade, preserved in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī's book of charity from the Prophet's list — belongs to the same economy. Al-Wāqiʿah does not cite it; it simply places extended shade among the middle class's goods and lets the audience draw the inference that shade, on that Day, is not meteorology at all.

**The Verse That Rebuilt the Qaylūlah**

That midday rest is not a marginal custom in the sūrah's world; the reports preserve it as practice alongside the noon prayer, and the day of the Ḥijāz belonged to it absolutely — the streets emptied at high sun, and the cool hours before dawn and after ʿaṣr carried all other business. Verse 30's "extended shade" is, read against that clock, the abolition of the schedule itself: the saved never again calculate their labor around the sun's transit, because the transit no longer rules. This is the verse's small revolution of time as thorough as the flood-inversion at 31 — the Garden does not merely have pleasant hours; it has no tyranny of hours at all — and al-Wāqiʿah teaches it without a single abstract noun. The audience heard "extended" and understood the end of the qaylūlah's necessity: a life in which rest is not stolen from the day's heat but is the day's shape. The shade is the sūrah's clock without hands.
verses.31:
> flowing water

**Maskūb: Water That Pours Itself**

The participle s-k-b is the verb of pouring — an intransitive image made passive: water poured out, running, ungarrisoned. Arabic's ordinary Paradise-hydrology is different: rivers "flowing beneath" the gardens, tajrī min taḥtihā, the settled irrigation-phrase of an agrarian afterlife, and the choice of maskūb instead of any form of that phrase shifts the water from canals to cascade. The sūrah's neighbors exploit the same verb for the opposite face of the Day: the seas "poured forth" in the overwhelming day (81:6), and the people of the left will, at verse 42 of this chapter, get "boiling water" in the same family of images (hamīm, a different word — but the chapter keeps water hot where they are, poured where the right are). Verse 31, in other words, is not a stream; it is water in the act of giving itself, three lines after fruit that gave itself off the tree, and the passive participle is the whole verse, as in verse 30, a roofless verb.

**Water as the Chapter's Chosen Argument**

No element in al-Wāqiʿah does more work. The sūrah's central interrogation will ask, point-blank, "Have you considered the water you drink? If We willed, We could make it salty — will you not then be grateful?" (68–70) — and that argument's premise is verse 31's promise made visible: water is the proof-text because no one can claim to have made it, and the Garden's "flowing water" is the same element stripped of its two terrors — drought and brine. The right-hand people's poured water is the answer to the question the chapter will ask the deniers, and reading 31 after 68–70 makes the architecture plain: the sūrah's orchard and its courtroom are built from one stock of facts, and the water that flows for the saved is the very water the lost drink boiling (55), the thirsty camels' guzzle, in the chapter's cruelest image (55).

**The Flood Inverted**

Arabic's most violent water is also its most nourishing, and the Book keeps the two faces together: Noah's drowning was a rain "poured down" in the Samaritan chapter's words — the heavens opened "with water pouring in torrents" (54:11) — and verse 31's maskūb cannot be heard by any trained ear without that resonance: the water that erased a civilization is, for the right, poured for drinking and irrigation in a Garden where it can no longer rise. The sūrah's theology of rain elsewhere is explicit — "We send down water in measured amounts and then give it to you to drink, and you are no hoarders of it" (23:18) — and the clause "you are no hoarders" legislates the exact miracle of verse 31: water no cistern can claim. Extended shade overhead, ungoverned water below; the two passive nouns of 30–31 describe a landscape without the two things that made landscape a contest at Makkah — sun and storehouse.

**No Cistern, No Quarrel**

The hydraulic society of the Ḥijāz ran on ownership of water: wells with tenancies, springs with clans, the camel-lines that queued, the law of first draw that the tribal code guarded with knives. Verse 31 gives the middle saved class a water with no owner because it has no source to own — it is "flowing," in the present translation's bareness, a participle without a noun for the vessel, without the word "well" or "river," and the grammar enacts the end of the water-law: nothing to fence, nobody upstream. That is why this three-word verse belongs in a sūrah whose hoard-argument runs from the mountains (5) to the sowings (63–67): al-Wāqiʿah's critique of property is not a sermon against riches but a description of the place where riches are incoherent, and poured water is its shortest exhibit. A gift that cannot be stored cannot be hoarded; a stream that cannot be dammed cannot be inherited; the right-hand people drink from the death of possession, and it is called, simply, flowing water.
verses.32:
> abundant fruit—

**Never Out of Season: Killing the Calendar**

The completion is verse 33's pair — "never out of season nor forbidden" (33) — and the first negation does the larger work. Maqṭūʿ means cut off, interrupted, and in the date-country it names the one fact every farmer knows: harvest is a season, and the rest of the year is storage and trade. To promise fruit that is "lā maqṭūʿah" is to abolish the calendar for the middle class of the saved — no glut and no famine, no "out of it," and therefore no preservation, no hoarding by the one who has it in February, no price. The Qur'an elsewhere describes this very blessing as the miracle given to Quraysh — the winter and summer journeys that feed the town (106:1–3) — and al-Wāqiʿah removes the journeys from the Garden entirely, because the journeys existed for what the trees of the right will not need. Time in verse 32 is no longer a ration; it is a season that never ends, and the abundance line is the sūrah's longest answer to short years.

**Nor Forbidden: Killing the Taboo**

The second negation, lā muḥarramah, landed in the audience's ears with a specific clatter, for the pre-Islamic sanctity-laws had made whole categories of food "forbidden" by vow and cult — the beasts and crops dedicated away from tables by the saʾiba, the wāʿila and the ḥāmī of the Heifer chapter's catalogue (5:103), with their rulings on who could eat what in what months. The verse's muḥarramah is the same root's adjective, and "never forbidden" promises the right-hand people an orchard without cult: fruit owed to no one, sacred to no altar, restricted to no gender, householder, or month, and it is the mirror-image of verse 18's cup, which the world's law had made forbidden and whose Garden-version removes the harm instead (19). Abundance plus no taboo equals provision with no priest — the sūrah's quiet republican sentence about food, which every class in the chapter eats out of, from the near-rank's chosen fruit (20) down.

**The Fruit of Two Classes, Compared Once**

Set verse 32 against verse 20 a final time, since the chapter has made the comparison inescapable. The near-rank were given fruit "they choose" — the grammar of preference, a wish with an object; the right are given fruit "abundant, never out of season nor forbidden" — the grammar of sufficiency, a supply with a guarantee. One class receives option; the other, assurance; and the sūrah's gradation is not that the right fare worse — no line in the chapter says the nearest get more — but that their portion was described in the terms of a banquet while this is described in the terms of a harvest, the most basic security a hearer could want. Read beside 69's parallel for the rewarded — where the given book in the right hand comes with "eat and drink, a reward for what you sent ahead, in sweetness" — the two late sūrahs agree that the middle of the saved eats first and asks no questions, and verse 32's single adjective, "abundant," is their shared summary of what enough means in a chapter whose God owns the seasons.

**Abundance in the Sūrah's Mouth**

Kathīr, the adjective's root, is the word the Qur'an uses when the world's numbers impress it and disappoint it: the party that said "we are more in number" (54:45, of the defeated host; the claim echoed by the Day-of-Judgment crowds), and the hoard-counting sūrah's rivalry in increase. In the Garden, kathīrah is applied only to goods, never to people, and never with the comparative edge the world's kathra carries — the abundant fruit outranks no one, and the right-hand census (39–40) that is "many" from former nations is a swarm of mercy, not of victory. The verse therefore reuses the audience's favorite metric and strips it of scoreboard; abundance is the one quantity al-Wāqiʿah blesses, and it blesses it in fruit, where quantity harms nobody. That is why 32 can end the orchard's middle without ending its argument: the many who eat the many fruits are the many whom the chapter's arithmetic was counting from verse 6, and the sūrah has quietly changed what its own word "multitude" means.
verses.33:
> never out of season nor forbidden—

The clause is built the way verse 19 built the cup: lā plus the first noun, wa-lā plus the second, a double denial on indefinite forms that shuts down two whole categories rather than two particulars. The parallel is close at hand in the chapter of The Raising of Hands, where the rewarded are told their fruit "will hang within reach" (69:23) — fruit that cannot be denied because it cannot be kept from the hand — and the sūrahs of the Mercy and the Event keep the same formulaic pair of negations for the Garden's produce: the two words always travel together because together they exhaust what scarcity is.

**What the Sacred Months Taught the Ear**

"Mutaharram" in the audience's usage was not only food-law; the same root named the months in which war was forbidden (9:5; 2:194) — a truce imposed on time itself, when roads were safe and markets held their fairs. That resonance means verse 33's "nor forbidden" is not simply the abolition of taboo but the generalization of the truce: the Garden is the sacred month that never exits the calendar, a place where the rules that made eating an occasion for peace or for priestly veto have been universalized into permanent permission. If the pre-Islamic sanctities fenced food by cult, and the months fenced travel by treaty, the right-hand orchard is the state in which both fences run out of business: nothing is barred, nowhere is unsafe, and the sūrah that borrowed the "people of the right hand" idiom from ancient judgment-lore finishes by borrowing the oldest Arab institution of protected time and extending it without end.

**Joseph's Seven Years, Answered**

The Book's most exact scene of "out of season" sits in Joseph, where Egypt stores grain through seven lean years after seven fat, and famine is the plot's hinge (12:47–49). Every hearer of al-Wāqiʿah lived, in the market's price of a measure of wheat, the memory of a season that cut food off, and lā maqṭūʿah speaks first to the stomach's calendar — the fruit never interrupted — before it speaks to law. The verse's genius is that it requires no miracle to be understood: no reader in the room missed that a garden without a lean month is a garden without a king, without granary-policy, without the rich buying up the year. Joseph's storehouse existed because seasons did; cancel the seasons and the whole apparatus of who eats when dissolves by itself. This is why the sūrah spends the line on negation rather than on description: abundance in the Garden is defined, as its drink was (19), by the subtraction of the mechanism that made the world's abundance a tool.

**A Note on the Verse's Afterlife**

The pair of negations outlived the sūrah in Islamic law's own debates about the Garden: the jurists asked, reading 33 against the Heifer's food-rules, whether any ruling of the world — the prohibitions of carrion, blood, and swine flesh (2:173) — has a mirror in Paradise, and the standard answer took this verse as its proof-text: the Garden abrogates prohibition itself, not its permissibility-by-exception that the world knows, where what is barred is licensed only in hunger. Verse 33 thus became, in the commentaries, the locus classicus for a theology of law's end: the saved majority eats with no mufti between them and the tree, and the sūrah, which had spent its courtroom half attacking tabus of cult (5:103's saʾiba was the audience's own inventory), closes its orchard by unhallowing hallowing. "Never forbidden" is the shortest sentence in the chapter for the shortest definition of the hereafter the Qur'an ever gives: a place where the only sacred is the safe.
verses.34:
> and elevated furnishings

**Furush: The Bed Before It Was Furniture**

The noun furush, plural of firāsh, is the Qur'an's own word for the earth as mattress — the verse of Ta-Ha praises the Lord "who made for you the earth a bed (firāshan) and the sky a canopy" (20:53), and this sūrah's opening cataclysm takes that bed away under the feet (4). What the chapter does at 34, accordingly, is not add a piece to an inventory but restore the primal good: the firm thing you lie on, back to being spread, and this time raised (marfūʿah), safe from the shake that unmade mountains. The root's domestic range is telling — firāsh is bedding, the saddle-cushion under the rider, anything spread to receive a body's weight — and the Garden's "elevated furnishings" keeps all of it: the saddle's rest after travel, the mattress after the day's work, the marriage-bed after the long betrothal. Al-Wāqiʿah gives the middle saved class not couches of state but the whole vocabulary of being received by something solid that stays solid.

**Marfūʿ: The List's Last Movement Is Upward**

Every item in the right-hand passage runs in a single direction, and the participle says it: the shade is stretched (mamdūd, 30) outward, the water poured (maskūb, 31) downward at will, the fruit stacked (29) toward the hand — and now the beds are "elevated," the last verb before the mates. The chapter's physics of the Day were vertical from the start: the earth flattened, the bodies "raised and debased" (3), the census sorted by height; and the right-hand estate answers that with furniture that lifts no effort, height without a stair. The near-rank had the higher word — thrones, surur (15), and they themselves were the "elevated" of 3 — while the right get the elevation moved down into their bedding. That is the sūrah's gradation, measured in inches: rank in the room above, dignity in the mattress below, and both in the same chapter's one act of raising, which verse 3 promised would, on the Day, belong to God alone.

**Why the List Stops Where It Does**

The orchard-run — trees, fruit, shade, water, fruit, beds — ends at 34 without the near-rank's pages and cups, and the omission is architecture, not poverty: the middle estate's passage is an outdoors, and beds are the last object a sky-room can hold. The next verses (35–37) will bring in the mates, and the chapter thus closes its furniture with the one piece that has no height in it: a bed is where a body is received, and after it, the sūrah needs no more "also." The translators' punctuation keeps the rhythm of the Arabic — wa-furushin marfūʿah, "and elevated beds," a phrase hanging in the same accusative as the fruit and the shade — and readers should notice that the grammar refuses to rank the items: strewn water and raised beds sit in one undifferentiated list, seven nouns of equal dignity. Al-Wāqiʿah does not itemize the saved majority's reward in tiers of value; it stacks nouns the way verse 29 stacks fruit, and the abundance of the middle class is, as promised, without order of precedence among its goods.

**The List Ends on the Body**

Notice the passage's last object before its verbs change: trees, clusters, shade, water, fruit, fruit's conditions — and then beds. Everything in 28–33 was environment, something the saved walk through or sit under; verse 34 is the first item that exists solely to receive a body, and the inventory therefore ends where it must, with lying down. The sūrah has described the Garden as the middle class would actually inhabit it — not as a view but as a rest — and the "elevated" of the beds is the list's final grace-note: the receiving thing is also lifted, so the body that arrives tired arrives, at last, above the ground that shook (4).
verses.35:
> Indeed, We will have perfectly created their mates

**The First-Person Plural at the Center of the Orchard**

After seven lines of passive, agentless nouns — stacked, stretched, poured, raised — the verse breaks into "Indeed, We created": the chapter's only direct "We" between the opening's "We" of 57 and the argument's, and the royal plural lands on the softest subject in the passage, the spouses. The switch of voice is the sūrah's own commentary on 28–34: the trees and beds were described as if self-assembling because that is how guests receive hospitality — nobody sees the host's hands — and when the text finally shows the hands, it shows them for the marriage. The emphatic inna and the perfect verb together answer the audience's probable question about the source of all this: the list has a maker, the maker is introducing Himself at the moment He introduces the intimate, and the sūrah thus binds, in one sentence, its theology of creation to its promise of companions — the same bind that the argument-half (57) will use for the first creation's proof.

**"Their Mates": The Possessive That Keeps Marriages**

The pronoun attaches the wives to the husbands as property of relation, azwājuhum in the idiom of the Book (2:25; 23:5) — "their spouses," the same possessive that the Thunder chapter uses when the believers enter the Gardens "and the righteous among their fathers, spouses, and descendants" (13:23). That continuity is a doctrine: the sūrah of the Event does not dissolve the married into the angelic, and the middle class of the saved are promised, not replacement companions, but their own — newly made. The promise of 13:23's family-reunion is not quoted here, but its logic stands behind the possessive; the audience who buried spouses in Makkah heard, at the center of an orchard-promise, a pronoun that does not let death file the marriage. Commentators noted the verse's tact: the near-rank got companions described by beauty, the right by making — the middle estate, whose marriages were worn with age and loss, receives the text's one explicit note of re-creation, as if to say: the love you knew is the love that will be, grown again from the seed of what God first sprouted (56:57–58).

**Perfectly: The Translator's Small Dogmatics**

The present line's "perfectly" renders a general perfection of the making — kamāl in the sūrahs' glosses — and the single bracketed word decides a whole old dispute: whether the new creation here means renewal of youth and beauty, or renewal of the very mode of being (the body of this world re-created as the Garden's body). The translators' adverb takes the first side; the verse's own doubling of the verbal noun takes the second, and both readings are sūrahs' — Ibn ʿAbbās's circle preserves "young again, and of equal age" (which 37 then legislates into the list), while the mutazilite readers noted that "We made them" after "We will raise the beds" answers the resurrection of bodies with the resurrection of persons, and the passage's placement — between beds and virginity — keeps the two questions touching. The bracketed "perfectly" is thus a miniature of the sūrah's whole reception: one word, three centuries of debate, and the audience's grief about aging bodies still addressed, gently, in the adverb.

**The Four "We"s of This Sūrah**

The chapter gives the divine plural to only four moments, and their distribution is its rhetoric. "It is We Who created you — will you not then bear witness?" (57) opens the argument; "If We willed, We could reduce [the harvest] to chaff" (65) and "If We willed, We could make [the water] salty" (70) are the argument's two threats; "We have made [the fire] a reminder and a provision for the travellers" (73) is its mercy-note; and one "We" stands in the promise — "Indeed, We created them [the mates] and made [them anew]" (35). The pattern is exact: in all this sūrah's Paradise, the only time God says We is when He makes spouses. The furniture, the streams, the shade, even the near-rank's thrones — all are described in impersonal passives; the first-person plurality is reserved for the one act the audience needed the Maker to take personal credit for, because it was the one they might doubt: that the marriages of this world arrive in the next intact, and newly made by the same hands that built the orchard around them.
verses.36:
> making them virgins

**Aṭhār: The Word, Its Range, and Its Grammar**

The noun is abkār, plural of ʿadhrāʾ, and the sūrah's sentence puts it in the accusative as a state (ḥāl): "We made them" — in what condition? "virgins." The grammar matters for how the verse should be read: the word describes the manner of God's making, not a status imposed on persons with histories, since the sentence's subject is the Creator who, at 35, sprouted the spouses anew. The present line's single word carries a whole aesthetic of firstness, and al-Wāqiʿah applies it, in the middle estate's passage, to the most intimate of the saved goods — the firstness, the chapter's orchard implies, of a condition that God's fresh making alone can give (35).

**The All-Merciful's Verse Beside This One**

The chapter of Mercy, the sūrah that stands before al-Wāqiʿah in the codex and shares its reward-lists, describes the Garden's companions with a formula close to this verse's: "maidens of modest gaze, who no human or jinn has ever touched before" (55:56; 55:74), the negative of mass (touching) repeated as pure fact." The pair of chapters is instructive, because Mercy's formula adds what our verse suppresses — the prior husband — and adds the gaze, the contentedness — while the Event keeps only the bare state, abkār. Between the two, the tradition's question surfaces: are these new women other than the wives of the world, and who, if remarried, is hers forever?

**Virginity as the Removal of the Past, Not of Memory**

The discomfort that modern readers report at this line — and it should be reported, not smoothed — belongs less to the adjective than to the world's habit of grading women by sexual history, a habit the sūrah actually undermines if it is read with 35. Verse 36's abkār is a divine passive's complement: God made; what was made has no prior, and priorlessness is stated of the making, not of the made. The ʿadhrāʾ-quality is an attribute of the new creation's grammar, and the chapter, which has just insisted at 61 that God can "transform and re-create" its audience "in forms you do not know," is not describing a body with a deleted past so much as a body whose past no longer functions as a category. The Garden's spouses do not forget their histories in the text's own sense of forgetting (they are "their" mates, 35, with the marriage kept by the possessive); what is abkār is the present of the relationship — nothing that has been handled, and therefore nothing used up, in the chapter's vocabulary for firstness.

**The Pearl and the Virgin: The Two Classes, Compared**

The near-rank received ḥūr "like hidden pearls" (22–23) — value defined by no hand having touched them — and the right receive mates "made virgins," the same property stated as the absence of prior handling in the estate where it is most existential for the spouses themselves. The sūrah, in its two registers of untouchedness, grants each class the identical core: intimacy without wear, possession without prior owner, and the pearl's seabed secrecy translated, for the middle estate, into human terms. The comparison also shows the near-rank's restraint and the right's precision: the foremost got a simile, and the right got an adjective of condition — and it is the adjective, not the simile, that the audiences have argued about for fourteen centuries, because "abkār," in a list about saved men who had been married in the world, asks the question "who exactly are these?" and 35's possessive has already answered.
verses.37:
> loving and of equal age

**ʿUruban: The Noun That Means Being In Love**

The first adjective is ʿurub (plural ʿuruban, as here) or ʿarīb, and the old lexicography — the lexica preserve it carefully — glosses it as the woman inflamed in love for her husband, ʿāshiqah in plain terms, the same root giving the verb for a wine that "goes to the head." Al-Wāqiʿah therefore places, between "virgins" and "of equal age," the one word in the orchard-passage that names a feeling rather than a property, and the sūrahs' most repeated note on it is this: the adjective is mutual in the real case, since the spouses' list began at 35 with "their mates" — a possessive of reciprocity — and ʿuruban supplies the interior the sūrah will not describe elsewhere even for the near-rank. The All-Merciful sūrah, whose companions are "of modest gaze, who no human or jinn has ever touched before" (55:56), supplies the other half of the psychology: restraint toward all else, flame toward the one. This is the sūrah's only love-word in its two Paradise portraits, and it sits on the middle class's spouses. The line drew the question the sūrah could not avoid provoking: if the saved are re-mated, whom does a remarried widow belong to in the Garden? The verse's equal-aged mutuality was read, by the commentators with the widows in mind, as the end of rivalry for a place, not the reassignment of it.

**Why Love Is in the List at All**

A final observation about the sūrah's place in the Book. Al-Wāqiʿah is recited in the tradition for provision and in the madhhabs for the dying, and its Paradise has — uniquely among the late Meccan pairs of chapters like it — a word of feeling in the reward-list. The Ranks sūrah describes its companions by the eye (37:48 — modest gaze), the Rising by faces (75:22–23 — bright, looking at their Lord), the chapter of Man by drink and garments; here the middle estate's passage closes on "loving." Whatever the codex's arrangement was meant to teach, the reciter who reaches verse 37 at a bedside finds the sūrah promising, to the family of ordinary believers, not scenery but the re-found tenderness itself, and equal footing for its exercise. The chapter's theology has been, from verse 1, that the Event sorts; verse 37 tells them what the sorted middle class gets to keep from the world — a love with nothing left in it to be embarrassed about — and the single adjective, among all the furniture, is the sūrah's own most human note, placed where the music of its orchard-list resolves.

The word's root also flavors wine in Arabic idiom — love that goes to the head — and the sūrah has already served that drink, minus its harms (19): in this estate even passion arrives side-effect-free.
verses.38:
> for the people of the right

**The Preposition That Dedicates the Orchard**

Li, the little dative, opens this verse — "for the people of the right" — and after ten lines of passive scenery it is the sentence in which the sūrah finally tells the reader who the scenery was made for, even though the answer has been announced since 27. The preposition of benefit and assignment does work the audience understood intimately: in the gift-language of the Arabs, "this is for you" is what turns an object into a given, and the sūrah now says it, formally, of the whole estate: the mates with their three epithets (36–37), the beds, the water, the thornless grove — all of it, for them. The bracketing of the present translation ("˹They will be˺" back at 28) anticipated the pronoun; the Arabic saves the dedication until now, so that the list stands between announcement and assignment, and the reader's question "who gets all this?" is answered exactly once, at the end of the answer. That is not redundancy; that is how hospitality is staged.

**"A Promise Made in Public: The Grammar of Assignment**

The translators print 38 as a fragment attached to what precedes, and the Arabic is exactly that exposed: no verb governs the phrase — the list simply turns toward its owners. Exegetes asked why the sūrah does not say "We gave this to them," and the best answer is that the bare dative keeps the giving continuous: a past-tense gift would locate the reward in one act, while "for them" states a permanent relation — the estate is theirs the way a promised dower is owed, without expiry. It is also, once noticed, the grammar of the whole chapter's hope: the saved are those for whom things are said — "for those who fear the Standing" is the All-Merciful sūrah's refrain (e.g., 55:46, 62, whose two gardens are both "for" someone), and al-Wāqiʿah, recited beside the same deathbeds, places its longest "for them" here, in the middle estate's dedicatory clause, where the ordinary believer, who is not the near one, learns the sentence is addressed to them.

**What "For" Excludes**

The dative, lastly, has a shadow: a list dedicated to one class is not available to the others, and the sūrah never softens that. Verse 38's "for" is the same preposition that will seal the left's accommodation, "this is their lodging on the Day of Judgment" (56) — "for" in this chapter is assignment, not invitation, and every "they will not be…" (33) that precedes it confirms that the orchard's boundaries are the estate's. Readers who want the sūrah's Paradise to be universal have to take the whole architecture, exclamations and all: the chapter counts, sorts, dedicates, and then, from 41 on, does the identical operation for the lost with its own terrible "for them." That severity is why al-Wāqiʿah has always been read, in the devotional literature, as a sūrah to be completed, never skimmed; the "for the people of the right" line at 38 means nothing without the lodging at 56, and the chapter's mercy — which is enormous, fruit without season, love without age, shade without noon — is, by design, not free for everyone in the same way, because the way it is given is exactly what the Day is for.
verses.39:
> ˹who will be˺ a multitude from earlier generations

**The Census Returns, and Changes Its Noun**

The chapter's counting device comes back for the second time, and the nouns are different in a way the translations hide at their edges. The near-rank were "a swarm from earlier generations" and "a few from later" (13–14), the swarm-word laḥq and the few-word qalīl; the right are kathrah, a multitude, "from earlier generations" and again "from later" (39–40) — the same min-partitive, the same paired halves, now filled with the opposite magnitude. Al-Wāqiʿah thus teaches its audience to read the census as a scale: the reader who heard 13–14 and flinched ("only the few?") arrives at 39 and is handed the many. The bracketed "˹who will be˺" is the translator's patch over the Arabic's ellipse — the line is a bare accusative of state — and the bareness is the style of these lists: classes as quantities, quantities as mercy, the arithmetic done by God.

**The Multitude of the Ancient Peoples**

"Earlier generations" — the same phrase that carried the near-rank's swarm — now does new work, because the right's multitude from the old nations is, in the sūrah's own theology of history, the crowd the old prophets actually saved. The near-rank's "swarm from the former" named the champions of each age; the right's multitude is the congregations: the followers of Noah, the rank and file of Abraham's household, the ordinary Israelites of the Exodus, the believing remnant of every destroyed city. The Qur'an elsewhere warns that "most of people" will not believe (12:103), and the sūrah's own courtroom half will call the left "the misguided deniers" (51) — but nowhere does this chapter quote a count of the damned against a hope of the saved, and verse 39's multitude from the former is the quiet surprise that balances the census. The multitude from the former is the sūrah's answer to any despair that only saints are saved: the middle estate is big, and its first citizens are the nameless believers of the old centuries.

**Why Repetition Preaches Better Than Novelty**

The chapter could have described the right's numbers with new language, and chose instead to re-run the device of 13–14 with the adjective inverted. That is repetition with a purpose the audience of a recited text feels: the second census lands faster, because the first taught the grammar, and the inversion is felt as a gift — the mechanism that said "few" for the heroes says "many" for you. The census even shares its halves — former and later — with the Day's whole gathering at 49–50 ("Most certainly, earlier and later generations will surely be gathered ˹together˺ for the appointed Day" (56:49–50)), so that the saved classes' counts are cut from the same cloth as the total roll-call.

**Multitude as Mercy, Not Majority Argument**

One caution the verse's defenders should keep: "a multitude" is not, in this chapter, an appeal to numbers as proof. The Qur'an's own charge against the crowds is sharp — "if you obey most of those on earth, they will lead you away from God's path" (the sense of 6:116) — and al-Wāqiʿah has just finished telling its hearers that the majority of history sat with the left (51–52 will say so in so many words). Verse 39's comfort is therefore not "most people make it"; it is that the saved middle is no elite club, that belonging to a multitude, not a spiritual aristocracy, is the normal shape of deliverance, and that the same warning chapters which say "few are My grateful servants" (34:13) here say the right-hand crowd is vast. Both statements come from one sūrah's God, and the tension is the chapter's moral instrument: do not count on numbers, do not despair of them either; be a member of the many, and let the counting be someone else's job.
verses.40:
> and a multitude from later generations

**The Second Half of the Pair**

Verse 39's multitude from the earlier generations leans on this line the way the near-rank's "swarm" (13) leaned on their "few" (14): the census is one statement with a hinge, and the hinge opens toward the audience. "Later generations" — al-ākhirūn — is the sūrah's own term for you: not the centuries of the prophets whose ruins the Makkān trade routes passed, but the communities the chapter's recitation would itself create. The sūrah's grammar keeps the later half in the accusative of state, a bare phrase appended to the scene, and the effect is a sentence the reader finishes by existing in it: every congregation that ever heard al-Wāqiʿah was, at the moment of hearing, a candidate for the multitude its final census line reserves. The text's temporality is a loop — a book about the end of time whose verse about "later" includes all readers to the Hour.

**What the Word "Kathrah" Has Learned to Mean**

The multitude here answers the chapter's own use of abundance since verse 32, where fruit's adjective was kathīrah, "abundant," and it completes the quiet re-education of the sūrah's favorite root. In the audience's life, kathrah was competitive — the rivalry in increase named by the short sūrah "You are diverted by rivalry in increase, until you visit the graves" (102:1–2), the counting of numbers as a civic sport. Al-Wāqiʿah now attaches the same word to a census of the saved (39–40) and to fruit (32) — multitude without rivalry, quantity that is received, not racked up — and verse 40 is the human end of that lesson: the later generations arrive as many, and their "many" cannot be credited to anyone's strategy, because the census is spoken by God before the Day. The verse's one-word adjective, repeated from 32, is the sūrah's way of converting the community's vice into its comfort.

**Generations, Not Elect**

Notice the noun doing the counting here: qarn, generations — the same as in the near-rank's census (13–14) and the Day's roll-call (49–50) — and qarn in Arabic is a unit of time defined by the people who share it, "the generation of such-and-such," with a neutral ring that elect-language lacks. The commentaries, reading 40 against 13–14, extracted the obvious pastoral: the near-rank are individuals, and the middle estate is whole cohorts, which is why the chapter gives the individuals thrones and the cohorts an open landscape of fruit and rain — the estate sized to the population. And the same word qarn binds 40 to the sūrah's repeated warnings about "the people of the former generations" whose fate was recorded (e.g., the Korah-type destruction narratives in the story-half of longer chapters): generations are the unit of history here, and the saved later generation enters, at verse 40, the same archive as the saved former one, file beside file.

**The Verse the Reciters Inhabit**

The last point is the reception and the verse are the same fact. Whatever the first listeners of Makkah — a persecuted handful in the 610s — could feel at "a multitude from later generations," the line has been fulfilled by the plain historical datum the sūrah's own recitation now proves: al-Wāqiʿah is chanted daily, in every century since, in millions of mouths, and each generation that heard it sat, textually, inside verse 40. No commentary should sentimentalize that — the verse promises multitude, not the multitude's virtue, and the chapter's two censuses for the left (51–52) will show the sūrah counting the lost just as massively — but the structural fact stands: a verse about "the later" written at the beginning of a community is, by the community's survival, one of the most literally vindicated lines in the Book.
verses.41:
> And the people of the left—how ˹miserable˺ will they be

**The Third Exclamation, and the Last**

The chapter now pays the full price of its own rhetoric: the exclamation that opened at verses 8–9 — "the people of the right, how ˹blessed˺ will they be; the people of the left, how ˹miserable˺ will they be" (56:8–9) — and re-run at 27 for the blessed, re-runs for the lost, and the third iteration is the last time the sūrah will use its signature device. The repetition has by now taught the audience to lean forward at the formula, and the lean is the sermon: the saved passages rewarded the expectation with orchards and companions, and verse 41 sets up the identical musical figure to do the opposite — the listener's body learns the pattern as comfort, and the sūrah strikes it as loss. That is the moral beauty of the verse's placement: the sūrahs of the commentators, long accustomed to this sūrah's repetitions, note how often re-echoed structures soften the ear before the blow falls, and here the softening is the sermon.

**The Bracketed Word That Answers 27**

In Arabic the two exclamations are identical: mā aṣḥābu-l-maymana, mā aṣḥābu-l-mashʾama — "what [is the state of] the people of the right/left?" The sūrah says nothing about bliss or misery; the translator decides, and the decision is now twice visible: ˹blessed˺ at 27, ˹miserable˺ at 41 (and at 9), the pair of English adjectives the bracket reveals as exegesis. Mercy, in this chapter's arithmetic, gets fourteen verses of scenery and two more in the soundscape; the left gets three lines of weather (42–44) and the cause of it.

**A Geography of Hands**

Al-Wāqiʿah takes a symbol whose badness the audience inherited and, in the chapter's physics, makes it literal direction: the people of the left are the same people verse 6 sorted when the crowd became three groups at the unfixing of the mountains. The sūrah does not demonize the left side; it finishes the sorting it announced, and the idiom — borrowed, ancient, bodily — bears the verdict without embellishment, which is why the verse needs no description of its own beyond the three nouns to come.

**"How Miserable": The Absence That Replaces the Answer**

Verse 27's withheld predicate, "how ˹blessed˺," was filled by the readers with lote and shade; 41's ˹miserable˺ will be filled by scorching wind, boiling water, smoke — but the sūrah's design keeps both classes, in their intro-lines, unspeakable: the saved are "too blessed to say," the lost "too miserable to name," and the identical grammar for both refuses the audience a voyeur's advantage in either direction. The present translation's brackets make the refusal uniform — two adjectives, one for each — and the verse's real teaching is in that uniformity: on the Day there will be classes whose condition outruns the chapter's own vocabulary on both sides, and al-Wāqiʿah, which has made its entire argument out of what the solid world cannot be trusted for, says here what it says in 56:74: God makes things, and the verdicts are His, and the human words for them (blessed, miserable) are bracketed inserts doing their best.

"Left-hand people" completes the idiom this commentary traced at verse 8: the Book of Matthew places the goats at the left hand as the sheep at the right (25:33), the ancient Near East knew the left as the inauspicious side (the left hand's eating and cleaning duties, the right hand's covenant-feasts), and the Arabic mashʾama, from sh-m-l — the shmal, the north wind's cold and leftward side — is already unlucky in the pre-Islamic poet's mouth.
verses.42:
> ˹They will be˺ in scorching heat and boiling water

**Samūm: The Wind That Is a Verdict**

The word ṣabāʿ, rendered "scorching heat" here, is ṣamūm in the Arabic — the wind of piercing, from a root of burning through and through, the sirocco that the audience fled at midday and that their poets made the counter-shade to the garden's. The sūrah's punishment is therefore not invented weather; it is the region's worst day raised to an estate, and the selection tells you everything about al-Wāqiʿah's method of hell: it subtracts from the known, it does not add to it. The near-rank's delights were their goods perfected — cups with no headache, beds elevated, shade extended — and the left's torments are their miseries, kept exactly. Verse 42's "scorching wind" is also, in the chapter's system, the answer to verse 30: the right are in stretched shade; the left are in moving air with no relief in it, and wind in a desert is, precisely, what shade is not.

**Hamīm: The Water That Cannot Be Water**

The second noun, maʾ, boiling water, ḥamīm, is the Book's fixed word for the drink of the lost, and the wider Qur'an supplies its exact profile so consistently that this verse needs no adjectives of its own: the Cave sūrah's parallel has them cry for relief and be answered with water like molten brass that sears the face, an evil drink and an evil companion (18:29) — and the Muhammad sūrah's rivers-passage ends by placing, opposite the four promised rivers, "water that tears their insides" (47:15, quoted above at this chapter's cup-section). Al-Wāqiʿah sets its own poured water — flowing, ungoverned, free — at verse 31, so that the two "waters" of the chapter, thirty verses apart, are the same noun family's two ends: maskūb poured for the right, ḥamīm boiling for the left, and the sūrah's hydrology is its theology of what a gift becomes when the Giver is refused. The translator's bracket ˹They will be˺ supplies, again, the bare locative: in these two elements, the verse says; they live inside weather that will not nourish.

**The Anti-Orchard in Four Words**

Compare the inventory of the estates at equal depth: the right stand "amid thornless lote trees, clusters of bananas, extended shade, flowing water, abundant fruit… and elevated furnishings" (28–34); the left are "in ṣamūm and ḥamīm, in a shadow of smoke" (42–43). The sūrah's parody is structural — where the saved had trees, shade, and water, the lost have wind, water, and a parody of shade; two of the three goods survive into the punishment only as their harmful twins, and nothing like fruit or bed is allotted at all. Al-Wāqiʿah, which built its whole argument on creation's water (68–70) and fire (71–73), conducts its the doctrine of the Last Day as applied cosmology: the same sky's products, two different relations.

**Prepositions of Placement, Once More**

A small grammatical fact carries the verse's doctrine: "in ṣamūm and ḥamīm," fi again — the same preposition the chapter gave the saved ("in the Gardens of Bliss," 12) and the mates ("for the people of the right," 38). Placement in this sūrah is, as at verse 15, the whole of the afterlife's grammar: nobody is shown walking toward their estate, earning the address, or leaving it; the classes are put in, and the put-in is described only by what surrounds them. That is why the left's two "in" items are elements rather than architecture — the wind and the water are total, un-housed, with no walls and no beds and no pages circling, and verse 42's bleakness is produced entirely by the preposition plus two nouns. The sūrah has no language for prison, because its language is for dwelling, and what it does to the lost is to give them a weather and call it their dwelling-place. The eloquence of that refusal is the verse's real sermon.
verses.43:
> in the shade of black smoke

**ʿIhab: The Word for a Sky That Has Caught Fire**

The noun ʿihāb carries, in Arabic's usage, both the leaping column of fire from a blaze and the dense smoke rising over it — the beacon the Bedouin read at distance, smoke meaning household or danger. The line itself says ẓill, "shadow," attached to the smoke, and the old glosses read the sūrah's companion-word yaḥmūm — which the Cliff chapter uses for scalding water: "except boiling water and ˹oozing˺ pus" (78:25) — as black because intensely hot; the present translation prints the color it infers, "in the shade of black smoke." Within our chapter, the domestic sense — smoke above a fire that burns — makes the punishment's skyline exact: the lost stand in the shadow of their own cooking-fires, while the near-rank sit beside water poured for them (31). The sūrah that denied the world any lasting solidity has, at minimum, given every class a skyline; the left's is made of what burning leaves behind, low enough to press on the head. And the "shade" here is, of course, verse 30's word minus its properties; verse 44 exists to do the subtracting.

**Blackness: The Sūrah's Palette**

Al-Wāqiʿah has kept its colors sparse, and the few it uses cluster here at the end of the description. The face of the near-rank was bright in the neighbors' Paradise (75:22–3, "On that Day some faces will be bright, looking at their Lord" — the chapter's own counter-light, quoted earlier at verse 16); the left's sky is yaḥmūm-adjacent black, the smoke's color; between the two the sūrah painted fire's whiteness ("crystal-white" is the Ranks' wine, 37:46, this chapter's neighbor) and the green of brocade nowhere. The palette is thus moral, not decorative: light and color in this chapter belong to description, black to the undescribed, and the smoke at 43 is the sūrah's only painted darkness — the shadow it throws is, the next verse says, unqualified by anything that would make it weather. The chapter that opened by pulverizing the mountains' color into "scattered dust" (6) ends its two estates with a grove (28) and a soot-cloud (43), and the two images are the whole the doctrine of the Last Day it offers: growth or smoke.

**"A Shadow" in a Chapter of Placement**

The preposition returns — "in the shade of black smoke," fi — and the reader of verse 42 will have heard the echo's chain: the saved are "in the Gardens of Bliss" (12), "amid thornless lote" (28), the lost "in ṣamūm and ḥamīm" (42), "in a shadow of smoke" (43). This sūrah's geography knows no open ground, no outside, no neutral landscape: every class is inside something, and the inside is the verdict.
