Smoke with shade under it is therefore, grammatically, a home; the verse says the lost have a dwelling, and the dwelling is the air on fire — and the near-rank's "elevated" beds (34) have their grim twin in the ẓill of a medium that lifts nothing, shades nobody, and has no floor at all. When the chapter, three verses before, called its classes a sorting at the Event when "you become three pairs" (6), the prepositions began closing around the audience one by one; verse 43, smoke-roofed, is the last ceiling the sūrah builds, and it is built of what a fire that needs no wood still makes.
verses.44:
> neither cool nor refreshing

**The Verse That Unbuilds a Word**

Ẓalla means to shade, and what it provides is two things the audience's proverbs never failed to enumerate: coolness (barad — "the coolest of shades," as the all-Merciful sūrah describes the Garden's best ẓill, 55:56) and benefit. Verse 44 denies both of the smoke's shadow, and the mechanism is the sūrah's signature: the left receive the word for relief minus the contents of relief, a shade that is neither cool nor useful. The two negated nouns, ḍarīb and nāfiʿ, are classical and debated — the old glosses take ḍarīb in the sense of something that strikes the body with good (dāriba: a spring that is hit by travelers and quenches them, or a shade that "strikes" with its coolness), and nāfiʿ in the plain sense of profit — and whichever etymology the reader prefers, the sense is single: the smoke-shade is a form of blessing preserved as a museum of blessing, everything it used to do for the body canceled, and the cancellation stated in two adjectives at the end of the estate's entire description.

**"Refresh": What the Water and the Shade Were For**

Nafʿ, benefit, has been the sūrah's hidden standard since its first description. The right's shade is extended (30), the near-rank's cups do not harm (19), the fruit is never cut off (33) — every amenity in this chapter exists for its use-value, stated in passive participles that promise the body will find them. The left's smoke-shade is the only "place" in the chapter whose properties are enumerated as absences, and the absence-word, nāfiʿ, is the commercial vocabulary of benefit — the same root the sūrah of the Iron spends its half on, the trade that does not lose its goods (35:29; 61:10-11, "a commerce that will save you"), the nafʿ that hoarded wealth never bought for its owner. In al-Wāqiʿah's economy the damned are not tortured so much as disinvested: the elements that profit everyone else are, for them, held out at zero yield, and "neither cool nor refreshing" is the ledger-line of an estate in which nothing pays.

**The Small Word That Ends the Scene**

The last noun of the left's first inventory is "benefit," and that is a ledger-word — the sūrah's whole introduction has been about gain and loss ever since it distinguished those handed their record in the right hand, who face "a reckoning, easy" (84:7, quoted at this chapter's own verse-8 commentary), from everyone else. Verse 44 closes the left's scenery on the word nāfiʿ and then the chapter, remarkably, refuses to escalate: the mockery (47–48), the gathering (49–50), the zaqqūm menu (51–55), the accommodation (56) all swim inside a condition defined twice as unprofitable, and the punishment is not enlarged, only witnessed. That is why 44 should be read as the sūrah's hinge: one line that says, in two negations, everything al-Wāqiʿah will ever say about loss — and then turns, from 57 on, toward what might still become profitable for these very listeners: their ejaculate, their seed, their water, their fire, and the stars.

**Neither Sun-Blaze Nor Bitter Cold: The Chiasmus**

The chapter of Man sets the Garden's climate in the mirror of this verse: in the Garden "you will see neither scorching heat nor bitter cold" (76:13) — the saved lack both extremes, because the shade is balanced; the lost have neither the sun's harm nor the cold's harm, but equally neither the sun's rising nor the cold's relief, because their medium is the in-between that smoke makes. The chiasmus is exact, and it is the sūrahs' standard way of reading 44 against 76: what Paradise gives is not the pleasant but the temperate — the removal of weather as a power over bodies — and what the left get is weather as pure presence, neither punishing usefully nor soothing at all. Al-Wāqiʿah's verse 44, ending on "nor refreshing," thus states the classical definition of hell in this literature: climate without season, exposure without end, a sky that neither rules nor serves.
verses.45:
> Indeed, before this ˹torment˺ they were spoiled by luxury

**Mutraf: The Passive Man of Pleasure**

The Arabic's word for the luxury here is takrafuf, the verb ismutrafa — "made soft, dandled, put at ease" — and the morphology is the whole sermon: the damned are not described as people who seized pleasure but as people who were laid into it, formed by it, the passive object of a life of ease, which is how this Book's political vocabulary habitually reads the rich of the old cities. The prophets of the Qur'an hear the phrase before this sūrah: when a messenger summons a town's assembly, the same title — "the eminent" — speaks from prosperity in the accounts of Nūḥ, Hūd, and Ṣāliḥ (e.g., 11:27), and the sūrah of the Heights says that God takes such people "by degrees, from ways they do not perceive" (7:182). That class-worried idiom stands behind verse 45, and when al-Wāqiʿah calls the left "mutrafūn in life," it therefore charges them with a condition, not a hobby: a world arranged so that nothing ever asked anything of them, and a self arranged by that world to find asking unbearable.

**"Before This": The Bracket That Times the Sin**

The sūrah's line is just "kānū fī takrafufi" — they used to be in luxury — and the translation's bracket ˹torment˺ decides what "before this" means: before this punishment, before this Day, before this announcement. The decision is right in context — the left's sin is stated as the antecedent of the estate — but readers should see that the bracket inserts sūrah-history's most famous Last-Day claim: the whole life of the damned is one "before." The Arabic of verse 45 is, precisely, an imperfect nominal — they were being in ease — the tense of ongoing background, and the Day arrives like a cut in film; the sūrah has been saying this in images since verse 4 (the earth shaken, the mountains to bits), and verse 45 now says it as plain past tense.

**Makkah's Own Mufassir**

Apply 45 to its first audience and the sūrah's situation becomes legible without any history book: Makkah's governing notables were precisely the class whose careers were built on the sanctuary's peace, the pilgrim trade, and the caravan schedules, and whose hymn at the Kaʿba disclaimed hunger — "We have found our fathers upon a path" — while claiming the house by right. The verse never names them; it just keeps the word their own culture prized, the "soft life," and says: that, continued, is the whole before of the smoke. The sūrah's restraint is worth registering — no accusation of wealth's acquisition, no demand for redistribution stated here, only the sequence "you were dandled, you persisted, now see what shade you are under" — and that sequence is the same one the chapter has run on every class, from census to bed: a habit, then a Day, then the habit's building. The Mufassir's point, in other words, is the sūrah's point: comfort un-thanked is slow stone-setting.

**Why "Indeed" Opens the Verse**

The inna at the head of 45 is the sūrah's own witness-word — "indeed, before this they were spoiled" — and its placement matters: the chapter's two descriptions of the estates so far have been pure gift, unprefaced, and the left's gets the emphatic particle before the accusation, not before the torment. The effect is a courtroom move: the punishment has been stated as fact (42–44), and now the sūrah produces its evidence, with inna, as if to forestall the left's own objection — the same objection they voice at 47, the incredulous "will we really be raised?" — and to tell the audience that the verdict's proof is biographical. Nothing in al-Wāqiʿah's hell needs a demon's résumé; the résumé is the soft life itself, attested by God in the chapter's loudest particle. "Indeed": that is the sūrah's last word about the before, and the mockers, in 47, will spend theirs about the after, and the reader is held precisely between the two "indeeds," which is the whole moral interval this sūrah calls the world.

The near-rank's opposite property is not austerity but vigilance: "men whom neither trade nor sale diverts from the remembrance of God" (24:37, whose commerce clause this chapter's own verse 25 answers in kind) — and verse 45's mutrafūn are that verse inverted: people diverted by nothing, because everything already belonged to them.
verses.46:
> and persisted in the worst of sin

**Istihlāʾ: The Verb of Keeping a Claim Alive**

The second charge's verb, aḥa, is stronger than "persisted" — its root carries pressing, insisting, holding on to a claim, and the sūrah's habitual construction (kānū yuḥiḍḍūna) makes the sin a posture maintained across time, not a single act. That fits the chapter's entire psychology: verse 45's spoilage was a condition, verse 46's persistence is a decision made again and again under that condition, and the two kānū-lines together are the sūrah's complete anatomy of hardening — circumstance, then repetition — the same grammar the saved were given at 24 ("what they used to do") with the sign reversed. The sūrah has no concept of an eternal punishment that is not also a persistent will; verse 46 is where that conviction sits, in one Form VIII imperfect.

**"The Worst of Sin": Which Sin Is Meant?**

Classical readers asked what al-ithm al-ʿaẓīm names here and answered from the sūrah's own sequence: the immediate context supplies mockery of resurrection at 47–48, and the chapter's opening supplied denial of the Day at 2 (the Day of Recompense whose truth "no one can deny" when it arrives). Many sūrahs preferred the widest reading — the unbelief that the Qur'an elsewhere calls the one sin God does not "overlook," the shirk the Book asserts directly as a wrong of greatness (31:13, Luqmān's charge to his son) — and the "worst" here (al-ʿaẓīm) is the superlative's plain work: within every sin this audience knew, the one that arranges all others against God. The translation's "worst of sin" captures the Arabic's definite-plus-superlative exactly; and the sūrah's strategy lets both readings stand: the persisted-in denial is, in the chapter's own file, at once the resurrection-joke and the theology that made the joke possible.

**ʿAẓīm: The Adjective Shared with the News**

The word "great" is not idle in this sūrah's world. The Qur'an's other late chapter calls resurrection "the tremendous News (anbaʾ al-ʿaẓīm) about which people disagree" (78:2–3), and the sūrah's own last verse puts the superlative on God as its final verb: "So glorify the Name of your Lord, the Greatest." (56:96) The sūrah thus builds a small ladder with one word: the News is great, the sin of mocking it is "the great sin," and the Lord whose name closes the chapter is the Majestic — and the left, in verse 46, are the people who attached ʿaẓīm to the wrong rung: they held fast to what is small in the face of what is not. The adjective is the chapter's moral ruler, and 46 sets against the sūrah's own use of it a lifetime of wrong measurements, persisted in, until the Day measures them back.

**"Persisted" as the Chapter's Verdict on Its Listeners**

Everything in the two halves of the sūrah is a consequence of one habit: the near-rank recline because they "used to do" (24) the same persistent, unglamorous righteousness, and the left choke in smoke because they "used to" keep a claim alive against the obvious. The sūrah's ethics are therefore, in the strict sense, a theory of habit, and verse 46 is its negative theorem — sin, persisted in, is not repeated but reinforced, each iteration making the next likelier, until the self that holds the position and the position are one, and the Day arrives to find only that unity. That is why no additional crime is itemized here: the inventory is done; what remains is the file's header, and it reads "persisted.".
verses.47:
> They used to ask ˹mockingly˺, “When we are dead and reduced to dust and bones, will we really be resurrected

**Dust and Bones: The Sūrah's Own Cosmology Turned on It**

The objection's materials are the chapter's: "When we are dead and reduced to dust and bones" borrows — the sūrah's audience would have caught the exact phrasing — the vocabulary of 4–6, where the mountains, crushed, "became scattered dust." The mockers speak as if pulverization proved impossibility: we will come apart into turāb and ʿiẓām, and who reassembles sawdust? The chapter has already answered at the level of physics: the same "becoming dust" they cite as their defense is, in the sūrah's telling, the Day's own opening movement — disassembly is not the denial of resurrection but its schedule, and the God who flattens mountains (5) does it to re-compose, which is why verse 57 opens the argument-half with "It is We Who created you. Will you not then believe?" The quotation at 47 and the cataclysm at 4 are thus one argument in two moods, the sūrah's audience able to hear the skeptics' dust as the Event's dust without a word of commentary.

**"The First [Life]" — What the Arabic's Question Actually Duplicates**

Readers of the English should know that the sūrah's line contains a word the present translation folds into "resurrected": the baʿth, sending forth, raising, and the object of the wonder — "will we really be sent forth?" — is the same verb the chapter uses for recreation at 61 ("We may transform you and bring you forth (yunshiʾkum) in a creation you do not know"). The mockers' noun is not resurrection as doctrine but resurrection as the word in the prophet's mouth, thrown back doubled; and the sūrah's placement makes the exchange grammatically exact: verse 47's interrogative (a-inna) is answered at 49 with the plain "qul: inna al-awwalīna wal-ākhiriina la-jāmiʿūn" — "Say: most certainly, earlier and later generations will surely be gathered" (56:49–50) — the chapter matching their questioning particles with a command to answer by decree, the two words (baʿth/jamʿ) the only theological vocabulary the sūrah chooses to concede them.

**The Ranks Sūrah's Identical Line**

Late sūrahs record the same objection again and again — 17:49, 25:15, 36:78, 37:16, 79:23 among them — and the closest in form and music is the Ranks sūrah's: "What! When we are dead and become dust and bones, will we really be resurrected? And our forefathers as well?" — in the present translation, essentially identical to ours — so that a listener moving between the two chapters heard one fixed quotation, a liturgical refrain of the skeptical, preserved verbatim. That the Qur'an reuses the sentence shows how real and how tired the objection was, and how the sūrah's answer differs by chapter: the Ranks answers with the single command "qul: al-awwalūna wal-ākhirona la-jāmiʿūna ilā mīqādi yawmin maʿlūm" — the same gathering-clause our sūrah borrows — while al-Wāqiʿah, at 57–74, adds its four interrogatives of semen, seed, water, and fire. The refrain belongs to the audience's history; the answers belong to the hour of each sūrah.

**The Question the Sūrah Answers with Bodies**

Verse 47's incredulous "we" — first person plural, four times across 47–48: we die, we are dust, we raised, our forefathers — deserves one notice, because the chapter's reply from 57 onward is built in the same person: "It is We Who created you... Have you considered what you eject (tumnee)? Is it you who create it, or We?" The pronouns lock: their "we" asks whether the body returns; God's "We/you" answers by taking the body apart at its first origin — semen — and asking who made it then. The sūrah's entire argument-half is, in structure, an exegesis of verse 47's grammar: the mockers' plural of disgust receives, line by line, the first-person plural of the Maker, until the same "we" can only mean "we who were once a despised fluid and were made by Someone." Al-Wāqiʿah never says this as argument; it is the mere shape of the sequence 47→57→59, and the shape is the answer the sneer asked for, spoken in bodies the skeptics claimed to own.
verses.48:
> And our forefathers as well?”

**One Line, Its Own Verse: The Art of the Follow-Up Sneer**

The sūrah gives the left's second breath its full verse-mark — wa-ābāʾunal-awwalūn — five words, an addendum, and in its brevity the most vivid line of their quotation. Grammatically it is not a new sentence but a tacked-on dative: "will we really be raised — and our forefathers as well?" The incredulity is all in the "and also": the first question mocked the individual's return, the addendum mocks the logistics, the sheer implausible scope — that the buried centuries, the ancestors of the audience's own pride, would have to be recalled too. And the sūrah's placement — immediately before "Say: most certainly, the earlier and the later will be gathered" (56:49–50) — answers the addendum first: the forefathers are in, the scope is exactly the objection, and the answer is one breath long.

**The Forefathers: Makkah's Strongest Noun**

To the first audience, ābāʾ were not merely ancestors but authority — the religion of the fathers was the standard defense of the sanctuary's order ("We found our fathers upon a path," the sūrah's own summary of the Makkān creed-formula in the Verse chapter's words, 43:22–23), and the Karbala of Arabic memory ran backward through them. The left's sneer therefore reveals, while dismissing resurrection, everything else they hold: the ancestors are the ones who must not be troubled; the dead of the old ways should stay in their honored ground; the claim that God re-raises the generations is offensive because it would summon, to the same questioning Day, the fathers who are supposed to be above questioning. Al-Wāqiʿah obliges: 49–50 gathers "the earlier and the later" without exception, and the sūrah's longer argument will insist, in its dying-scene, that "We are nearer to him than you, but you do not see" (56:85), a nearness no forefather has. Verse 48 is thus the chapter's quietest demolition of ancestor-culture: it lets the mockers name their idol in a subordinate clause and then books him into the census.

**"Bring Our Forefathers If You Are Truthful": The Book's Taunt Returned**

The Qur'an elsewhere turns this very word back on its users. To the claim that paradise belongs to Israel alone the Heifer chapter says: "Bring your forefathers, if you are truthful" (2:111) — produce your ancestors as witnesses — and in the Poets chapter Moses, defying Pharaoh's court, names the Judge by their own oldest title — the God of their Lord and of their forefathers, Lord of the East and the West (26:26–29) — the forefathers not as defense but as summons. Al-Wāqiʿah's 48 rhymes with both usages without quoting either: the sneer's own logic — "and our forefathers as well?" — assumes the fathers stand outside the summons, and the sūrah's theology of the gathering has already made them the first names on the roll. The audience who heard 48 in Makkah heard themselves, precisely where they felt unexamined: the dead whom no one questions will be questioned first, and the question-mark the mockers put on the fathers will, the sūrah implies, be turned back on the sons.

**Anaphora of Doubt: What Quotation Does in Recitation**

Structural note on the chapter's ear: verses 45–48 run "Indeed they used to be (kānū) spoiled… and used to persist (kānū)… they used to say (qālū: in the Arabic, continuing the kānū-chain)… and our forefathers as well?" — four lines of habitual past carrying the audience along a rhythm of "they used to," and the quote lands inside the rhythm like a stone in water. The verse-mark after "as well?" then opens the "Say" of verse 49 like a lid, and the reciter is made, briefly, to hold the sneer in the mouth before the answer is allowed — a small, severe pedagogy of empathy-by-inversion, in which the audience tastes, for one line, how a claim on God sounds from the side of the spoiled, before they are invited to be glad they are not them.
verses.49:
> Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Most certainly, earlier and later generations

**The Certainty-Grammar of Verse 49**

The English "most certainly" stands for two Arabic particles working together — the sentence's inna (indeed) and the lam of emphasis (la-jāmiʿūn) in its predicate — a construction Qur'anic recitation reserves for verdicts: not "the gathered will come," but "they are, assuredly, gathering-to-be." The sūrah, which has been describing, now swears, and the shift in register is the listener's cue: everything from 50 to 56 hangs on this lam. Commentators noted that the verse carries no oath-formula (no "by the Lord of such-and-such") — the certainty is asserted, not sworn — while the chapter's only sworn passage is its own great oath to the Book — "So I do swear by the positions of the stars" (56:75). The design places two unshakable statements side by side: the Day's gathering, without an oath; the Book's truth, with one — as if the sūrah's architecture wanted its audience to notice that both rest on the same God's word and no human evidence, the resurrection and the revelation, each "most certainly," and each asked to be taken before being seen.

**"Generations" Again: The Sūrah's Unit of History**

The noun left unquoted above deserves a sentence. The sūrah's "earlier and later" are, in Arabic, generation-words — qarn, "the people of a time" — not "dead" or "souls," and the choice keeps the chapter's census material, corporate, bodily: the unit that rises is a whole era of people, not a cloud of spirits. Al-Wāqiʿah has consistently resisted every temptation to speak of the afterlife as disembodied (the semen, the sowings, the water, the fire in its argument-half all insist on bodies and fields), and verse 49, the chapter's great gathering-line, extends the same policy across history: what is raised is every generation, in its body, together, and the audience listening in Makkah — a town that dated itself by its generations of custodians — hears that their whole chronological pride will file into one assembly-line whose only distinction is the one the chapter has been drawing since verse 6: class, of their own choosing, sorted by what they used to do (24).

**How Verse 49 Ends the Sūrah's First Half**

Readers with an ear for structure should note where the qul lands and where its paragraph ends: the sūrah's description-unit — three classes, two estates fully shown, the left's sneer and its answer — closes at 56 with "This will be their accommodation on the Day of Judgment" (56), and 49–50, the gathering-decree, is the hinge inside the left's own passage that also pivots the whole chapter: from here the text turns from scenery to testimony (57–74), from Day to Book to death (75–87), and the three-class census resumes at the bedside (88–94). Verse 49, in that map, is the chapter's waist: the last verse of the vision, the first of the argument. The "say" is handed to the prophet exactly where the sūrah's showing ends — and the command to speak, not to demonstrate, is the chapter's own definition of what revelation is for the unshown: "most certainly," the word for the half of reality the eye has not yet reached.

**The Answer's Address**

Notice also who the qul makes the speaker: not God in the first person — the chapter's own "We" waits until 57 — but the Prophet, quoting the decree. The left's mockery at 47–48 was aimed at the messenger ("will we really be raised?"), and the answer returns through his mouth, so that the sūrah stages the refutation as the very office the mockers denied: a man, saying God's certainty, to people who wanted proof. Between 48's sneer and 49's "Say" there is no argumentative connective, only the imperative — the chapter's judgment, made grammatical, that the question of resurrection is not answered by evidence at the bar but by the weight of who says it, and that the bar itself is the Day. When the audience later hears the four "Have you considered?" questions, they will discover that the sūrah, in fact, does have the evidence it declined to produce here; verse 49's bare "Say, most certainly" is the verdict, and 57–74 is the summing-up that follows it, not the proof that earns it.
verses.50:
> will surely be gathered ˹together˺ for the appointed Day

**Mīqāt: Contract-Language for the End of Time**

The sūrah's word is mīqāt, from w-q-t, the noun of measured appointment; the present line's "the appointed Day" renders mīqāti yawmin maʿlūm, a day with a date, and the idiom is the audience's own: a mīqāt is a fixed deadline agreed between parties — the same noun family that carries, in the Heights, the forty nights of Mūsā's tryst with his Lord (7:142). The sūrah thus speaks of resurrection in the register of contracts kept: the Day is not a spontaneous eruption but an appointment the deniers themselves have been served papers for, and the mockers' incredulous "will we really?" (47) lands, grammatically, on a date already set. That is the quiet terror of verse 50: the Hour behaves like a creditor's patience — nothing is rushed because nothing can be renegotiated.

**"The Known Day": Why the Arabic Insists**

Mīqāti yawmin maʿlūm — for an appointed, known Day — and the "known" (maʿlūm) is one of the Qur'an's most theologically loaded adjectives: the Day is known to God, known through the preachers, "known" the way a court date is known to both parties, while al-Wāqiʿah keeps the plain force: this Day is knowable — announced by preachers, calendared in revelation, "known" the way a tryst is known to both parties — and the Ranks sūrah, whose Garden-list our chapter keeps beside its own, attaches the identical adjective to the reward ("a known provision," 37:41), so that Day and recompense share one epithet within the same pair of late texts. The Day's "knownness" is thus part of the evidence: an appointment the accused can produce no excuse for having missed.

**The First Half's Closing Cadence**

Listen to 49–50 as one line across two verses: "Say, 'Most certainly, the earlier and the later will surely be gathered for the Day of the Appointment'" — inna…la-, qawāfil, maʿlūm — the sūrah's longest run of heavy emphatic particles, and its last before the argument turns colloquial ("Have you considered…?" ×4). That cadence is the chapter's own structural signal: the vision has been stated at its maximum certainty, and everything after 50 is evidence, address, and oath — the menu of the left (51–56) and the four questions (57–74) both unfold from the decree, not toward it. Preachers have read the cadence pastorally for centuries: the sūrah's audience is not invited to weigh probabilities about the Hour but to accept a date — and then, in 57, to look at their own bodies and crops, where the sūrah says, the proof of that date has been quietly growing all along, in fluid and in seed, for anyone who will consider it.

**Three Words for the Date, and a Fourth Already Spoken**

The sūrah's small library of Last-Day nouns could be read as a lesson in the audience's calendar: maʿlūm, the known day; mawʿūd, the promised, which the Qur'an's skeptics mock in the same breath they mock the dust — "when is this promise, if you are truthful?" asks the sovereign chapter of the dominion of the same doubters (67:25); and mīqāt, the appointment that does not require their agreement to bind them. Al-Wāqiʿah's contribution to the set is its deployment of all three registers inside two verses — "appointed," "known," and, at 56, "the Day of Judgment" (yawm al-dīn, the Day of Recompense of verse 2 by another name) — a single event named four ways: promised, dated, known, and owed. That quadruple naming is not stylistic surplus. The sūrah is answering verse 47's "really?" from every angle the audience's own contract-vocabulary could supply: you were told, it is on the book, it is a fixed date, and the payment is being withheld by no one — the debt is yours. The Day, in al-Wāqiʿah, behaves like a judge who has already stamped the file at the first hearing (2), and verse 50 says so in the market's own nouns, forty-four verses before the chapter asks the deniers why they take the whole message lightly (81).

The verb's root is the same as the Qur'an's name for Friday's gathering and for the the end of the world it foreshadows — the sūrah of Hud calls it the day on which all people will be gathered, a day of witnessing (11:103), and the sūrah of Consultation names it the Day of Assembly about which there is no doubt (42:7) — while our verse's form, la-jāmiʿūna, says it plainly: they will be gathered, and the sūrah adds no place, only the Day, because in al-Wāqiʿah's geography the place is the weather and the address is a class.
verses.51:
> Then you, O misguided deniers

**The Turn from "They" to "You"**

Through verses 41–50 the left were talked about; at 51 the sūrah turns and talks to them — "Then you, O misguided deniers" — and the shift of person, what the sūrahs' rhetorical science calls iltifāt, is the verse's whole argument. Report addresses a jury; summons addresses the accused. The audience, who have been listening to a description of some third group's smoke, suddenly stand inside the address, because the "you" has no quoted speaker other than the God the chapter has been asserting since 49, and every hearer must decide which "you" they are in. Classical readers of the Qur'an's rhetoric list this turn among its most forceful devices precisely because it happens without warning — no verse-divider announces that the court now speaks to the defendants — and al-Wāqiʿah's placement at the hinge of its second half makes 51 the loudest single line of the left's passage, a line consisting, in Arabic, of nothing but a conjunction, a pronoun, and two nouns.

**"Misguided": The Verb of Losing the Road**

The second title, al-ḍāllīna, is the sūrah's word for going astray, and the root is travel-language: ḍalāla is losing the road, missing the way across open ground — the worst thing that can befall a people whose survival is navigation. The Qur'an uses the same word for its messenger's own prehistory, in the chapter of the Morning-Hours, "He found you unaware of the Scripture and the faith, and He guided you" (93:7) — guidance and being-guided are the pair the word lives inside — and so verse 51's insult is, at bottom, directional: these people are not the wicked but the lost, and the Day they denied is, in the sūrah's physics, the point at which being lost becomes a fixed address. The audience of caravans and star-reading understood ḍalāla as the final danger, and the chapter's choice to name their enemies with it — instead of the vocabulary of crimes — keeps the sūrah's mercy intact: every ḍāll could still be hadā, and the smoke at 43 is what it looks like when the road has been refused until the map is taken away for good.

**Vocation as Last Courtesy**

It is worth stating plainly what the address does not do: it does not revile. "O misguided deniers" is an appellation, not an abuse, and the sūrah at this its most hostile moment stays inside the terms it used for them at 2 and 45 — no epithet of their persons, no cursing, no wish. Commentators on the Qur'an's rhetoric note that divine vocatives of rebuke ("yā ayyuhā al-ḍāllūna" — the sūrah of Ya-Sin's "willfully wronged" are a kin-case) function as summons to responsibility, not as exclusion from it: a lost person addressed is a lost person still able to hear. The irony the sūrah permits itself is the irony of timing — "then" — the address arrives in the verdict, when hearing changes nothing, and the reader who is not yet in the verdict is the one meant to take the vocative as a last courtesy rather than a last insult: the name the Day will give you, offered now, while names can still be refused.

**The Two Titles, Read Once More Together**

"Guiding-losers who call-false": the vocative stacks its nouns without "and," and in Arabic's economy that asyndeton makes ḍalāla and takdhīb one condition — lostness consisting precisely in calling the guide a liar. The sūrah has, since verse 2, treated denial as an act (no one denies the Day except one who has been spoiled into refusing the claim), and 51's double title compresses the psychology: nobody strays into disbelief, in this chapter's view, by honest wandering; the ḍāll of al-Wāqiʿah is the mukadhdhib who has learned to love the road he lost. That is why the verse needs no further description of them before the menu begins — the two words are the inventory of their sin, and the eating to come, from 52, will be its mirror image: what you called false is now your food, and the road you loved is the smoke that surrounds the table.
verses.52:
> will certainly eat from ˹the fruit of˺ the trees of Zaqqûm

**The Fruit That Answers the Mockery**

Context gives the verse its logic: the left denied being raised (47), the gathering was affirmed (49–50), and the address comes (51), and now, at 52, the verdict is not fire as such — it is eating. The Ranks sūrah runs the same menu earlier in the Book — a tree sprouting in the bottom of the Hell, fruit compared to the heads of devils, bellies filled with it, a drink of hamīm after the eating, and a return to the Blaze (37:64–68) — five notes in the same order our 52–56 will play, and the point of a food-punishment is that the deniers made their bodies their argument: "when we are dust and bones, will we really be raised?" The answer is a body that eats forever and is nourished by nothing — resurrection granted in its most terrible form, flesh restored only to the function of swallowing. Al-Wāqiʿah's mockers get their resurrection, in the first tense it will be felt: the throat.

**"Eat From the Trees": The Botany of the Two Estates, Compared**

Set verse 52 against its twin in the right-hand passage, and the chapter's agricultural system appears complete. The saved eat fruit (faakihah, 20, 32) that is never cut off and never forbidden, from thornless lote and clustered trees (28–29); the lost eat "from the trees of zaqqūm," and the Arabic's shared construction — min plus tree-language — is the sūrah's own cue to compare, estate against estate, tree against tree. The pairing encodes the chapter's theology of provision: food is not neutral stuff but relationship, and in this sūrah every people get the vegetation their covenant produced — the near-rank fruit of choice, the middle fruit of abundance, the lost a fruit that is the opposite of cultivation, a plant of the root of Hell that the Ranks sūrah says God "made a trial for the wrongdoers" (the same idiom of trial the verse 73 below will re-use for the world's fire). The Garden and the Fire are, in al-Wāqiʿah's vocabulary, two orchards, and only one of them grows in answer to gratitude.

**The Certainty-Lam Returns, Third Time**

La-tā-kulūna: "you will certainly eat," the emphatic lam of verse 50's la-jāmiʿūn repeated and now attached to swallowing. The sūrah has rung that particle three times — gathering, eating, drinking (50, 52, 54) — and the recurrence is what turns a menu into a sentence: no new threat is being introduced, only the certainty-grammar of the verdict being pressed, item by item, into the left's mouths. Commentators note that the Qur'an reserves this doubled emphasis (inna plus lam) for what the deniers find impossible — resurrection, punishment, the Book's truth — and 52 belongs to that family: the thing the mockers said could never happen is the thing they will never stop doing. There is, in the sūrah's arithmetic, a grim symmetry between the two estates' verbs of certainty: the near-rank were given no lam at all — their pleasures were simply "for them" (38) — while the left receive certainty three times over, because the verdict's function at this point in the chapter is evidentiary, not executive: the audience is being shown that the Day's food will be as sure as its gathering, and the swallowing that will not nourish is the guarantee that the raising that will not end.

One reception-note completes the entry: zaqqūm became, in the literature of warning-sermons across the centuries, the Qur'an's emblem for the punishment of appetite, and the preaching literature turned the tree into the food of every worldly injustice the audience could name — the devourer of orphans above all, after the Women chapter's line that such a man eats fire into his own belly (4:10).
verses.53:
> filling up ˹your˺ bellies with it

**Fullness Without Nourishment: The Punishment of the Apposed Appetite**

The Arabic participle mal'ūna — "filled up" — describes the bellies as being stuffed (mal'a, the verb of filling a skin or a bucket to the brim), and the torment's genius is that the wish for satiety is granted: the left will not hunger in this scene, they will be full, permanently, of what cannot nourish. The Qur'an elsewhere defines the damned's food by exactly this pair of failed functions — in the Overwhelming chapter, "they will have no food except from a thorny plant, which neither nourishes nor satisfies hunger" (88:5–7) — and al-Wāqiʿah, which never says "neither nourishes," states the same truth by the absurdity of the image: fill the belly and offer it nothing but a tree that was never food. Verse 53 thus punishes the appetite not with deprivation but with completion, and readers who know the animal satisfaction of a full stomach will notice that the sūrah has made that satisfaction itself the instrument: the body's one reliable pleasure, turned into its one permanent grievance.

**"With It": The Instrumental of Nothing Else**

Minhu — "from it/with it" — ties the filling to the tree alone, and the exclusivity is the sentence's sharpest edge: no second course, no water that quenches (that comes at 54, as fire on the fullness), no variety, no season, no choice, nothing "they desire" (compare 21, where the near-rank's birds are "what their souls desire"). The saved estate's grammar of options — choose, wish, select — has here been reduced to a single accusative of instrument: you will be filled, with this. Al-Wāqiʿah, whose whole Paradise is built on the removal of constraints on appetite (no season, no ban, no hangover), builds its Hell as appetite with all removals reversed — one object, no exit — and verse 53 is the verse that locks the reversal into the body. Monotony is the punishment's aesthetic; the bellies are full of the proof that a desire, fed forever one thing, is a prison rather than a pasture.

**Passive Again: Even Their Fullness Is Done to Them**

The chapter's grammar of placement — the saved are "in" gardens, "on" thrones, "amid" lote (12, 15, 28); the lost are "in" samum and hamīm (42) — now adds, at 53, the last and most intimate of its passives: they will be filled. The verb is not "they will stuff themselves"; the bellies are full-ed, and the left, who in life were mutrafūn (45 — people dandled, spoiled, done-to by their ease), receive in the next world the same grammatical fate with the sign reversed: in both existences they are acted upon. That symmetry is the sūrah's most severe claim about the damned self — that its passivity is continuous, a softness that chose, once, to be shaped by nothing else, and is now shaped forever by the one thing it mocked. Al-Wāqiʿah has no theory of autonomous damnation; verse 53 insists that even here the verb belongs to God, and the left are the object — and readers who flinch at that theology should remember that the same passive voice, with the same verbs of filling and receiving, describes the Garden's every gift, and the sūrah's point is that the only active voice left in the whole the end of the world was the one sentence at 47: "will we really be raised?" They asked; the answer fills them.
verses.54:
> Then on top of that you will drink boiling water—

**"On Top of That": The Sequence of a Host's Care, Inverted**

Thumma ʿalā dhālik — "then, upon that" — is the sūrah's way of keeping the manners of serving in the scene of punishment: in the etiquette the audience knew, the drink comes after the food, the host does not let the guest's throat go dry at the end of the meal, and the Ranks sūrah, narrating the same menu, says it with the same phrase — "Then on top of that they will be given a blend of boiling drink" (37:67), the line our verse paraphrases. That courtesy, exercised upon the damned, is the verse's chosen irony: the left are served, hosted, attended to — their estate is, as 56 will name it, an "accommodation" (nuṭub, hospitality) — and the sūrah thus refuses to depict hell as neglect. Nothing here is forgotten, withheld, or left to chance; the punishment is administered with the precision of a host who has planned the whole meal, which is far more terrible than abandonment, because it means the left are as certainly in God's hands as the near-rank are, and are being attended to with the same intentionality.

**Hamīm, the Third Time: Water as the Estate's Medium**

The word ḥamīm has now sounded through the left's passage at three functions: the element they are "in" (42), the drink they are forced to (54), and the hospitality they will be given at the Day's final summary (93). Water is the chapter's master-medium, and this is where its theology of water completes itself. The same Book that made the deniers' argument about the ordinary element — "Is it you who bring it down from the clouds, or are We? If We willed, We could make it salty" (68–70) — places them inside water boiling and makes them drink water boiling: the salted water the argument threatens is, in the the doctrine of the Last Day, already arrived. Al-Wāqiʿah's left do not lack water; they have only water, in its unusable form — and a reader who has felt the irony of being offered a drink you cannot want has the whole verse. The chapter's hydrology is thus its theodicy: the same rain is the proof of mercy to the grateful (70, "will you not then be grateful?") and the instrument of verdict to the refused, because in this sūrah substances carry no blessing of their own.

**"Like Molten Brass": The Neighboring Description**

What this verse declines to say about the drink, the Book says elsewhere, and the sūrahs line the passages up as commentary on each other: the Cave chapter's hell-folk, when they cry for aid, "will be aided with water like molten metal, which will burn ˹their˺ faces" (18:29), and the Dazzling chapter's "boiling in the bellies" image for the tree-food of the sinner (44:45–46) — the same belly that 56:53 filled, boiling with what the neighbors say is molten brass. The present sūrah keeps all such comparison back; 54 states only "of ḥamīm," the noun it has already defined in the estate's air (42), and lets the hearer's memory of the other chapters do the work. The restraint fits the chapter's method throughout the left's passage: scenery in three nouns, cause in two lines, and no gore added to what the audience's own experience of heat, thirst, and bad water already supplies — al-Wāqiʿah's punishment is, repeatedly, the familiar made inescapable.
verses.55:
> and you will drink ˹it˺ like thirsty camels do.”

**Ḥīm: The Image the Desert Needed No Gloss For**

The comparison's noun — hum, plural ahyām, from the root of the thirst that unmakes the brain — denotes the camel driven mad by thirst, the animal that will not leave the trough, drinks and drinks and comes up empty, in the old lexicography because the beast's disorder prevents its body from receiving water at all. To an audience whose wealth walked on four legs and whose worst day was the camel's death by thirst, the sūrah needed no further word: "you will guzzle like him" is the entire sentence of punishment, and the translators' bracket ˹it˺ marks the object their verb carries on its own. The simile performs the classic degradation of the Qur'an's damning imagery — humans reduced, not to demons, but to livestock: the chapter of Muhammad says the deniers "eat and enjoy as cattle eat and enjoy" (47:12), in a plain assertion of the same zoology — and here the very act of drinking, which the near-rank perform from ewers with no harm (18–19), is given to the left in its beastly form.

**The Sūrah's Similes, Counted**

Al-Wāqiʿah uses similes four times, and their distribution is its aesthetics. For the cosmos: the mountains elsewhere become like carded wool (70:6), while this chapter's mountains are crushed to pieces and become scattered particles of dust (5–6) — and at 75–76 the stars' positions carry an oath instead of a comparison. For the near-rank: "like hidden pearls" (23), beauty defined by untouchability. For the left: "like molten brass" is not here, it is the neighbor's; this chapter gives them only "like the him." The pattern is precise: the saved get a simile from the treasury (the pearl, the thing hoarded and safe), the lost a simile from the pasture (the animal, the thing perishing at the water), and between them the sūrah's oath-sworn stars — the middle of the chapter's sky, unowned. Verse 55, the last of the left's images, is therefore the chapter's lower term: the audience's most cherished livestock, rendered in their most humiliating death, handed to the mockers of resurrection as their likeness forever, and the sūrah's economy of comparison is closed.

**The End of the Quotation**

Verse 55 closes, typographically, the sūrah's last word spoken to the left: the present translation ends the line with its final quotation-mark, and after 55 the damned receive no further address, only description — the accommodation (56), the created you (57), the questions, the oath, the bedside. That closure is the chapter's design: the speech of the left, their one sneer quoted at 47–48, has been answered; God's vocative runs through 51–55 and stops at the camel-drinking, and what follows is verdict, argument, and doxology. The audience, who heard the "you" of 51–55 as their neighbors' indictment, are meant to feel the silence that falls after 55 — the moment when addressing stops is when the case is no longer before the court — and turn, with the sūrah, toward the four "have you considered" questions, where the only "you" left in the chapter is the one still able to believe it. The thirsty camel's line is thus, in the most literal sense, the end of the conversation; the diction of the remainder is the diction of what comes after words are wasted. And a commentary that has followed the chapter verse by verse can add only this: the sūrah's last image of its deniers is a beast at water, and everything the sermon said afterward, from 57 on, is addressed to the men who still can.
verses.56:
> This will be their accommodation on the Day of Judgment

**Ḍiyāfa: The Word for Hosting, Used as a Sentence**

The noun the present translation renders "accommodation" is ḍiyāfah — hospitality, the guest-right, the whole etiquette of receiving the traveler — and its choice, once felt, changes the verse's temperature entirely. The sūrah calls the Fire's menu a hospitality. The Book uses the same noun, with the same irony, in the Ranks chapter's sequence: "that is their ḍiyāfa, so let them taste it" (37:68), and — for the other side — "Is the accommodation of Paradise better, or the tree of Zaqqūm?" (37:62), where ḍiyāfa appears at the head of the blessed estate's description too. The two usages prove that the word belongs to the chapter's moral vocabulary: hosting is what one does to the arrived, and the Day of Judgment is, in al-Wāqiʿah's design, an arrival at what was always being prepared — the near-rank's "elevated furnishings" (34) and the left's ḥamīm are both, in this sūrah's grammar, things a guest is given. Nothing could be more offensive to Arab honor-usage than calling the Fire a ḍiyāfa, which is precisely why the sūrah calls it that.

**This: The Deictic of Arrival**

"Hādhā" — this — is the verse's first word, and the pointing is the passage's whole the doctrine of the Last Day in a pronoun: the left will not be told about their accommodation in advance forever; at the Day, the deictic arrives, and what was prophecy becomes this. The sūrah, which has spent its description in futurate verbs and state-nouns, ends the scene with the one word that cancels futurity: there will be no more "then" after the drink of the him (55); there will be this. Preachers from the sermon-literature onward made the same observation about the chapter's style — the Qur'an's future tense is a courtesy, a delay, and every "on that Day" is the closing of a distance — and verse 56 is that courtesy ending: the distance at which the mockers had stood to say "when we are dust and bones" (47) collapses into the pointing of the demonstrative, and the sūrah lets its audience feel, for one syllable, what the Day will be like to those for whom it has become the only pronoun. The smallest word in the verse is the one with the most theology in it.

**What the Verse Adds to the Threat: Nothing, Intentionally**

It is worth counting what verse 56 declines: no duration ("eternal" is not said here — eternity in this sūrah belongs to the Garden's nouns, never the Fire's), no angels of punishment, no catalog of torments beyond the drink, no "they will not die." The sūrah ends the left's scene with the flattest possible summative — this, their hospitality, that Day — and goes immediately to "It is We Who created you; will you not then bear witness?" (57), to argument, not to escalation. That restraint is al-Wāqiʿah's most characteristic severity: it gives the punishment its verdict and refuses it its drama, because drama would make the left interesting, and the sūrah's theology requires that they be, finally, only what they made themselves: guests of their own denial, hosted by the One they called liar, in the accommodation they spent a lifetime ordering for themselves, dust and bones and all. Everything the chapter will still say about them — the deathbed reprise of this exact wording at 92–94 — lives inside the flat summation of 56. The Day of Judgment, said once, is said enough.
verses.57:
> It is We Who created you. Will you not then believe ˹in resurrection˺

**The "We" Returns, Now on the Stand**

Through the descriptions the chapter gave creation in polite passives — water poured, shade stretched, mates fashioned — and reserved its first-person plural for three moments: the mates (35), and now, four times in five verses, the argument's opening. "It is We Who created you" is the sūrah's thesis-statement for 57–74, and the fronting of "We" (inna-hu naḥnu khalaqnakum) makes it an exclusive claim: whoever else the audience credited with their making — the stars their soothsayers watched, the ancestors their genealogies honored, fortune they blamed for the chaff — is being answered by pronoun before verb. The bracketed ˹in resurrection˺, the translation's insertion into "will you not then believe," is correct exegesis: the object of belief the verse needs is not creation (which the deniers admitted) but the second act the first makes easy, and the sūrah argues, as it has all chapter, from the conceded to the denied.

**"Then": The Small Adverb That Runs the Chapter**

Fa-lā — the "then" the translation keeps in each closing question — is the sūrah's hinge-word, and it carries its double work from 3 to 96. At the beginning, "when the Event takes place, then no one can deny" (1–2); in the middle, "It is We Who created you, will you not then believe" — the then is temporal and logical at once: at the Day you will believe, and right now the premise should force the conclusion; the sūrah's whole argument lives in that ambiguity, which is why the chapter can be recited at weddings and deathbeds with the same sentences. The translators' bracket ˹in resurrection˺ pins the object of belief, but the verse's own force is the fa: belief here is not a new doctrine but what the already-known Event, when genuinely considered, produces in any mind — the small word does the heavy lifting, and any reader tempted to call this argument circular should notice that the circle is the intended geometry of reminder: creation → Day → creation, each "then" a radius.

**The Verse in the Chapter's Arithmetic of Questioning**

Finally, a census of the half: 57–74 contains four "have you considered" openings (58, 63, 68, 71), four disjunctive challenge-questions ("is it you… or are We?" ×3, with the fire-verse expanded to "who produced its trees"), two "if We willed" threat-clauses (65, 70), and three closing appeals (57, 62, 70) before the doxological fourth (74, "So glorify the Name of your Lord, the Greatest"). Verse 57 is the argument's overture, stating the thesis ("We created you") and the required response ("believe"), and everything after is four variations on that single chord, each in a different register of the audience's daily life — fluid, seed, water, fire — the four things a Makkān household touched every hour of its day. The sūrah's rhetoric of the commonplace begins here: the denier will not be convinced by the heavens (he is a trader, and the caravan's sky is a tool), so God argues from the things his hands cannot deny, starting with the one whose making he would be ashamed to claim.

**Creation as the Chapter's Own Definition of God**

One final fact about 57: in a chapter that has spoken of God as maker of water, fire, harvests, beds, spouses, and deaths, this verse states the thesis in the barest possible form — "We created you" — and then, until the doxology at 74, says nothing more about creation except to point at four ordinary processes. Al-Wāqiʿah's God is not introduced here as omnipotent; the attribute doing the work is creativity, and the required response is belief "in resurrection," not in power. Late Makkān monotheism, at its most economical, says: you are made, therefore you will be remade, and the "therefore" is the whole of the sūrah's middle, the way the "then" of verse 2 was its beginning.
verses.58:
> Have you considered what you ejaculate

**"Have You Considered": The Verb That Sees**

The formula a-fa-raʾaytum — the present line's "have you considered" — uses the Arabic verb of sight for an act of thought, and the sūrah's epistemology is in the pun: the way to know is to look at what you already do, closely, as though for the first time. Late Makkān preaching is full of this imperative to see (the Neighbor chapter's "have you not seen what your Lord did," 89:6, the Elephant's "have you not seen how your Lord dealt," 105:1), and al-Wāqiʿah turns the eye inward: its four "consider" questions will scan semen, seed, water, fire — the four substances of the household — without once asking the audience to contemplate the stars, which the oath at 75 will do for the Book's sake. The verse is thus the argument's manifesto of method: no cosmological subtlety, only the nearest body-function, held up for inspection.

**Maniyy: The Euphemism That Is Clinical**

The verb tamnū — "you pour out" — is Arabic's own discretion: the fluid (umniyyah) named by its spilling, no anatomy, no stage, no clot. The Qur'an speaks about semen without shame and without detail elsewhere — "from a fluid ejected, issuing from between the backbone and the ribs" (86:6–7, a description that is functional, not physiological) and "did he not used to be a drop of ejected fluid?" (75:37) — and 56:58 stands in the same register: what is asked is not a biology lesson but the admission that the fluid is not, at the moment of its pouring, anyone's achievement. Commentators of the sūrahs read 58's bluntness as pedagogical: the audience's boasting was of lineage (nasab), and the sūrah reaches into the very act from which all their genealogies are made and asks the one question pride cannot answer — did you make that drop? The euphemism makes the question possible for public recitation; the question, once asked in the mosque, unmakes the boast.

**What the Verse Does Not Say**

Equally instructive is the verse's silence: no embryology, no "wonders of development," nothing the apologetic literature of later centuries loves to supply. Modern readers are often tempted to hear in "what you ejaculate" a foreshadowing of histology — and the temptation should be named and let go: the sūrah's argument needs the drop to remain what the audience knew it to be, a lost bit of the body, because its logic is about agency, not about complexity. The Qur'an describes the stages in its own places (23:12–14, 22:5), and those descriptions serve the reminder of formation; here the point is narrower and deeper: the fluid is your only raw material, and even it arrives in you from what you do not control — you eat, you drink, you pour, and none of it was manufactured by your will. Argument from the mundane, kept mundane, is the verse's discipline.

**The Second Person Plural of Daily Life**

The verb's subject — "you" plural — includes every hearer in the act being discussed, and this is the sūrah's audacity, felt more in recitation than in print: the assembly, men and women of Makkah, is addressed about the most private thing all of them have in common, and the sūrah will then immediately repeat the pronoun for the seed-sower and the water-drawer (63, 68). The "you" is never accusatory; it is inclusive — the sermon's first move, in this chapter, is to make every listener a witness in their own case rather than a juror in someone else's, which is why the argument-half reads so differently from the denunciation-half: no "they" survives inside 57–74 except in the threat-clauses of verses 65 and 67.
verses.59:
> Is it you who create ˹a child out of˺ it, or is it We Who do so

**"Or": The Question With No Third Door**

The Arabic's disjunctive am ("is it you… or is it We") frames a choice the sūrah refuses to widen: there is no third answer in which the fluid makes itself, or chance does it, or the ancestors do it — the question's shape is the argument's whole content. Al-Wāqiʿah's theology of creation is, at this point in the chapter, radically simple, and the simplicity is the Makkān point: the audience's gods were sharers, partners "who own" and "who intercede," and the Qur'an's recurring demonstration is that partnership requires, at minimum, one act anywhere that another agent performed — the drop being the case in point, because no claimant — not al-Lāt, not al-ʿUzzā, not the family's own memory — has ever put a soul in semen or taken one out. The verse does not enumerate what God did in the embryo; it asks who did it, and its two-option grammar is how the sūrah closes every loophole at once without arguing a single loophole.

**"Create It": The Verb That Exceeds the Fluid**

To the audience's own craft-vocabulary, "creating" (kh-ل-q) meant what a maker does: shaping leather, weaving cloth, forging the head of a lance — and the sūrahs record that Arab poets could call a fine poet "the best of those who shape (khāliq)" in the idiom of making, which is why the verse's verb stings: it asks whether their making reaches into the making of a person, and quietly answers no maker, however skilled, has ever made what he worked with. The Believers sūrah ends its embryological sequence with exactly this coronation: "blessed be God, the best of shapers" (23:14), a verse that knows the audience's praise-formula and redirects it — and 56:59, in its plainer Makkān accent, does the same work by question: "is it you who create it?" The craft is honored; the creation is claimed; the sūrah never says the maker is nothing, only that making is not the same as giving being, and the fluid's first being is the proof.

**"Or We Who Did It": The Modesty of the Evidence**

The second half of the question is the sūrah's only positive assertion in this pair, and its reserve deserves notice: "or it is We Who do so" — no description of formation, no claim about ensoulment, no timetable, nothing a skeptical reader can test, dispute, or over-read. The sūrah's claim, here and throughout the argument-half, is about the direction of credit, not the mechanism of embryology, and readers who want the Qur'an to "anticipate science" in these lines find only an assertion of divine authorship — which, as it happens, is the one part of the argument no science can retire: whoever maps the stages, nobody made the map out of nothing. The present translation's bracket ˹a child out of˺ supplies the object the Arabic elides ("create it"), and the elision is the iʿjāz the sūrahs admired: "is it you who create it, or We?" — the whole of the soul's biography in six words, the pronoun "it" pointing at the drop and at the child at once, because in the sūrah's grammar those two are the same thing, which is precisely the point the mockers at 47 could not grant.
verses.60:
> We have ordained death for ˹all of˺ you, and We cannot be prevented

**Qaḍāʾ: Death as a Completed Act**

The verb is qaḍā — to decree, and also to finish, to carry through to the end (the same root gives the Day "of Decision," yaum al-faṣl) — and the sūrah does not say "We will make you die" but "We have ordained death among you": a settled matter, filed and closed, its grammar as certain as the decree it states. The audience's own poet had written, as poets did, that death is the one thing a man cannot outrun, avert, or buy; the sūrah converts that fatalism into a personal appointment with a first-person verb, and the conversion — fate to decree, decree to address — is verse 60's quiet revolution in the Arabia of "fortune (dahr) does it.".

**"Cannot Be Prevented": The Image of the Race**

The Arabic's last word, masbūqūn, is from racing — "We are not to be outrun, forestalled, got ahead of" — and the metaphor fits a people who measured honor in the speed of their camels and the escape of their clients: no one has ever arrived anywhere before God's decision about them. The Heifer chapter's line about those who fled their towns "in their thousands for fear of death" — and God caused them to die, then gave them life (2:243) — is the same doctrine told as story; and the verse 60 here tells it as the unlosable race whose every entry is already decided: you cannot be first to evade what is ordained to you, and — the sūrah's next word — the defeat is productive, not terminal, which is the one sentence the fatalist's Arabic never had. Read against the mockers' "when we are dust, will we really be raised?" (47), "We cannot be outrun" means: your dust is, specifically, our turf; the race you imagined against annihilation, you have already lost on our terms, and our terms say re-creation.

**"And We Cannot Be Prevented" as Comfort, Not Threat**

Modern ears hear the clause as menace; its first listeners, mostly, would have heard the double-edge the sūrah always runs: the God who cannot be outrun in killing is the same who cannot be outrun in raising — verse 61 proves the syntax ("We are not to be outrun ˹in Our power to˺ substitute…"), and the near-rank's serenity and perfume (89) prove the theology. The verse's pastoral register deserves the note precisely because the sūrah was recited at bedsides: "We have ordained death among you" spoken to a dying person is not a sentence of despair in a chapter whose God has just described the dying as "serenity and perfume and a Garden of Bliss" — it is the assurance that what is happening is inside a decree that cannot be reversed, delayed, or bargained with, and therefore needs no more struggle, and the struggle's end is 61's "transforming and re-creating." The threat-mode and the comfort-mode are one verse; the difference between them, al-Wāqiʿah has said from the start, is class — which class you were busy becoming (24, 45–46).

**"For You" and "Among You": The Pronoun's Double Hold**

The Arabic's prepositions around the decree — ʿalaykum, among you — give the death sentence a legal ring, the phrasing of an ordinance "against" a people, and the same double hold (for you / upon you) will re-appear at the chapter's end, where accommodation is "for them" the boiling drink (93). The sūrah thus binds the decree's universality and its personal address in one construction: death is not a fate that befalls the third person, it is a ruling filed against every listener by name — and since 57 has just said "We created you," the same "you" who were made are the "you" on whom the ordinance stands, which is exactly the verse's contribution to the resurrection-argument: the Maker's jurisdiction opens with creating and closes with dying, and the mockers who grant the one cannot plead exemption from the other.
verses.61:
> from transforming and recreating you in forms unknown to you

**The Verse's Quiet Argument Against the Dust-objection**

Set 61 back inside the mockers' sentence and it answers them at their own hinge. Their objection at 47 was: dust and bones do not reassemble — the materials are too ruined. Verse 61 concedes the ruin entirely: you will not reassemble; you will be transformed and brought up new, in forms not in your inventory of materials at all. The sūrah's resurrection is not archaeology, and 61 lets no reader pretend it is: the "re-creation" (nashʾ) verb, chosen in the same chapter where God "made the mates anew" (35), makes the risen body, like the Garden's spouses, a fresh sprouting rather than a repair — and the mockers' physics is thus answered not by a stronger physics but by a change of category: what God does with dust is not gather it but graduate it. The argument-half's logic (58–59: the drop you did not make) generalizes here: just as the body's origin was not an assembly you performed, its end will not be one you can object to.

**"In Forms You Do Not Know" in the Sūrah's Economy of Surprise**

Notice how often this chapter withholds its images behind the word "know" — "positions of the stars," an oath "if only you knew" how great it is (75–76); the Book "touched by none except the purified" (79); and here: forms unknown. Al-Wāqiʿah's epistemology is that the biggest realities are, right now, informationally closed to the audience, and its ethics is that living as though they were open is what the saved do. Verse 61 puts the review body inside that same closedness — not a mystery to be solved by the pious, but a form to be received without preview — and the effect on the reciter is instructive: one practices, on this verse, the very relation to the unknown that dying will be. The chapter that opened by telling its hearers what happens when nothing solid stays solid ends its first argument by telling them they are, already, on their way into a shape that has no file in their imagination, and that the Only Shaper (59's verb again) is the one sentence they do need to know.

**Why "Recreate" Shares Its Verb with the Mates**

The final fact of the verse is its word: nush'a is the noun family of inshaʾ, and the chapter has now used the family twice — of the spouses made "in a [new] creation" (35, where the present line's bracket reads "perfectly created") and of the selves made over after death (61). The sūrah's readers have always noticed verbal echoes as architecture, and this one is load-bearing: marriage and resurrection share a verb because, in al-Wāqiʿah's theology, both are the same act — God introducing what is worn into what is new, without cancelling the relation (the mates are still "their" mates; the self is still "you"). Verse 61, on that reading, is not only the argument's next move; it is the promise-section's hidden stanza: the body that will not fit its imagination and the love that will not fit its history are, in this chapter's single vocabulary, equally a sprouting — and the unknown forms are, for the near-rank, precisely the Garden: what you cannot picture is what you were being made for.

And the clause's mercy within its severity is worth one last plain word: "unknown to you" means that nothing you dread about the body's future is what you will get, and nothing you have earned for it is lost in the changing — the forms pass, the address ("you") does not.
verses.62:
> You already know how you were first created. Will you not then be mindful

**Tadhakkur: Forgetting as the Disease the Sūrah Treats**

The closing verb, tadhdhakkar, is the root of dhikr — remembrance — and in the Qur'an's anthropology the sin of the deniers is rarely ignorance; it is inattention, the un-remembering of what is conceded. Al-Wāqiʿah has already staged it: the Event "no one can deny" (2), the forefathers the mockers cite as if they were beyond summons (48), the Book they "take lightly" (81). Verse 62's "will you not then be mindful" prescribes against that disease with the sūrah's own name as medicine — the Qur'an, in its self-designation, is "the Reminder (dhikr)," sent so that what the soul already knows is not lost (the Book's claim, paraphrased in the Heifer and the Qāf chapters: "a Reminder to whoever has a heart" — the Qāf verse's exact idiom, 50:37) — and the verse's placement right after the "unknown forms" of 61 makes the logic complete: the future body cannot be known, but the past origin can be remembered, and remembering the lesser is the sūrah's way of making the greater credible.

**The All the more Engine of 57–74**

Read 62 as the argument's thesis-key: if you were made once from nothing you did not prepare, the second making is not harder but easier, and the mockers' difficulty ("dust and bones?") is therefore not an objection but a forgetting. The Book states this syllogism aloud elsewhere, in the chapter of Ya-Sin, where the man who crumbles the bones is answered: "Who will give life to bones while they are decayed? Say: He will give them life who produced them the first time" (36:78–79, cited in plain paraphrase because the sūrahs count them as one argument) — and al-Wāqiʿah, which never quotes Ya-Sin, runs the identical demonstration inside its own four "consider" questions: first creation (57), drop (58–59), decree of death (60), transformation (61), and the reminder of the knowing (62), five rings of one chain.

**Why "Then" Ends the First Movement**

Verse 62 is the last line of the chapter's first argument-movement before the sowing-passages (63–67) begin, and its fa-lā — the "then" of all three closers (57, 62, 70) — closes the movement on the listener's obligation, not God's: the sūrah's verdict after creation-and-death is "be mindful," a verb the audience can perform in the next breath, in the market, at the well. That is why 62 needs no threat, no promise, no image; its two clauses complete 57's question ("will you not believe") with its memory-variant, and the third, gratitude (70), will close the whole half like a chord. The sūrah's rhetoric here is at its plainest and, in the classical judgment, its strongest — late Makkān passages that argue without ornament are rare in the Book, and commentators of the sūrahs treated 57–74 as a specimen of the "argumentative sūrahs (ḥujajiyyāt)," whose verse-divisions fall on the audience's duties (believe, remember, thank) rather than on God's acts.

**The Verse at the End of the Census It Began**

One structural circle deserves closing: verse 6 began the chapter "and you become three pairs," and verse 62 ends the first argument with the same second-person plural — "you were created," "you know," "you will be mindful" — the three classes of 6–14 now reduced, in the reasoning, to one "you," which is the sūrah's final statement about the Day's sorting: the classes are the future tense of the shared past. Every census-line from 8 to 52 ("the people of the right," "the people of the left," "the foremost") subdivides a humanity that 62 insists is continuous in origin, and the effect is that the chapter's terror and its comfort come from the same fact: you, who know where you came from, are being addressed about where you are going, and the sūrah's one question at the hinge — will you not be mindful — can be answered by anyone, in any of the three pairs, while the knowing lasts. That is al-Wāqiʿah's whole pastoral, and 62, the plainest verse of its middle, is where the sūrah says it without images.

The Ranks chapter will later press the point in the Book's own terms — man created "from a dust, then a drop of fluid" (the sūrah of Prostration's reminder, 32:7–8, in plain paraphrase) — and verse 62 declines to cite even that: your knowing, it says, is pre-scriptural, lodged in the fact that you exist and were born.
verses.63:
> Have you considered what you sow

**The Second Consideration: From the Body to the Field**

The argument-half runs on one repeated imperative — "have you considered" — applied to what you eject (58), what you sow (63), what you drink (68), and what you kindle (71), and the sequence moves outward from the body through the field to the sky and the hearth, the four domains a Makkān household actually inhabited. The second, at 63, is the one the audience's wealth was built on: grain was the south's money as much as its food, the storehouse was the bank, and the sūrahs of the South Arabian terraces are a civilization's autobiography told in irrigation. By placing sowing next to semen the sūrah has made both into the same class of evidence — acts every man performs and no man completes — and the verse's brevity ("what you sow," two words in Arabic, the verb zaraʿa and its object) does the rest: the sermon will not allegorize the seed here, though later readers loved to; it simply puts the furrow beside the womb as second witness to verse 57's thesis, "We created you," in a court of one exhibit per room.

**The City Without Fields**

One contextual fact sharpens the verse: Makkān scripture is honest that the sanctuary-town was agricultural nonsense — the Heifer chapter's own account of Ibrāhīm's prayer makes the valley's barrenness the premise of the settlement ("a land without cultivation," 14:37), and the city's fame was the trade that carried grain into it, not the grain it grew. "Have you considered what you sow" therefore addresses, at 63, an audience for whom sowing was a profession of neighbors (the Ṭāʾif farmers, the Yemeni terraces) and an import, and the sūrah's argument reaches them through the thing they bought weekly: to live at Makkah was to depend, every loaf, on rain and growth you could not station guards around. The verse's choice of sowing over reaping — the act of putting seed in the ground, the gesture of pure expectation — fits that listener exactly: Makkah's piety, like its economy, was a bet placed on what someone else's fields and heaven's water would do.

**Seeds Elsewhere in the Book**

Al-Wāqiʿah cites no seed-parables here, but the audience's scripture was thick with them, and the verse's "what you sow" is a compressed intertext: the Heifer's "a seed that splits the sprout" (6:95, plain paraphrase), the Heifer's own parable of the grain that puts forth seven ears, a hundred in each (2:261, paraphrased), and the Victory chapter's sower whose shoot "He sprouts, then makes it grow strong" (48:29, in plain paraphrase), and the Kafrūn sūrah's devastating "you certainly know" structure — "not are you worshippers of what I worship" — which verse 68's format will imitate. The Qur'an's agriculture is, across these passages, a single argument: growth is the clearest case of un-owned power, and the seed, because it must leave the hand to live, is the object that best dramatizes trust. Verse 63 places that whole scriptural stock, without quotation, behind four words — "have you considered what you sow" — and lets the listener's own familiarity with the Book's farming do the exegesis.

**The Verse Before the Threat**

Finally, notice what follows and why: 64 asks who grows it, 65 says "if We willed, We could make it crumbled stubble, and you would keep on wondering." The sūrah's second consideration is thus the only one of the four followed by an explicit "if We willed" clause — a threat hung on the field and not on the fluid — and the asymmetry makes verse 63 the hinge between the two registers of the argument: the body is God's proof, but the harvest is God's leverage, because the audience's survival, unlike their generation, could be bargained with, taxed, salted, and lost, and the sūrah exploits that vulnerability. To "consider what you sow" is, in al-Wāqiʿah's court, to consider the thing that can be taken; semen cannot extort a verdict from a denier, wheat can, because he feeds his children from it and knows it. The verse is gentle in form and ruthless in placement: the second question in a chain whose second answer is famine.
verses.64:
> Is it you who cause it to grow, or is it We Who do so

**Nashz: The Root That Grows Crops, Mates, and Bodies**

The verb of the challenge — "is it you who cause it to grow?" — carries the sūrah's own root for sprouting: n-sh-ʾ, to bring up, to cause to rise, and the same root has already done duty twice in this chapter and does so once more below: God "made the mates in a [new] making" (inshaʾan, 35), "We could transform and bring you up in a form you do not know" (nunshiʾakum, 61), and here, the growth of what the farmer buries (tunshīʾūna? — the sūrahs read the verb as the raising of vegetation). One root, therefore, runs from the re-creation of spouses to the resurrection of bodies through the daily sprouting of grain, and the sūrah is making its case with morphology as much as with questions: in al-Wāqiʿah's vocabulary, marriage-freshness, harvest, and the risen body are the same act of God, one verb wearing three contexts. The earth's sprouting is also, elsewhere in the Book, the earth's speech — the Quake chapter has the ground "tell its news, because your Lord has inspired it" (99:4–5) — and the mockers at 47, who dismissed the reassembly of dust, are answered by the dust that rises every spring on their own terraces, speaking, testifying, sending up what nobody put there.

**An Open Question the Hearer Cannot Exit**

The disjunctive form — "is it you… or is it We" — is identical to verse 59's, and the repetition is itself the argument: the audience, having conceded the "or" for the child's creation, cannot withdraw it for the crop's growth. The verse demands no doctrine, only the choice between two options its hearer already knows, and the sūrah is confident the field will answer "We" the way the womb did. What the sūrah also declines is a third option — no "nature" slot is offered, not out of discourtesy but because the audience's nature was their weather, and verses 68–70 will argue the rain separately and reassign it in the same form. By its shape alone, 64 closes the loophole the denier always tries, the concession that God made the first push and then things just grow: the question has already put the whole growing, this season's included, inside the same unanswered "or.".

**"We Cause It to Grow": The Continuity of Creating**

The present tense of the divine verb — "We are causing it to grow," the sūrah answering in its own imperfect — puts the making of the crop not in a past-deity but in ongoing act, and that tense is the sūrah's contribution to its own resurrection-logic: if growth is something God is doing now, the second growth (nushuʾ, 61) is a continuation of the same verb, not a new argument.
