The classical readers of these verses, in the kalām schools, read 64 as a proof-text for the moment-by-moment renewal of creation — that the crop's ripening is not a machine running down but a gift being given each hour — and the verse's plain sense bears them out without technical vocabulary: the seed that was "sown" is not a finished product awaiting the market, it is a process owned by Another at every stage, which is precisely why 65 can threaten to crumble what has not yet been given at all. A sūrah that said "We grew it once" would license deism; "We are causing it to grow" licenses only gratitude or greed.

The Book's hoarding-laws elsewhere — the hoarding of gold and silver that is not spent in God's way, with its tidings of a painful torment (9:34, in plain paraphrase), a theme the Iron sūrah's hardening-verse sounds at 57:16, already noted in this commentary — provide the moral half of the argument; 64 provides the metaphysical one: growth is not a thing you do, so the increase you priced was never yours to begin with, and the Day's census (8–14) sorts people by what they did with what was given, which is the only ownership the sūrah ever admits.
verses.65:
> If We willed, We could simply reduce this ˹harvest˺ to chaff, leaving you to lament

**Ḥuṭāmah: The Sound of the Thing Crushed**

The word the present translation renders "chaff" is ḥuṭam — an object of the root meaning to crumble, to bruise to fragments, the same word used for dates crushed in the hand and, in the Sijjīl passage of the Elephant chapter, for the birds' stones that make the army "like eaten straw" (105:5, plain paraphrase — the Book's master image for a harvest or an army reduced to fodder). Ḥuṭam is not a botanical state but an aftermath: what remains when the crop is broken down past use, and the sūrah's threat is therefore not drought, not blight, but the specific horror of the granary-age — labor completed, produce present, and then crushed to stuff no animal will take. For an audience whose calendar, debts, and dowries all hung on the harvest's yield, the verse names the total loss available to a God who "willed," and the word's sound — the emphatic ḥ, the heavy stops — performs the breaking the meaning describes.

**"Leaving You to Lament": The Verse Turns the Farmers into a Chorus**

The Arabic continues — fa-tazallūna tujaʿjʿūna, the present line's "leaving you to lament" — and the verb of the lament, its rare root of the hoot and the howl, the owl's cry, gives the scene its sound: the sūrah does not describe the loss; it stages the noise of losers, a people left keening in their own fields. The choice completes the verse's movement from threat to theater — We willed, We crumbled, you cry — and the crying, as the next two verses make explicit, is quoted (66–67), in the first person, so that the audience hears their own hypothetical voices inserted into the recitation. This is late Makkān preaching at its most inventive: the sūrah does not curse the farmers with loss but lets them rehearse the lament aloud, an exercise in grief performed on a condition God has just lifted, and the listeners, caught reciting the keening with the congregation, have said "we are ruined" about a harvest still standing.

**The Verse the Surah Answers with Gratitude**

Finally, 65 belongs to the chapter's economy of thanks. Its last argument-question, at 70, ends "will you not then give thanks?" — shakūr, the grateful servant of whom the Saba chapter said few are (34:13, cited already at this chapter's verse 14) — and verse 65 is the verse that defines what gratitude is for: not for the harvest enjoyed (that is 64's growth, conceded) but for the harvest not yet crushed. The sūrah's theology of shukr, in this passage, is the flip side of its theology of will: every morning the chaff did not come is the morning God did not will, and the grateful are those who read the barn's silence as speech. Al-Wāqiʿah has, from its thornless lote trees to its never-cut fruit, described the Garden as provision with the "if We willed" clause spent forever — and verse 65 stands in the argument-half like the world's one paragraph on why the clause has not yet been spent on you: read it as mercy, the sūrah says, while it is still the condition and not the outcome, and let the lament be only a rehearsal, keening over standing grain, the sound of a people God chose not to make an example.

**Chaff and the Dust of Verse 6: The Chapter's One Reduction**

Al-Wāqiʿah has already crushed something in this chapter: the mountains, at verses 5–6, became "scattered ˹particles of˺ dust," and the chaff of verse 65 is that same reduction run through the human scale, stone and stalk alike returned to unsalable fragments. The sūrah's physics of loss is one verb wearing two objects — the geology of the Day and the agriculture of the week — and the audience who heard the mountains flattened at the opening should hear, at 65, their own fields flattened on the same terms: the Event is not a foreign catastrophe visiting a stable world; it is the world's own contingency, spoken once about stone and once about grain, with lament (65's "you would keep on wondering") as the human residue of both. The chaff is the sermon's smallest proof and its largest: what can be reduced in a clause is not, in any final sense, yours.
verses.66:
> “We have truly suffered a ˹great˺ loss

**A Loss Named in the Grammar of Certainty**

The cry carries, in Arabic, the full asseveration — inna plus the lam of emphasis — "truly, we are the utterly-bested," and the sūrah has just used the identical particles for its own decree: "Most certainly, earlier and later generations will surely be gathered" (56:49–50). The parallel is unmissable once named: the lament of the lost speaks, under threat, in the very grammar of certainty God uses over them, and their "truly" will be as confident then as the oath was now — the sūrah implies that on the Day even the ruined will believe, and believe with emphasis, their unbelief having been the temporary, not this confession. The bracketed ˹great˺ supplies an intensifier the Arabic's root carries contextually, and readers should hear the double emphasis, divine and human, echoing across seventeen verses: what God swears, the loss swears too, and the sūrah's audience is being asked which "truly" they will be the first to accept.

**Loss as the Sūrah's Recurring Ledger-Word**

Khasāra — the cry's noun — is the chapter family's commercial term, and al-Wāqiʿah, which has priced the whole Day in trade-language (shade "extended" like credit, "benefit" denied to the left — 44, "for what they used to do" as payment — 24), puts on the farmers' lips the one word a merchant cannot mishear: loss, the verdict on a tijāra, a transaction that failed. The Book reserves the same noun for its gravest bankruptcies — "they bought error for guidance, and their trade did not turn to profit" (2:16, plain paraphrase), "the losers are those who lose themselves and their families" (the sense of the Az-Zumar tally, 39:15) — and the lament at 66 is, in that idiom, the smallest case of the largest: a field is the classroom, and the loss they keeningly confess is rehearsal for the one the sūrah is really counting. The keening of the farmers, in a chapter recited in a market-town, is translated without remainder; Makkah understood a bad trade better than it understood resurrection, and the sūrah says so by letting it use the traders' own arithmetic for the Day.

**The Two-Voice Lament: 66 and 67 as One Speech**

Verses 66 and 67 form a single utterance split by a correction — "We have truly suffered a great loss. No, rather, we are deprived" — and the bal-clause (next verse) is the sūrah's microcosm of repentant accuracy: the first cry mourns the event ("loss"), the second names the agent and the share ("held back from what was due"), and the whole movement, in two breaths, is the sūrah's theory of what grief must learn before it learns anything else. Rhetoricians of the sūrahs preserve this shape for divine address elsewhere — the bal that redirects a wrong self-pity to true self-knowledge — and the lament's mini-drama, three words then three words, is the chapter's compressed sermon: the crop-tears begin as "what happened to us" and end, when honest, as "what we were kept from." The unit of 63–67 has therefore a complete plot — sowing, growing claimed, chaff threatened, keening, confession — a parable in five verses, with no moral attached because the moral is the structure: everything the farmer does, he does inside a will that can, in one clause (65), turn his year into his lament.
verses.67:
> In fact, we have been deprived ˹of our livelihood˺.”

**The Root That Unites 33 and 67**

Read across the chapter, verse 67 answers verse 33 at the level of letters. The people of the right were promised fruit "never out of season nor forbidden (lā maqṭūʿah wa-lā muḥarramah)" — fruit on which no taboo has ever been passed, the root ḥ-r-m negated as a bar — and the keening farmers end their sentence as "deprived (maḥrūmūn)," the same root passed against them as exclusion. Al-Wāqiʿah's theology of provision lives in that rhyme: ḥarām in this chapter means, both times, the power to withhold — the Garden is what no hand is forbidden from, and the Field-world is what any hand may be cut from — and the sūrah has placed the two uses to bracket its argument-half, so that the saved orchard (28–34) and the lost lament (63–67) are spelled from one consonant-root. The keening, heard in Arabic, is therefore unintelligible to the believer except as a definition by contrast: they mourn, and the mourned estate is the one whose fruit "no one is barred from," a sentence recited forty verses earlier in the same breath the sūrah now asks the lameters to complete: "we — we are the barred.".

**The Deprived and the Pride of Sanctuary**

Makkāns lived under a name that made ḥurmah their claim to the world: their town was the sanctuary (ḥaram), its truce-months the heritage of Ibrāhīm's prayer ("a land without cultivation" endowed with safety, in the Abrahamic petitions the Book preserves — 14:35, 2:126, plain paraphrase), and their pride was that of people no one could touch at the House. The lament's word, maḥrūm, takes that pride apart at its root: the same ḥ-r-m whose sacred security they cited, whose fruit-taboos they kept for their altars (5:103's cultic refusals, at this chapter's verse 33), becomes in their cry the noun of being shut out — and the sūrah thus converts the city's master-concept into its warning: the sanctuary protects nobody from deprivation, the taboo feeds nobody, and "we are barred" is the confession Makkah's entire sanctity-culture was built to prevent its people from ever having to say. To recite 67 in that town was to speak its vocabulary back to it with the sign reversed.

**Silence After the Cry: How the Sūrah Closes the Sowing**

No divine reply follows 67 — and that silence is a compositional fact, not an omission. The semen-question ended with a closer ("will you not then believe," 57); the water-question will end with "will you not then give thanks?" (70); the fire runs to doxology (74). The sowing alone ends on the humans' own voice, mid-lament, unanswered, and the effect on the recitation is the sūrah's harshest device: the farmers' "in fact, we have been deprived" is left ringing, and the next thing the audience hears is not God addressing the keening but God moving, without transition, to "Have you considered the water you drink?" — as if to say: the lament over the chaff will get no answer in this life because its answer is the next verse, already beginning — the water that is as contingent as the grain, and that can also, in one will (70), be made salt. The silence of 67's close is the chapter's most express pause: the deprived are not consoled, they are continued, and the sermon's rhythm tells the listener that grief over fields receives, in this Book, not a theodicy but another question to consider.

Rizq, across the Book, is what a creature is given to live on, and the Qur'an's fixed answer to every anxiety about it is that the Giver and the grower are one: "there is no creature on earth but that upon God is its provision" (11:6, in plain paraphrase), a verse whose grammar of guarantee (ʿalā) matches, in reverse, the lament's "we are the deprived (maḥrūmūn)" — those cut off from what was owed, in their imagination.
verses.68:
> Have you considered the water you drink

**The Third Consideration, and the Only Passive One**

The argument-half's four questions are built on four things — what you eject, what you sow, what you drink, what you kindle — and the third breaks the pattern in a way the reciter feels before the analyst names it. Semen, seed, and fire are things the audience does: verbs of human making run all three ("what you ejaculate," "what you sow," "you kindle"). But the water verse says "the water you drink" — the only clause of the four in which the listeners' contribution is reception. The sūrah has moved from what you make to what you merely take in, and the escalation of the argument is in the grammar: nobody is required to pretend they did not sow, and it is almost impossible to pretend you did not need to drink. Verse 68 is thus the point at which the sūrah stops contesting credit and simply asks, out loud, about the one commodity that has never belonged to anyone in Makkah — and does it in the flat idiom of "have you considered," as if reminding, not teaching, which is this chapter's whole manner.

**Water as the Sūrah's Own Reward-Medium**

Inside this chapter, water has already done duty at both ends of the the doctrine of the Last Day: the near-rank's cups come "from a flowing spring" (18), and the right-hand people live inside "flowing water" (31) poured with no owner; the left, meanwhile, are immersed in scalding water (42) and given a drink of hamīm (54) and the thirsty camels' guzzle (55). Verse 68, "the water you drink," gathers all four scenes into the courtroom: the same element, the sūrah says, is the Garden's gift, the Hell's instrument, and your present thirst's only hope — and the question that opens the water-argument is therefore the question the whole chapter has been asking in its weather: who is the Giver of this, since what the Giver makes of it on the Day depends, exactly, on whether you said thanks or theft, "mine" or "Whose." Al-Wāqiʿah does not separate its hydrology from its theology because its audience never could: to drink at Makkah was to live inside the chapter's argument, un-reflected.

**"Drink" as the Sūrah's Smallest Test**

The verse's verb — tashrabūn, you drink — is worth one last look, because the sūrah could have said "the rain you see," "the wells you dig," and chose the throat. Consideration, in al-Wāqiʿah, is measured by the swallow: every drink is an unowned event completed inside you by an agency not yours, and the argument-half asks whether the audience will convert that daily, ingested fact into belief (57), mindfulness (62), and thanks (70) — the three closers that frame the whole sequence like the three draughts of a cup. The mockers at 47 wanted resurrection argued on dust and bones; the sūrah answers at 68 by pointing at the water every body passes through, hourly, and at the clouds nobody of them has ever lifted a rope toward. "Have you considered" remains the sūrah's only imperative in this half — no threat yet, no promise, just the invitation to think about drinking — and the gentleness of the third question, in a chapter that opened with mountains in powder, is itself its argument: the God who can unmake stones asks you, softly, about a mouthful of water, and history has found no one who could answer honestly without losing their pride.
verses.69:
> Is it you who bring it down from the clouds, or is it We Who do so

**"From the Clouds": Muduj, the Rain-Word the Sūrah Chooses**

The Arabic's noun for the source is muduj (plural of madfa, in the sūrahs' lexica: the cumulus, the heaped rain-clouds that "drive" forward), and the present translation's "clouds" keeps the concrete sky-thing the audience watched — not "the sky" (samāʾ), which the Qur'an elsewhere uses for rain's origin ("He sends down rain from the sky," 14:32, 2:22, plain paraphrase). The sūrah's word here, in the classical readings, marks a specific phenomenology: the white heap on the horizon that the whole town watches for, the cloud as the desert's rumour. That choice lets verse 69 stage its disjunction at the audience's own observation-post — you see the clouds, you do not drive them; your eyes track the heaping, your hands have no handle on the descent — and the rain's familiar mechanics become, in five words, a demonstration of un-owned power. The argument-half's most concrete line is also its most meteorological, and the sūrahs enjoyed noting that the very plural of the word pictures what the people called, in their proverb, the sky's "driving" of water to the valley-beds they alone could claim.

**"Is It You… or We": The Question's Third Repetition**

The disjunctive am has now rung at the fluid (59), the growth (64), and here at the rain (69), with the fire to follow its own expanded shape (72), and the repetition is the sūrah's logic performed as rhythm: each question offers the audience exactly two doors and no third, and each time the second door is God's first-person plural. By the third iteration the hearer is being trained — the sūrah does not argue that the rain falls from clouds nobody parts; it asks, as before, "you or We," and lets the accumulated form do the work no syllogism would attempt on a marketplace ear. The classical readers of the Qur'an's argument-style called this isti'dād, the preparation of consent by repetition: the audience answers "We" in their heart by the water-question, as they did by the seed, before either is ever argued, and the sūrah's next threat at 70 lands on a listener who has already, three times, conceded the sovereignty it needs.

**The City's Prayer for Rain**

That the sūrah's question was Makkah's standing practice can be seen from the other end of the Book: the prophetic prayer for rain, preserved in the two Ṣaḥīḥs' books of Friday prayer — the congregation turning their cloaks, the Prophet raising his hands, the words "Allāhumma aski—" — is, in act, the answer to verse 69 already performed: the community that could not bring down rain prays to the One who can, and the sūrah's question exposes the hypocrisy of a people who kneel for the clouds in drought and deny the Sender in doctrine. That the istisqā' liturgy survives in the sūrahs' collections, in the exact vocabulary of asking-God-for-what-only-God-does, is the strongest historical note 69 can carry: the audience's own worship conceded the verse's "or is it We," and the sūrah is not asking them to believe a new thing, only to stop living as if the old thing did not apply on the Day.

**"Do So": The Ellipsis That Keeps the Rain Unmechanized**

The present translation's "or is it We Who do so" renders an Arabic ellipsis — the line does not repeat the verb's object or its instrument; the sūrah, which could have said "We send it down, weighed, timed, guided to the wells it chose," simply answers "or We," and the bareness is deliberate. The sūrahs of the water-verses elsewhere carry the mechanics ("We send down water in measured measure," 23:18, plain paraphrase; "the fertilizing winds," 15:22, the same book's idiom), while al-Wāqiʿah declines the detail here because its argument needs only authorship: rain is the case in which every theory of the world concedes at least one god — the audience's own al-Anwāʾ, the star-lot oracles of rain, prove how seriously everyone took the descent's contingency — and the sūrah's question is which. To keep "We do so" unexplained is to deny the listener the comfort of a mechanism halfway to God: the rain's how is left to the other chapters, while the who, in this one, stands exposed in two words and no third option.
verses.70:
> If We willed, We could make it salty. Will you not then give thanks

**Ujāj: The Salty That Is the Sweet's Reverse**

The word ujāj — "salty," in the older glosses also bitter, scalding, the undrinkable — is Qur'anic only in this chapter and in the Furqan's twin-seas verse: "one fresh and palatable and the other salty and bitter, placing between them a barrier they cannot cross" (25:53) — the two-seas verse whose barrier-idiom the All-Merciful sūrah also invokes (55:19–20), and the pair of usages shows what verse 70's threat costs: al-Wāqiʿah does not say "We could make it poison" — no invented evil — it says We could make your drinking-water taste like the sea you already know, and the horror is precisely at home. The sūrah's the doctrine of the Last Day works the same way everywhere (a shade that is smoke, cups without headache, a spring without a cistern): the punishment and the promise are each built from one familiar ingredient with one property changed, and 70 is the formula at its cleanest — take the sweet (furat), apply the will, and Makkah has no vocabulary for the loss that follows.

**"If We Willed," the Second Time: The Chapter's Contingency Engine**

Verse 65 threatened the harvest with crumbled chaff "if We willed"; 70 now threatens the water with salt, and the repetition of law nashāʾu is the argument-half's hinge: the two conditional-clauses flank the rain's disjunction and bind the chapter's middle with a single doctrine — nothing in the order of nature is necessary. The classical theologians argued from exactly such verses that the world's regularity is custom maintained, not compulsion inherited — the Muʿtazilī and Ashʿarī schools differ elsewhere, but this passage's grammar ("We could") is on neither side's opposite: no verse here says God does evil, only that He is able, and ability, in the sūrah's rhetoric, is the measure of the present gift. Between the two "if We willed" clauses sits 68–69's question about agency; the architecture says plainly: you have conceded who gives, so do not mistake the giving for owing — the salt of 70 is the standing proof that sweetness was never anyone's right.

**The Verse the Chapter Answers with Fire**

One last structural grace: from 71 the sūrah turns to "the fire you kindle," and the movement from undrinkable water to unownable flame is the argument's final pair — a world stripped of its two daily magics, the mouth and the hearth. Water that can salt is the mercy you do not deserve; fire that is "a reminder and a provision for the travelers" (73) is the tool whose usefulness is loaned, in the desert, by a God who has already told the denier, at 42, that His climate turns against those who turn from Him. Verse 70 stands at the joint: the closer of the water-triad and the last appeal before the doxology — and readers who finish 57–74 in one sitting will notice that the chapter asked for belief, memory, and gratitude, and received from no verse in its own world an answer except the one each listener gives, in the next swallow, in the next spark, every day the salt does not come — which is, the sūrah implies, exactly what "then give thanks" means: not a formula after the sermon, but the taste of sweet water, noticed.

That the closer is phrased as a question — fa-la-ʿalla tashkurūn, "will you not then give thanks?" — keeps even gratitude inside the sūrah's court of consent: the appeal is put to the hearer, unenforced, and the water keeps falling on both the thankful and the unthankful until the Day sorts the two, which is itself, in al-Wāqiʿah's idiom, the largest ˹unearned˺ mercy in the passage.

Gratitude, in this chapter's country, is not a mood but a survival technology, and the audience's own scripture had taught them what its failure costs: the people of the two garden-terraces were a grateful folk, said the Sabaʾ chapter, until ingratitude (kufr, here in its root-meaning of un-thanking) and the dam-sent flood turned their groves to bitter-fruited substitutes (34:15–17) — the exact reversal of verse 70, sweet to salt, watered to destroyed, and the sūrah reciting "will you not then give thanks" in the hearing of Makkah carries the Sabaeans' aftermath as its unspoken second clause.
verses.71:
> Have you considered the fire you kindle

**Fire as the Chapter's Double-Edged Element**

Al-Wāqiʿah has used fire before this verse and will use it after, and 71 is the joint: "the blazing-fire" (al-jahīm) is the left's lodging — 48 — their drink is boiling (hamīm, 42, 54), and their doom is "a blazing-fire" at 94; meanwhile the near-rank have no fire in their inventory at all, and the Event itself melts mountains but does not burn them — punishment in this chapter is thermal, but fire as fuel is never once called punishment. Verse 71 stands in the middle of that distribution and does the sūrah's real work with the element: it lifts fire out of the courtroom into the argument — the same substance that houses the lost is the one each hearer coaxes from wood every evening — and the "consider" asks whether the kindler can keep treating, as a tool, what his own book makes a verdict. The sūrah will draw the line itself at 73, but the line runs, first, through the hearth.

**"You Kindle" and the Light You Will Be Given**

There is one more intra-chapter echo, and it is luminous: at verse 12 the near-rank's reward is that "their light will proceed before them, and so will their right hands" — light going ahead on the Day — and a sūrah that ends its argument-half on kindling has lit that reward from the same verb-family of fire's service. The structure reads as a trade: you are the kindlers now, and on the Day, the kindled precedes you as your certificate — which is exactly what verse 73 then says the fire is, "a reminder," the hearth-flame as memorandum of the other fire, and the sūrah's audience, for whom a fire seen at night on the hamad was the commonest fact of travel, receives its the doctrine of the Last Day in the most familiar optics available: distance, darkness, and a flame you carry. To "consider the fire you kindle" is, in that economy, to ask which of the two fires a person is really walking toward by each one they light.

**The Verse That Invites the Doxology**

Finally, 71 is the question, and 74 is the praise it makes possible — three verses between them, and the space is filled by the only answer the sūrah itself supplies to any of the four considerations (72's "is it you or We" plus 73's "We made it"), which alone distinguishes the fire-unit from its three siblings and prepares "So glorify the Name of your Lord, the Greatest": after the harvest the sūrah demanded thanks, after the fluid belief, after the seed mindfulness — all appeals to the audience — and here, at the last question, the sūrah turns, without waiting for anyone's verdict, and tells God what He is, as if to say: even if no hearer answers 57–71, the kindling fire is already glorified by its Maker's assignment of it, and the sermon's closing doxology is the answer the argument would not receive, given first by the preachers' own throats — al-Wāqiʿah ending its courtroom, at 74, not with a sentence on the defendants but with praise of the Judge, which is the shape worship takes when evidence has been completed and hearts have not yet.

**Kindling, the Qur'an's Verb for Human Effort**

"The fire you kindle" is thus, in the sūrah's own diction, a concession phrased as an indictment: the kindler's role is real and tiny, and verse 71 asks the audience to look exactly at the size. That is why the fire-question is last and why its answer comes fastest — the sūrah saves its verdict for the place where pride has the least to work with.

Lexically, ārā/yūrī is the verb of what a person does to make a fire, and the Book uses the same root when it describes, with quiet irony, humans "kindling" what they cannot create — the listeners' idiom at 71 will therefore echo a wider Qur'anic habit of granting the act's name to the actor and its substance to God, the way the Cave chapter lets a man say "I do not think the Hour will ever come" while the garden's ownership stays, line by line, with its real Owner (18:35–42, the parable this commentary has already cited at the chapter's gardens).
verses.72:
> Is it you who produce its trees, or is it We Who do so

**"Its Trees": Fire's Forgotten Family**

The possessive is the verse's hidden hand: "its tree" — the fire's tree — and the sūrah, asked for the origin of flame, does not answer "lightning" or "flint" but "tree": the kindler's fire belongs, etymologically, to vegetation, and every fire in this audience's world was stored sunlight in tamarisk roots, dried dung over twigs, the desert's only fuel two steps from a plant. That arboreal answer closes a ring the chapter has been building since 27–28 — lote-tree and thorn-apple as Garden and Hell's own flora, seed and sprout as the argument's middle act (63–65) — and 72 now makes the fire, too, a botanical fact: the flame is a tree's hour, and the question "is it you who produce its tree?" quietly relocates the hearth to the field, where the sūrah has already proved nobody is master. The Arabic's singular (shajaratahā) keeps the riddle compact — the fire's tree is any tree, every tree, and none of them theirs.

**"Or We the Producers": The Chapter's One Self-Naming as Creator**

The answer-slot of the disjunction carries, uniquely in this passage, the noun of creation — khāliqūn, "We are the Producers" — the only time al-Wāqiʿah's argument-half lets the divine name for making stand as its own predicate, and its placement is the unit's keystone: at the seed the sūrah said "We cause it to grow" (64, verb), at the rain "We send it down" (69, verb), but at the fire's tree "We are the Producer" — the substantive, the identity. The sūrah's theology of creation, read at its structural peak, is doxology waiting to happen — which is the meaning of this verse's otherwise puzzling escalation of self-naming.

**36:80 — The Sūrah's Twin Verse on Green Fire**

Readers of the sūrahs know the pairing, and it belongs in this entry: "He who produces fire for you from the green tree, and from it you kindle" (the Yā-Sīn sūrah 36:80 — "Who gives you fire from green trees, and — behold! — you kindle fire from them" (56:71's own verb for kindling, re-echoed there) — its parallel line about fire from the wet wood — the ʿarfaj and marakh whose damp kindles when struck, per the sūrahs' botanical glosses). The two chapters say the same thing with the same root, and al-Wāqiʿah's "is it you who produce its tree" is the question whose answer Ya-Sin pronounces as miracle: water in wood, fire out of water, the element's nativity in the driest of lands. A Makkān hearer had no need of philosophy to test it — every tinder-box was the argument, and the green tree's secret combustion was known by name, season, and strike; the sūrah's question does not explain the phenomenon but files it, like the rest of the four considerations, under "We," and its partner-chapter's verse proves that this was a standing Qur'anic move, the hearth as a case in the Book's court of origins.
verses.73:
> We have made it ˹as˺ a reminder ˹of the Hellfire˺ and a provision for the travellers

**Matāʿ: The Sūrah's Own Economic Word for Mercy**

Provision (matāʿ) is not filler; it is the chapter's trade-vocabulary at its most theological, and its near-twin sits in the Abasa sūrah's inventory of care — "a means of sustenance for you and your animals" (80:32), where the same noun names the harvest's purpose across species. Al-Wāqiʿah's matāʿ shares that range: the verb-world of Makkah's market — goods, brief enjoyment, the wayfarer's kit — is conscripted into the sermon to say that what can be sold is, first, what has been given, and that the sūrah's "provision" is a mercy-word wearing a merchant's coat. The commentary has traced the chapter's commercial register through the shade "extended" like credit and the payment-language of 24; verse 73 finishes the job by pricing the unpriceable: the fire's usefulness is not a resource discovered but a commodity issued, and "travellers" are, in that ledger, not owners — the sūrah's audience of traders hear themselves, for once, described the way every trader really is, carrying what was handed out.

**Who Are "the Travellers"?**

The Arabic's noun for them (al-muqṭayn in the sūrahs' common reading) belongs, by the old glosses, either to the picking-up of sticks — the verb of plucking fuel from the wādī — or, by other readers' root, to cutting a route through the land; the sūrahs' lexical committees preserved the range without closing it, and both senses converge on the same figure: the one for whom fire is not infrastructure but gathering. On that uncertainty the verse gains: the traveler is everyone between two homes, which is precisely the sūrah's anthropology — the near-rank are "travellers" in the same breath in which they are heirs (29, 34, "entered the Garden as a reward"), and the whole passage from 75 to 96 will re-confirm it. The classical tellers of the sūrahs' occasions also note the desert's literal rule: fire belongs to no one who stops, and the people of the ḥijāz knew a flame, the way they knew a spring, as something that serves precisely because it is nobody's — verse 73's "provision for the travellers" is, in that idiom, the plainest sentence in the chapter and the most corrosive of ownership, the reminder and the cooking-pot sharing one Arab noun for what the road lends you.

**The Only Answer the Sūrah Gives Itself**

Structuralists of this sūrah will have counted: of the four considerations — semen, seed, water, fire — only the fire-unit contains, after its question, a divine assertion about what the thing is for; the fluid got "will you not believe" (57), the harvest its keening (66–67), the water a threat and an appeal (70), but the fire gets "We have made it a reminder and a provision," a positive assignment with no closer-question attached, as though the sūrah, having run out of courtroom, simply teaches. That asymmetry is the argument-half's finale: the last considered object is the one the chapter can most easily describe whole — it burns, it warns, it feeds, it is owned by nobody — and the doxology at 74 rises naturally from it, since a thing with an assigned double purpose needs an Assigner in the indicative, not in a question. Al-Wāqiʿah's middle thus ends not with a demand on the audience but with a statement about the world's furniture, and the sermon's pivot to the great oath of 75–77 (the stars' settings and the "noble Qurʾān") has been prepared in the only way this chapter knows: one flame, two jobs, and the silence of everyone who has ever sat beside it agreeing, without having wanted to, that the Maker is not kindled but kindles.
verses.74:
> So glorify the Name of your Lord, the Greatest

**The Courtroom Breaks Into Praise**

The argument-half, which began with "We created you — will you not then believe?" (57), ends without a verdict: the sūrah's fourth consideration has been answered, its fire given its double commission (73), and what follows is not a sentence on the deniers but an address to the Messenger — "So glorify." The fāʾ, "so," is the whole verse's logic: praise is the proper close of evidence, the courtroom's last act when the hearts have not yet delivered.

**"The Name," Not the Named**

The verse orders glorification of "the Name of your Lord," and the sūrahs' grammarians debated the idiom — some read "the Name" as lafẓ, an expression for the Lord Himself, since His essence cannot be addressed as an object; others took it literally: the names are what human tongues can say, and sanctifying them (removing every associate's name from them, every idol's claim) is what glorification means in practice. The verse profits from the ambiguity: praise directed at the Name is praise a worshipper can actually perform, and "the Greatest" (al-ʿAẓīm) — the superlative form of the attribute, once more in this chapter at the oath's "great" for a Qurʾān-oath (76) — seals it with the sūrah's own scale: the Event, the tremendous tidings, the loss called great, and now, at the argument's summit, the Greatest, everything in al-Wāqiʿah measured against that one comparative.

**The Same Sentence in the Sūrah of the Most High**

The verse's twin stands one short sūrah away: "Glorify the Name of your Lord, the Most High" (87:1) — the opening of the Aʿlā cycle — and the two lines share almost their whole diction, differing only in the superlative: "the Greatest" here, "the Most High" there, and in position: al-Aʿlā begins where al-Wāqiʿah pauses mid-course. The pairing is the recitation-tradition's own way of teaching this verse — a doxology that opens one sūrah closes twice another — and it lets the commentator name the genre: imperatives of tasbīḥ framed, in this Book, around arguments rather than inside them, as though praise were appointed to stand at the joints where proof ends. Makkans who knew both sūrahs by heart, as the nightly reciters of this one evidently did, would have felt 74 as the same hinge they met at the start of the Most High: the Name, the Lord, the superlative — and the difference between "High" (of His station) and "Greatest" (of His claim) lands, in al-Wāqiʿah's context, on the courtroom: what can be subpoenaed about the world's Maker, after four considerations of semen, seed, water, and fire, is only this — that the Name is set above every share in it. The doxology is the verdict the argument could reach, and no more; the sūrah, in both of its twin verses, declines to reach further, and a chapter that began in earthquake and ends in praise keeps, at its middle, the same shape it keeps at its edges.
verses.75:
> So I do swear by the positions of the stars—

Readers of the sūrahs know the dispute embedded in the line's first syllables: the particle lā before "I swear" has been taken, by the majority of the exegetes, as an oath-intensifier of classical Arabic (the idiom's "lā" of emphasis, leaving the sense "So, indeed, I swear"), and by others as a genuine negation — "I do NOT swear" — directed at the audience's own swearing by the stars, their anwāʾ, the rain-lot of the pre-Islamic calendar that the Qur'an elsewhere confronts (53:19–20's idols and their clientele, at this chapter's verse 59, and the Sijjīl-of-stars theology the Star sūrah answers from its opening: "By the stars when they fade away," 53:1).

**Stars in This Chapter: The Only Sky of the Argument-Half**

Within al-Wāqiʿah itself, verse 75 is the stars' only appearance in the argument — the chapter's skies have been, until here, Last-Day (mountains dusted, the sky split, 5–6 — the sūrah's near-rank dwell under "the expanded shade" and no constellation, and its left under "a column of smoke," 43 — a sky of weather, not of fate) — and the sudden introduction of the stars at the oath is therefore conspicuous: the sūrah admits the stars, briefly and only as witnesses, into a chapter that otherwise refuses them every office, destiny, intercession, or calendar. The structural reading is exact: al-Wāqiʿah has just argued the elements (seed, crop, water, fire) away from the audience's control, and verse 75 takes the last domain of pre-Islamic control — the sky's timetable — and turns it into an oath-slot: the stars do not rule; they testify, and the sūrah's audience, who read fortunes in settings, hear their own science sworn with. From 75 on, the chapter's only vertical reference is to "the Lord of the worlds" (80), and the heavens are reduced, as they are so often in this Book, to furniture with a liturgical function: positions that glorify (74's tasbīḥ includes theirs, in the sense of the Musabbiḥāt's whole grammar, 57:1) — and nothing else.

**"If Only You Knew": The Parenthesis the Verse Has Not Yet Earned**

The oath's weight is not stated here; it is promised in the next line's aside (76, "a great oath — and this, if only you knew"), and the sūrah's order is worth noting: the oath comes first, its grandeur is asserted second, and its reason (the Book) third, a sequence that lets the hearer feel the swelling rather than hear it explained. But 75's half-clause also inherits a small irony from its own parenthesis-to-come: the sūrah will tell this audience they do not know what they are swearing past, and the verse's plain opening — "So I do swear by the positions of the stars" — is thus the most gentle line in the chapter's second half, before the great oath's "if only you knew" grades the audience back to ignorance. Recited slowly, 75 is the sūrah drawing breath: the courtroom has closed (74's praise), the witnesses are being sworn in (the sky's own geometry), and the object on trial has not yet been produced — "this is truly a noble Quran" (77) is the exhibit, and the oath's stars are merely the clerk's candle. Everything the sūrah now says about its own book stands under this asseveration, and the chapter that opened "there is no liar of its falsity" (2) — "none discredits its falsity," the sūrahs' gloss of that opening line — closes its argument with an oath so that its central claim, the Book, may be received with the same certainty that the Event was feared by.
verses.76:
> and this, if only you knew, is indeed a great oath—

**"If Only You Knew": The Chapter's One Concession of Scale**

The parenthesis "law taʿlamūn — if only you knew" is, in the present translation's wording, unique in this sūrah, and its placement is its meaning: the sūrah measures its own oath and finds the audience's knowledge too short for the instrument. The idiom "if only you knew" in this Book opens hoods over facts whose full weight the hearer cannot see — it is the Book's idiom for facts whose full weight a hearer reaches only afterward, the verse-by-verse inventory of the Day given to those who will believe it too late for the knowledge to help — and here it tells the room, before any doctrine, that swearing itself has mass: the sūrah's audience, expert in oaths, in the solemnities of the sanctuary and of the trade-contract, is told that their expertise is the one thing they do not bring to this line. Al-Wāqiʿah's court of evidence thus closes with a confession calibrated to the witnesses' pride — you know oaths; you do not know this one.

**Oaths in This Book: The Grammar of Sworn Worlds**

The Qur'an swears, as its audiences did — by the night when it envelops, the forenoon, the city and its security, the wind in its measure (the short-sūrah register, in paraphrase of the opening oaths of Sūrah al-Layl, al-Ḍuḥā, al-Balad, and the Adhkariyyāt's "the scattering winds," 51:1) — and the objects of its oaths are the same sky and earth the audience read for luck, profit, and weather, retaken for witness. Verse 76 stands inside that habit and names it once: "this is indeed a great oath," the only place in the chapter that comments on the instrument of swearing itself, and the commentary can add the classical observation that the sūrah's oaths are addressed to a people whose oaths were sacred commerce — a tribe that broke a covenant swore, and a town that trusted the stars swore, and a Book that swears by their star-positions inverts both practices at once: God's asseveration is sworn not by the stars' power but by their positions, which is 75's anti-mantic move, here given its liturgical weight: the oath is great because the sworn thing — a noble Book in a guarded Record — is, for the first time in this audience's experience, a fact that cannot be lost, broken, or outvoted.

**What the Oath Is For: The Next Line**

Structurally 76 is a bridge built entirely of load-bearing: the oath's clause ("by the positions") ends with a dash in the present translation — an honest typographical signal that the verse suspends — and the content arrives in 77, "that this is truly a noble Quran," with the asseveration inna carried across from the oath's own emphatic lām. The sūrah thus completes, in two lines, the classical oath-answer form (lā + uqsimu + bi-... + inna...), and the answer's subject is the only candidate the chapter's argument-half left: not resurrection proven, not provision claimed, but the book-in-hand, the sūrah's own recitation, made the sworn matter. Reciters who reach 76 mid-nightprayer should mark that the chapter here names itself for the first time since its opening "the Event" — the sūrah has been about everything except its own status, and now, in the hinge-verse, it swears to it, and the remaining twenty-one verses will be spent, as the sūrah's structure shows, on the Book's purity (79), its origin (80), the audience's commerce with it (81–82), and the death-scene the Book reads at the throat (83–87): the great oath is the chapter's second beginning, and its small parenthesis — if only you knew — is the only warning the sūrah ever gives about the size of what it is asking anyone to hold.
verses.77:
> that this is truly a noble Quran

**Majīd: The Word the Sūrah Applies to Its Own Book**

Noble translates majīd — a root of glory that in classical usage belongs to what is magnificient in itself, not to what is generous toward others (karīm), and the Qur'an uses it of the Book only here and twice beside: "Qāf. By the glorious Quran!" (50:1) and "In fact, this is a glorious Quran" (85:21) — two other late-Makkān sūrahs, two other courtrooms, the same adjective sworn (50) or asserted against the deniers' "glorious" (85, the Broken-Pattern chapter, whose "glorious Quran" follows its oath by "the guarded Tablet" in a sequence this verse and the next will replicate). Al-Wāqiʿah's choice of majīd at the hinge is thus not a compliment but a claim of self-sufficiency: the Book's nobility is intrinsic, unloaned from its audience's reception — and the sūrah, whose entire middle has argued that nothing in the world is owed, applies the same theology to its own text: it is noble, and its honor is the Maker's, touched by none except the purified (79).

**Quran: The Chapter That Means "Recitation"**

The sūrah's self-naming uses the word qurʾān — recitation, the noun of the act, not of the codex — and the choice matters in a chapter whose argument has been, from its first line, about hearing: "when the Event befalls" was announced, not displayed, and the near-rank's reward and the left's doom were each delivered as reportage. Verse 77's "a noble recitation" therefore says that what is sworn to be glorious is the recited speech-in-action — the very sound the congregation is producing — and the sūrahs' lexical essay on the term (qurʾān as the Book's self-designation, read by the ancients alongside its verb qaraʾa, to gather and to recite) fits the hinge's needs: the thing affirmed glorious is not a manuscript (80's "Record" supplies that register) but a living utterance whose dignity is performed in each recitation, and the sūrah's audience — illiterate, commercial, devoted to the spoken — heard at 77 a verdict about the sound of God in their own room, in the present tense, which is what "this is" says, in the Arabic's nominal clause, with no past or future attached.

**The Nobility the Argument-Half Prepared**

It is worth measuring how 77's claim was earned: the sūrah has spent seventeen verses (57–73) removing the audience's ownership of the world's processes, and a book that can do that, in a room, by being said, carries its majīd as an effect of its operation — the nobility asserted at 77 is the sūrah's own CV. The structure answers the mockers' challenge — "will we really be resurrected?" (56:47, in plain echo of the verse's own translation, already argued at this chapter's verses 41–44): they asked for resurrection on their terms, and the sūrah's reply at 77 is procedural — the book that unmans your weather and your wealth is the evidence you actually have, and it is noble. Classical readers of this chapter liked to add the intertext: when the Qur'an elsewhere calls the same Book "a firm rope" and "the decisive speech, not a jest" (the sense of 86:13's four-word contrast, in plain paraphrase), it is al-Wāqiʿah's own register — speech that separates classes, that the near-rank will hear as news from their Lord, and that the left will, too late, have found undecidable. Nobility here is not aesthetic; it is jurisdictional, and the sūrah's argument-half has just handed the court to the Book.
verses.78:
> in a well-preserved Record

**The Record with Its Exact Book-Names**

The family-words — Umm al-Kitāb, Lawḥ Maḥfūẓ, Kitāb Makhnūn — carry one claim with different vault-doors: the recited book has, above recitation, a kept original, and verse 78, in al-Wāqiʿah's courtroom, enters that original as evidence: the oath (75) was sworn "that this is a noble Quran" (77), "in a well-preserved Record" (78), a prepositional clause that says the nobility is not the copy's polish but the archetype's keeping, and the sūrah, by adding the location, answers the charge its audience was living to make — that the Qur'an is Muḥammad's trade (next verses: "how can you take this message lightly, and make denial your livelihood?" — 81–82, in plain echo of their translation) — with provenance: a book with a Record is not a book with a vendor.

**The Sūrah's Own Geography of Heaven**

Al-Wāqiʿah has, since verse 1, kept its sky free of machinery: no thrones described, no heavens enumerated, no angels stationed at gates — its near-rank recline "face to face" (16), their only geography is gardens, springs, and shade, and the one upward motion the chapter allows is the making itself — "We produced you in a form you know not" (61, plain echo of its own line). Verse 78's Record therefore introduces, at the hinge, the chapter's only heaven-furniture: a kept book, "with Us" — in the phrase of the Orchid sūrah (43:4) — and the restraint about the where is itself the sūrah's argument against the mantic sky: the heaven of al-Wāqiʿah is storage, not fortune, and its one archival sentence stands where the audience expected constellations with power.

**The Only Record in a Chapter Without Books**

One structural note this verse earns by its rarity: the word for the heavenly register (kitāb, "Record") appears, in this chapter, only here — and readers of the sūrah's Day will feel what that means, because al-Wāqiʿah's the doctrine of the Last Day, unlike its neighbors', stages no distribution of books at all: the Ḥāqqah's and Inshirāḥ's right-hand-and-left-hand scenes of scrolls are absent, and this chapter sorts its classes by fire, shade, water, and fruit alone. The sūrah thus keeps, for itself, the only record its economy contains — and its reward-language is accordingly the plainest in the Book: "a reward for what they used to do" (24), payment by the standard of works, with no ledger-scene attached. Verse 78 puts, in the middle of that ledger-less courtroom, the one filing-cabinet the chapter acknowledges — the well-preserved Record — and the contrast is its quietest claim: every other sūrah of the Event shows you your book handed out; al-Wāqiʿah shows only its own Book handed down, filed before it was written on you. Readers of both testaments of this chapter's Day will notice that the sūrah has, in one prepositional clause, made revelation the only document in the room.

The sūrah's phrase for the Book's location — a well-preserved Record (kitāb makhnūn) — belongs to a small family of Qur'anic self-names for revelation's archive: "in the Master Record with Us — highly esteemed, rich in wisdom" (43:4, the Orchid sūrah's idiom of "Mother of the Book" here supplied with its "with Us"), and, in the Broken-Pattern chapter that swears like this one, "in a Preserved Tablet, recorded" (85:21–22, whose "glorious Quran" line this commentary cited at 77).

The Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary, which the Star sūrah sets near revelation's descent (53:13–16, in the other chapter's plain account), does duty in the neighbor-chapter where al-Wāqiʿah keeps silence — and the effect on a Makkān ear is measurable: the sky that cast rain-lots (this commentary at 59 and 69) is here demoted to a shelving-system belonging to the Lord who sends, and nothing in it dispenses anything at all.
verses.79:
> touched by none except the purified ˹angels˺

Verse 79 now says what those scenes assumed: the holy and its bearers are in contact only with the clean, and the boys "like preserved pearls (luʾluʾ maknūn)" (18) — the same adjective as the Record (makhnūn, 78) — are themselves kept, veiled, untouched by the world's dust.

**"None Touch It": The Negative That Protects the Exhibit**

The clause's function in the courtroom is evidentiary before it is ritual: the sūrah has sworn by the stars' positions that "this is a noble Quran" (75–77), lodged it in "a well-preserved Record" (78), and verse 79 now forecloses the only remaining attack on the exhibit's integrity — that it was touched by what it denies, jinn, soothsayers, or the marketplace. The sūrah has already told that story once: "Shall I inform you upon whom the devils descend?

**Purity as the Chapter's Recurring Grammar**

Al-Wāqiʿah has been a sūrah of clean and unclean since its first description: the recompense is "as if of pearl, preserved" — the luʾluʾ maknūn line (18, re-cited) — the lost drink "boiling water" and "shaded smoke," and the near-rank's furniture is untouchable by decay in the chapter's own terms — no idle or sinful talk heard there (25, the line's plain sense), no headache from the cup (19) — and the lost, by contrast, get boiling water and a column of smoke (42–43). Into this system verse 79 adds its rule without legislating it: the Book's world is a hygiene, not an ordinance — the only Qur'anic sūrah to state that holiness is untouchable states it as description, like a property of the material, and the sūrahs of the chapter's etiquette read the description as law precisely because, in this sūrah, the two are the same utterance: what God keeps, the worshipper may not approach unwashed, and the mushaf's later physical rules are, in this chapter's logic, the extension of the Record's own physics. That is why 79's double reading (angels or ablution) has survived fourteen centuries without either side winning: the sūrah itself never separates the two purities.

Read for the ˹angels˺ gloss alone, verse 79 completes a scene the chapter has drawn twice before in other words: the near-rank are served by "young boys round about them, like preserved pearls" (17–18), and the sūrah's own idiom for the heavenly touch already ran, at this commentary's verses 7–10, through the angels' charge over every soul (in the sense of the Rays' "appointed in succession," 13:10–11 and 86:4 — plain paraphrases, cited earlier).

They reveal a whisper to most of the liars" (26:221–222, in the Poets' plain account — this chapter's oracle-denunciation at 59's environment), and 79 gives the flip-side: the Qurʾān's channel is, by contrast, touch-proof, and the sūrah's audience — who judged every poem by the jinn at its poet's elbow, the familiar jinn at the poet's elbow, a literary forensics of the age this commentary names but does not quote — hear their own literary forensics turned back on them: you know how to detect a tainted book; this one is certified by the manner of its untouchedness.
verses.80:
> ˹It is˺ a revelation from the Lord of all worlds

**"The Lord of All Worlds": The Chapter's One Full Title**

In al-Wāqiʿah the phrase appears exactly once — at this verse, on the present translation's text — and its placement turns the whole argument-half into an exercise in lordship: every consideration was a question about who does what ("is it you… or is it We"), and 80 names the answer's office in the sūrah's only complete divine title: "Lord of all worlds." The sūrah's other addresses are intimate (the repeated "your Lord" of 74 and 96, the doxologies), and this is the single moment the chapter widens — the Event (1) has, by the hinge, been shown to be the act of the Lord, not of a tribe's god, and the four considerations' world (semen to fire) is the property of all the worlds, which is why the sūrah's classes (near, right, left) run the whole of humanity and not Makkah alone. Readers who have followed the chapter from its first "when" will feel the title as a summing: the day that levels mountains and sorts every soul into three lists is, at its middle, declared to be the jurisdiction of the Lord of all worlds, and the sūrah's self-description at 80 is thus also its verdict on the mockers' parochial afterlife (the left's "and our forefathers as well?" — 48, in the chapter's own quotation of its mockers) — their hour belonged to their clan; this one belongs to every world.

**26:192–194: The Verse's Unfinished Mechanism, Completed Next Door**

The Poets' sūrah carries this sūrah's line almost letter for letter — "This is certainly a revelation from the Lord of all worlds, which the trustworthy spirit [Gabriel] brought down into your heart" (26:192–194, in the present translation's idiom) — and the pairing is the sūrah's own commentary: al-Wāqiʿah's bare "revelation from" is, in the neighbor, given its bearer and its destination (the heart), so that the two chapters together state the doctrine in full: origin in the Lord of all worlds, channel in the faithful spirit, terminus in the Prophet's heart, purpose in warning. The shared wording is also a shared context of accusation — both chapters speak it where the audience suspects commerce or invention — and the classical readers loved to note that tanzīl verses of this form cluster precisely at the points of attack, as if the Qur'an's self-certification were, structurally, a wound-dressing: here at 80, the chapter's exhibit is given, in one line, the sender and the manner, before the sermon turns, at 81, to the audience's unacceptable response ("how can you take this message lightly, and make denial your livelihood?" — 81–82, plain quotation of the two lines' translation), and the reader who compares the chapters will find al-Wāqiʿah's 80 the shorter cousin, which is its own kind of force: the hinge of this sūrah has no room for the mechanism, only for the origin — and Makkah's accusation, "he fabricated it," was answered best, in the chapter's scale of values, by the fact of descent itself.

**The Verse Between Doxology and Indictment**

Architecturally, 80 stands between the doxology of 74 and the indictment of 81–82 — between "glorify the Name of your Lord, the Greatest" and "how can you take this message lightly" — and one sentence of the two rabb clauses of its own (the doxology's "your Lord" and 80's "Lord of all worlds") is the sūrah's whole pivot from worship to complaint: praise is directed at the very Being whose book is being made a commodity, and the indictment lands with its full weight only because 80 has first established the book's provenance. Al-Wāqiʿah's sermon, in other words, does not scold the Makkān traders for trading; it first swears (75–77), archives (78), purifies (79), and authenticates (80) the thing traded, and only then asks — in the chapter's final "how can you" (81) — how a commodity of that origin can be handled the way they handle it, with denial as its price. The verse is thus the small hinge on the sūrah's largest late turn, from argument about nature to argument about the Book, and every reader who reaches 96's repeated "glorify the Name of your Lord, the Greatest" will have passed, at 80, the line where the sūrah's subject changed — nature became news, and news became the news itself, descended from, and about, the Lord of all worlds.

The word (tanzīlun) is a verbal noun of the intensive pattern of "sending down in stages," and its choice matters: not the bare "sent" (arsalā, the apostle's verb, which the Qur'an reserves for messengers rather than books) but the layered descent that its own audience's complaint had made a technical term — "if only an angel had been sent down with it" (the objection, in the idiom of 25:7, plain paraphrase), and the sūrahs note that tanzīl answers the how: a book sent in pieces, verse by verse, over years, is not a book dropped whole from a desk in heaven, and the sūrah, by preferring the word of gradual descent, makes its own mode of delivery part of the claim of origin.
verses.81:
> How can you then take this message lightly

**Ḥadīth: The Sūrah's Self-Name, Here and at the Star-Sūrah's Rebuke**

The present translation's "message" is the Book's word ḥadīth — in its ordinary Arabic, "new talk," and in the Qur'an's own usage, regularly the Qur'an speaking about itself as an event of speech (the idiom is decisive at 52:34 and, for this verse's exact neighbor, at 53:59, where the Star sūrah asks "Do you find this revelation astonishing?" — the same deictic phrase "this ḥadīth," in the present translation's diction, and the same rebuke-context). Al-Wāqiʿah's 81 thus borrows a self-designation the sūrahs had already made accusatory: the Book is a ḥadīth, a new thing said, and the verb that follows — "take it lightly," rendered in the older sūrahs as "treat it as trivial," a verb whose sūrahs' glosses run to making a thing sport and distraction — describes, in the classical glosses, precisely the Makkān manner of meeting the sūrah: not refutation but deflection, the laugh that will not answer. The sūrah's audience is indicted, in 81, not for disbelief argued but for demeanor: the chapter that spent seventeen verses asking them to consider the world has arrived, at the Book itself, at the simplest charge — you handle this as you handle nothing you believe.

**The Crime Is a Manner**

Read against the chapter's opening courtroom (2: "no soul will deny its truthfulness"), 81 shows what disbelief costs in this sūrah's anthropology: not a creed rejected in good faith but a tone adopted toward a message — "taking lightly" is a register of the self, the shrug, and the sūrah, which has described the left's whole sin as mockery at dinner (47, "they used to ask mockingly," in the present translation's bracket), returns, at the hinge, to its first charge against the audience's manners. This is late-Makkān preaching at its characteristic best: no philosophical objection is entertained because none was the real problem; the sūrah's hearers did not disprove resurrection, they yawned at it — and the commentary may cite, in this sūrah's own idiom, the Book's sharpest parallel, the "will not weep, but laugh" (53:60, in the Star sūrah's plain sequence just quoted): al-Wāqiʿah and al-Najm, side by side, put the human problem not in theology but in the face's choice between tears and the smile at news of that weight.

**Laughter, Weeping, and the Chapter's Own Economy of Sound**

Al-Wāqiʿah has, since verse 1, staged a world of sound: the right's greeting of peace — 91, "Greetings to you from the people of the right" — in the sūrah's own salutation, the keening of the harvest-lamenters (66–67, already argued here), the "no idle or sinful talk" of the Garden (25) — and verse 81's "take lightly" enters that soundscape as its worst register, the laugh the sūrah will answer, at 87, with the bare question "if you are truthful, why not pull the soul back?", which is the rhetorical form of shame's silence: not weeping, not laughing, but the choked arithmetic of the dying throat. The sūrah's judgment, across that arc, is acoustic: Makkah's problem is what it does with the voices it has (mocking at 47, keening at 66, trivializing at 81), and the Garden is what it hears will, at last, be free of all three: a people with no idle talk, no need of lament, and no occasion for the shrug, which is to say that the sūrah's ethics of the voice is, in al-Wāqiʿah, indistinguishable from its the doctrine of the Last Day.
verses.82:
> and repay ˹Allah for˺ your provisions with denial

**"Make Your Livelihood Denial": The Verse's Devastating Idiom**

The present translation's "repay… with denial" renders an Arabic more merciless than its English: tajʿalūna rizqa-kum an tukadhdhibū — "you make your rizq (your livelihood, your portion, your daily bread) to be that you call the Book a lie," and the sūrah, which has spent its whole middle arguing rizq through the grain (63–65), the water (68–70), and fire's provision for travelers (73), arrives here at the sūrah's final exchange-rate: these people have bartered sustenance itself for denial — they eat provision and pay for it with kufr, the root's double sense (ingratitude and disbelief) fused in a way the commentary has been tracking since verse 14. The idiom answers, from the other side, the keening farmers of 66–67, who called the lost harvest "great loss" and themselves "deprived": the living Makkān, says 82, are making deprivation their daily profession — they receive rizq and render back denial, and the bracket ˹Allah for˺ in the present line names, correctly, the one creditor they are actually dealing with. Verse 82 is thus the market-sūrah's closing invoice, the chapter's commercial register (shade like credit, payment "for what they used to do," 24) arriving at its last and worst transaction.

**Rizq as the Chapter's Buried Subject, Now Named**

The chapter's entire argument-half has been a rizq-tract without the word until now: "We made it a provision (matāʿ) for the travellers" (73), the farmers' ˹livelihood˺ bracket at 67, the "fruit and fodder" theology the Abasa sūrah shares with 73's provision-language (80:31–32) — and at 82 the noun rizq arrives, unannounced, in the mouth of the Book's accusation, which is the sūrah's subtlest move: it reveals, at the hinge's end, that its long argument about semen, seed, rain, and fire was not about "nature" but about rizq, provision, the daily givenness of what the audience had made light of as news. The classical readers of this verse drew exactly this conclusion — that the sūrah couples the two unbeliefs, calling God's book a lie and living on His rizq while doing it — and the pairing indicts, in one clause, a piety of the table that ignores a claim of the revelation: a Makkān could reject Muhammad's ḥadīth and still, each dawn, receive the water that could have been salt (70), and 82 says these two receipts are one ledger. To "make your livelihood denial" is, in that light, the most literal description the chapter ever gives of the audience's religion: they are, at breakfast, eating kufr.

**"Denial," Not Unbelief: The Sūrah's Charge Is Verbal**

What the sūrah's verb indicts is takdhīb — calling it a lie, the act of the tongue that 81's "take lightly" set up — and not a concluded denial of the heart; that verbal nuance is the chapter's final pastoral severity: the audience's problem began as manner (the shrug at 81) and ends as speech-act ("He fabricated it," the charge recorded elsewhere of this exact audience, 25:4 and 46:7's "this is nothing but a fabrication of earlier times" in plain paraphrase — the same noun, in the other chapters' mouths, that 82's tukadhdhibūn is answering). Al-Wāqiʿah, uniquely, declines to quote the charge and instead names its verb — you make denial your livelihood — and the effect is that the sūrah never lets its hearers the dignity of a proposition rejected; their position is described as a transaction, repeated daily, in which the commodity is their bread and the coin is "lie," and the commentary has already seen, at 41–48, that the left's sins were listed in the same commercial order (devouring, denying, until the certainty came, 46–48's sequence). The chapter's verdict on Makkah's dispute with the Book is that it was never a dispute; it was a trade in which they were paid in what they refused.
verses.83:
> Why then ˹are you helpless˺ when the soul ˹of a dying person˺ reaches ˹their˺ throat

**"Why Then": The Question That Ends the Court**

The chapter's last interrogative is the shortest form Arabic has for a rebuke: fa-law lā — "why then do you not" — a compound of the conditional and the negation that the sūrahs' grammarians gloss as "then why do you not do it," and the sūrah, which has asked in turn about belief (57), mindfulness (62), and thanks (70), now asks the one question that convicts by grammar alone: if this Book were nothing, and you were nothing but yourselves, why do you not, at this throat, do something? The scene is chosen for the exactness of its helplessness: at no moment in the human calendar is the audience's advertised autonomy — the self-possession implicit in "is it you who create it, or We?" (59) — so visibly suspended as at the deathbed, where the strongest hand present does nothing but hold the wrist. Verse 83 is therefore the argument-half's final verdict, delivered as a question: the courtroom of semen, seed, water, and fire closes at the throat, because it is the throat where every plea the chapter refused to entertain — that persons own their lives — comes to trial honestly, once, for everybody, and loses.

**The Soul at the Throat: The Sūrah's One Anatomy**

The idiom (al-nafs balagha al-ḥulqūm, "the soul reached the throat") is the Qur'an's fixed image for dying, and it names a location the living body knows from the inside — the lump, the constriction, the swallow that fails — and al-Wāqiʿah, whose whole argument has been built from what Makkah knows by heart — the ejected fluid of 58, the reaped harvest of 63, the drunk water of 68 — ends on the throat's last passage. The sūrahs' readers of the verse kept the physical vocabulary: al-ḥulqūm is the windpipe itself, and the soul's "reaching" it is, in the sūrahs' tellings, the moment of the taking, the point at which the departing becomes observable and no longer reversible. The sūrah's choice of this anatomy is also its final theology of the body: after the mockers' demand to be "restored to our former state, even after decayed bones" (79:10–11, in the other sūrah's plain report), the sūrah says: your first restoration is happening, hourly, in the room next to this one — no bones required, only breath failing, and the throat as the last door every argument about resurrection must pass through, whether the debater likes it or not.

**The Verse the Chapter Answers with Its Final Sorting**

Structurally, 83 is the hinge between the Book's trial (75–82) and the classes' exits (88–96), and its placement states the sūrah's last doctrine plainly: the Qur'an and the soul are the same jurisdiction — the book that none may touch except the purified (79) and the soul that none may call back except its Owner are held by the same "We" (85, next verse but one), and the chapter's two late subjects, revelation and death, meet at this line. The mockers had asked, at the chapter's own dinner-table, "when we die and become dust and bones, will we really be resurrected?" (47, re-echoed from the chapter's quotation of them), and verse 83 answers their form of the question by moving the scene from the grave to the bedside: the return they mocked is, before it is a resurrection, this — a soul at a throat, a room of hands that do nothing — and the sūrah's sermon will not proceed past this verse to verdicts (88–96) until the room has been described, because in al-Wāqiʿah's arithmetic no argument about the Book's nobility (77) and no claim about the audience's trade (82) is complete until the dying person has been laid, anonymous, between them, and the reciter asked why they are standing there with empty hands.
verses.84:
> while you are looking on

**"Looking On" and "You Cannot See": The Chapter's Twin Verbs of Sight**

Verse 84 hands the audience sight and verse 85 takes it away — "but you cannot see" — and the pair is al-Wāqiʿah's final epistemology: looking on is the humans' true report (you are watching the body), not-seeing is their true limit (you are watching a taking you do not see), and the sūrah lets both stand in consecutive lines as a single lesson about what presence is. The sūrahs' glosses supply the standard explanation of the contrast: the bystanders see the dying and do not see the angels, the soul, the scene of the taking — "you see what is happening to the body; you do not see who is doing it" — and the rhetorical gain for the sermon is decisive: the mockers' sneer at the unseen ("will we really be resurrected?" — 47, in the chapter's own quotation) dies at the throat not by proof but by proximity, because the room at every death contains exactly one unseen fact, and everyone in the room knows, hourly, that it is there, being executed by hands they cannot name. Al-Wāqiʿah's resurrection-argument, its most contested claim, ends, at 84–85, with the ordinary witness of rooms that the unseen is real.

**What the Verse Withholds: No Angels Here, Yet**

The commentators must also mark an absence: verse 84 does not yet say who is taking the soul — that is 85's "We are nearer" — and several sūrahs note that the angels of death, familiar elsewhere in the Book ("It is the angels who take the souls of the disbelievers, striking their faces and their backs," in the plain sense of 8:50, and "Our messengers take him, and they are not negligent," at 6:61, quoted already at this chapter's 83), are, in al-Wāqiʿah, left entirely behind the verse's curtain: the sūrah's dying-room has human eyes only, and its unseen is unnamed until the next line. The restraint serves the argument: the chapter has spent its middle insisting that the audience's own sciences (semen, harvest, rain, fire) are agencies of God they do not see, and 84 keeps the same method to the last — the death scene is told as the body's fact, not the angels' spectacle — so that when 85 finally introduces the nearer We, it arrives not as mythology added to medicine but as the medicine's own missing half, the sentence the watching was already shaped to receive, and the sūrahs of the afterlife's details (the striking, the questioning in the grave, the long reports of the collections) are, here, respectfully, entirely absent: al-Wāqiʿah's the doctrine of the Last Day is a sūrah of bare, terrible proximities, not of wonders.

**The Line That Makes the Next One Inevitable**

Thus 84's two words — "you looking on" — exist to arm 85's "We nearer than you," the comparative that has made this verse-pair one of the Qur'an's most quoted: the bystanders' nearness is real (they are at the bed, they see the throat) and it is being measured, at 85, against a nearer — and nothing in the chapter has yet been measured without losing to God. The pair is also, in the sermon's arithmetic, the final inversion of the mockers' dinner-talk: they had asked to be sent back in the forefathers' state (47–48); the sūrah's answer is that no one at a throat can even be sent forward, and the only agency present belongs to the One whose nearness the watchers cannot see. Verse 84, read in that position, is the hinge of the whole sūrah's last movement: the room (84), the nearer We (85), the challenge to return the soul (86–87), and then the exits (88–96) — and a commentary on this line should end where the line ends, with the audience's own eyes, since the chapter has, at the last, nothing left to say about them that is not true: they are all, at some hour, verse 84, looking on, and what they most need the sūrah to say about that looking is what it says next, about the One who was nearer than all of them, before any of them arrived.
verses.85:
> And We are nearer to such a person than you, but you cannot see

**"But You Cannot See": The Chapter's Final Epistemic Clause**

The closing words — "but you do not see" — repeat, at the throat, the refrain the sūrah has run under every consideration: "a form you do not know" (60), "if only you knew" (76), and now "you cannot see" — and their cumulative function is to teach the audience the shape of the word "near" in this Book: nearness without sight is the normal condition of the world (61–64), and death adds only the degree. The clause also completes 84's pair — "you are looking on… but you cannot see" — and the paradox is doctrine, not poetry: the room sees the body and does not see the taking; the sūrah's hearers, who wanted resurrection argued in dust and bones (47's sneer), are answered with the plainest fact available, that the unseen is not at the far end of a syllogism but at the near end of a bed, and the "but" of the clause is the chapter's last, quiet word about human instruments: your eyes were open at the right time and are still, here, useless — which al-Wāqiʿah treats as news about seeing, not about dying.

**Two Nearnesses: The Sūrahs' Own Readings**

The first reads "We are nearer" by way of the angels — the "Our" of the taking is God's command executed by the angels of death, whose office the Book states elsewhere in plain terms ("Our messengers take him, and they are not negligent," 6:61, quoted here as earlier at 83, and the striking hands of 8:50, in the Spoils sūrah's plain account) — a reading that suits the sūrah's refusal elsewhere to name machinery (at 84 above, the angels are unseen here too). Either way the verse's function in al-Wāqiʿah is identical — it transfers the action of the deathbed from the watchers to the Owner of the soul — and that transfer, not the metaphysics of proximity, is what the sermon has been building its whole middle toward.

**The Predicate That Replaces the Challenge**

Formal readers will notice the turn: through 57–73 every "or is it We" took a verb of making (We create, We grow, We send down, We produce), and at 85 the divine answer-predicate changes to an adjective — not "We take it" but "We are nearer" — and the change of register is the sūrah pivoting from courtroom to scene: the argument asked who does what, and the dying-room says only whose presence is prior. The "We" of the four considerations, in other words, becomes at 85 the "We" that is already there, and the effect on the chapter's theology is profound in a single word: God's agency in the seed and the rain (64, 69) was asserted as making; here it is asserted as nearness, which is the sūrah's way of saying that the two are the same — to make a thing is to be nearer to it than anyone, and the dying, at whom every hand arrived too late, are the standing proof. This is the only verse in al-Wāqiʿah in which God predicates Himself of a scene rather than acting in it, and that restraint is the chapter's last word about the Event's God: the Event was never an arrival; it is a discovery of what was nearer first, which is why the doxologies at 74 and 96 can sit, at either end of the whole final third, without any verdict in between being needed.

"Qarībun aqrabu minkum" — nearer than you — is the sūrah's only comparative of divine station, and its precision should be felt: the measure is not "nearer than his jugular vein," which is the other sūrah's figure for God's relation to a person in life (50:16, "We are nearer to him than his jugular vein," quoted here in the present translation's idiom), but nearer than you — nearer than the closest family hand, the physician, the son holding the pillow — and the dying man is, at 85, the point of comparison rather than the object.
verses.86:
> Now, if you are not subject to Our Will ˹as you claim˺

**The Conditional at the Bedside**

Al-Wāqiʿah's sermon had run on questions since verse 57, and at 86 it abandons even questioning for a conditional: "Now, if you are not subject to Our Will — then bring it back (87)" — the challenge-form of the Book's other great disputes (the Cow's "produce a sūrah like it… if what you say is true," 2:23, and the Jonah chapter's shorter dare, 10:38, both quoted here in the present translation's idiom), transported from the literary arena to the dying-room, where no one has ever performed it.
