The grammar matters for the whole chapter's trajectory: the mockers had demanded resurrection be proved to their taste (47), and the sūrah now grants them, hypothetically, the one doctrine under which no proof is needed and none is possible — that they answer to no one — and stakes everything on its corollary: if no Lord, no reckoning, and no reckoning, then the soul at the throat is yours to call back, and the verse hangs its "if" open in front of a room that cannot fill it, the gentlest way a book has of executing an argument by experience.

**"Madīnūn": The Word with Two Reckonings**

The Arabic's single adjective (from m-d-n) was preserved by the sūrahs' lexicographers with two construals, and the verse is stronger for carrying both. The first is the one the present translation chooses — "subject to Our Will," read as not being reckoned, answerable, judged (the dīn-family's office: "you are not being requited," so free of a Lord in the claim) — and the sūrahs' readers also transmitted, as the plainest sense for this verse, "if you are not maintained": madīn as the one whose sustenance is spent on him, the kept, the provided-for — the same audience's own livelihood-word (rizq at 82), turned back on them as a conditional: if you are not, at any rate, kept — and both senses are answered by one scene, because the soul at the throat is neither reckoned with by the watchers nor maintained by them. That the verse holds judgment and provision in one word is al-Wāqiʿah's last theology: to be judged and to be fed are the same Lord's offices, and the audience's pretended autonomy ("as you claim") is, in this sūrah's physics, the single error of denying both — a point the brackets of the present line (˹as you claim˺) mark, in the Book's idiom for zaʿm, an assertion without a witness.

**The Sūrah's Last Concession**

Formally, 86 is the argument-half's final grant — the chapter that had refused its hearers credit for semen, crop, rain, and fire now refuses them, provisionally, even the one sovereignty they thought they kept for themselves (the sovereignty of the unaccountable), by conceding it hypothetically to expose its poverty: "if you are not subject to Our Will" — suppose it true; the only visible consequence is the impotence of verse 87, and the sūrah has thus, in two verses, executed the classical reductio: the autonomy that cannot reverse a dying is not worth arguing against, only exhibiting. The commentators will note that this is the same method, in miniature, as the chapter's opening: the Event arrives, "its falsity no soul will deny" (2), and every position is tested at the point where it would have to act — semen that cannot choose its shape (59–60), water that cannot refuse its salt (70), and here a will that cannot hold the soul it claims to own — and al-Wāqiʿah closes its long argument, at 86, exactly as it began its whole sermon: by putting its hearers, not in a debate, but in a scene, with their doctrine in their hands and a dying person between them, and asking them — one last, last time, softly, in an "if" — to do with it what they promised themselves they could do.
verses.87:
> bring that soul back, if what you say is true

**An Imperative Nobody Has Ever Obeyed**

Urdidūhā — "bring back that soul" — is the only imperative the sūrah ever addresses to its deniers, and its content is a command to reverse the one process the chapter has spent its whole middle declaring sovereign: if you own nothing in the making (57–73) but your claim to be unaccounted for (86), exercise that ownership at the throat, now, on this one soul, and return it to the body it has just left. The sūrahs' readers marked the form: divine challenges in this Book come in escalating generosity — produce a sūrah like it (2:23), ten (the Hūd chapter's dare), or call witnesses to help (10:38, both in the present translations' wording) — and al-Wāqiʿah's is the shortest and the most local: no literary performance, no assembly, only the reversal of a dying in the room you are standing in. A challenge measured to the strength of the opponents' actual position — "if what you say is true" — and the sūrah, by accepting no substitute deed, makes the verse's silence (no one ever has, anywhere) the last testimony in the courtroom: the chapter does not need to refute the claim of the unaccountable; it hands the claim the only instrument its own doctrine recognizes, the will, at the only scene where the will is on parade, and lets the failure speak.

**"That Soul": The Demonstrative's Intimacy**

Arabic's hādhihi — "this/that" — points, and pointing at a death is different from speaking about deaths: the sūrah has said "the soul" (83) and "such a person" (85) in the general case, and at 87 the grammar comes close, "bring back that soul," the one now in the room, now at the throat of the person whose pillow the strongest bystander is holding. Al-Wāqiʿah, which began by denying that any soul would disbelieve the Event (2: "no soul will deny its truthfulness"), ends its argument by staging a scene in which everyone present, believers and mockers alike, believes one thing with equal clarity: the soul has gone, and it is not coming back, and the "that" of verse 87 is where the chapter finally catches its audience — in a certainty they share with each other, in a room, over a body, before any doxology tells them what to do with it.

**"If What You Say Is True": The Sūrah's Own Truth-Test**

The formula "in kuntum ṣādiqīn" — "if what you say is true" — appears, in this Book, almost always attached to a dare (at the Cow's verse quoted above and the Jonah chapter's, but its cousin-noun sits in this chapter's own opening: "no soul will deny its truthfulness (takdhīb)" at 2, the very noun the mockers were charged with making their livelihood at 82), and its placement at 87 completes a ring that has been running since verse 2: the chapter opens with the Event that nobody can disbelieve, and closes its challenge with the truth-test nobody can pass — and between the two, the sūrah has defined truth-telling, in its own vocabulary, as the only thing the human will has ever reliably been able to perform: consider, admit, thank, glorify — the four small verbs of 57, 62, 70, 74. To "bring that soul back" is the one act that would make the claimants' cosmology true, and the sūrah, at 87, is not asking them to perform it; it is asking them, one last time, to tell the truth about it — to say, looking at the throat, "this was never mine" — which is, in al-Wāqiʿah's entire moral world, the exact sentence that opens the door of the people of the right, three verses from here, and the only sentence the deniers of 47–48 had spent their whole lives, at every bedside they attended, refusing to say.
verses.88:
> So, if the deceased is one of those brought near ˹to Us˺

**The Participle of the Brought-Near, Read After the Verse of Nearness**

The double vocabulary is the hinge of the whole chapter's theology of proximity: near to all as Lord, near to some as welcome — and the dying person of 83–87, whose throat was about to be the scene of the universal nearness, is now, at 88, addressed in the possibility of the particular: which nearness did your life befriend? The sūrah does not say "if he was noble" or "if he was pious"; it says "of the brought-near," a phrase whose passive forces the reader to ask by Whom — and the whole argument-half already answered: only the One whose first-person verbs owned the semen, the crop, the rain, and the fire can bring near, and can refuse to.

**"If He Was": The Conditional That No Longer Challenges**

The sorting-clauses of 88, 90, and 92 all open with "fa-ammā in kāna" — "as for, if he was" — and the conditional particle, at this late point in the chapter, is doing something new with its old work: 86 had used "if" to test a claim ("if you are not subject to Our Will, bring the soul back"), and 88–92 use "if" to sort a file — the difference is between a dare and a verdict, and the sūrah's grammar marks its own transition: the room where the challenge rang (87) is the room whose occupant is now conditionally classified, and nobody is being asked to perform anything anymore. The commentators will note that the Arabic of these verses contains no verb but "was" (kāna) — the copula of settled identity, not of act — and that this is the last verb the sūrah will lend its classes: everything they did has collapsed, at the throat, into what they were, and the sūrah's ethics of habit (it has repeated "they used to" (kānū) again and again, in the left's "they used to ask mockingly" at 47 and the right's "they used to do" at 24) arrives at its tense: past, complete, and, on this side of the verdict, final. "If he was" is the sūrah's plainest and most terrible question, because it asks what has, by definition, stopped being answerable by new action.

**"One of" — Partitive Mercy in a Chapter of Lists**

The phrase "one of the brought-near (min al-muqarrabīn)" uses the partitive "min," and the sorting at 88, 90, and 92 all run on it — a dying person is "one of" a class — and that small grammar has earned its commentaries: the sūrahs read the partitive as the sūrah's mercy on the individual, since "of" allows a man to be counted without being totalled, a servant to be among the near despite himself, and the later schools — pressed by their own doctrines of assurance — debated whether a believer may testify "I am one of the people of Paradise" and often answered that the sūrah's own grammar permits humility and hope at once: every "if he was" is a fact only God verifies, and every "one of" is a company wide enough for the imperfect.
verses.89:
> then ˹such a person will have˺ serenity, fragrance, and a Garden of Bliss

**Three Nouns With No Verbs: The Welcome as Pure Gift**

The apodosis of the near-rank branch is three words — fa-riḥun wa-rayḥānun wa-jannatu naʿīm — and the sūrah, which has spent its whole final third attaching rewards to verbs of past service ("a reward for what they used to do," 24; "We shall requite," in its repeated idiom of giving-back), gives its highest class, at the throat, three bare nouns and no sentence: rest, fragrance, garden — a welcome, not a wage. The grammarians of the sūrahs read the nominal clause as immediacy: the dying muqarrab does not receive after the Day; what arrives at 89 arrives now, at the moment the soul reaches the throat (83), before reckoning, in the sūrah's own compressed time in which the Event and the dying are the same verb. And the near-rank's estate, unlike the right's in the chapter's earlier panorama (28–34), has no furniture listed here at all — the sūrah reserves its orchards, spouses, and cushions for a different register — because the entry of the nearest is a greeting scene, and the commentary's long observation at this chapter's first description of them (11–14) found the same subtraction: the nearer the class, the fewer the nouns.

**"Jannata Naʿīm": The Garden Word and the Question It Will Ask**

Bliss translates naʿīm — the noun of soft, untroubled living — and the sūrah's audience met its family at 45: the left were "spoiled by luxury (mutrafīn)" (45) in the life before, and the naʿīm of the near-rank is the same root's honest form: luxury become gift, softness become garden, the wealth Makkah worshipped re-sown for those who were not worshipped by it. Al-Wāqiʿah does not pose that question at 89 — the near-rank are past questioning — but by naming naʿīm it files the saved under the verse the whole community lives by: what you were asked about, you were given; what you were not thanked for, was taken; and the Garden of Bliss is the naʿīm of the Guest of God, not the spoiling of the mutraf — the same softness twice, once owned and lost, once received and eternal.

**"Then such a person will have…" — The Sūrah's Third-Person Pity and Honor**

The pronoun is the last the chapter will use for the dying: "such a person" — the sūrah, having addressed the whole room in the second person through 87 ("you are looking on… if you are not subject to Our Will… bring it back"), now returns to the third person, and the shift has a double edge worth marking: the near-rank die in the middle of an address — the sermon turns from the watchers to the man, and the man is no longer spoken to, only about, by the room — and the sūrah keeps even its honors in that oblique case, because al-Wāqiʿah's the doctrine of the Last Day is, formally, reportage: what is said of a person after they can no longer hear it said, said well, in the past-tense conditional (88) and the future-of-the-noun (89), is the sūrah's entire theory of the last words. The commentators who read this line at the dying — the bedside practice traced above, in the lore recorded at 23, 26, 83, and 84 — are, by the sūrah's own grammar, doing what the sermon does at 88–89: speaking over, not to, and letting the three nouns be the whole of what the room may affirm. There is no verse in this chapter that consoles a mourner more precisely, and none that a sūrah could more honestly place at the end of a sermon about ownership: at the throat, the dying are, at last, only what was said about them, and al-Wāqiʿah makes sure the sentence begins "rest.".

The word rayḥān has stood, in this sūrah's earlier passage, at the cups of the near-rank — "and fragrance (rayḥān), a Garden of Bliss" — and this commentary weighed it at verses 18–19, where its double sense (the sweet plant and the ease of soul) divided the sūrahs: the present verse, repeating the noun at the bedside, decides nothing and doubles the gift: the nearest dying are welcomed with a scent that is also relief, and the sūrah, whose left receive "a column of smoke" (43 — samūm in the other chapters' word, ṣaʿīr here and samūm at 43's neighborhood) a drink of hamīm (93) — and in the other chapter of the mounting hour, the striking wind called samūm paired with hamīm itself (52:16, plain paraphrase) — defines its near-rank by olfaction as sharply as it defines the lost: two economies of smell, the garden's rayḥān against the smoke and the scorched wind.

The pairing completes the chapter's economics: it indicted making denial one's livelihood (82, at this commentary's verse), promised gratitude as the rarer harvest (70), and now gives the near-rank the naʿīm whose every hour the unthankful spent pretending was theirs — and the sūrahs' hearers would have known, at the word, the companion-verse they recite when the garden's name is spoken: the Rivalry chapter ends by promising that every person will, that Day, be questioned about the naʿīm — the delights they were given (102:6–8, in plain paraphrase).
verses.90:
> And if the deceased is one of the people of the right

**The Middle Branch of the Dying**

"Fa-ammā in kāna min aṣḥāb al-yamīn" — the second of the chapter's three bedside clauses (88, 90, 92) — reopens the census the sūrah took in its opening third ("and you will become three classes… the people of the right — what are the people of the right?" — 7–9, in the chapter's own repeated formula), and the repetition of the census-formula is the device by which the final third claims to be the first third, spoken at a nearer microphone: what the chapter narrated cosmically at 7–40 it now whispers individually at 88–96, and the middle class, largest of the saved, is where its hearers hoped to be listed. The verse supplies nothing new about the people of the right — no gardens, spouses, or cushions (the panorama's furniture at 28–34) — and the restraint is the point: at the throat, the saved are not re-described; they are re-counted, and the sūrah, which opened its Garden-material at 12 with "in the Gardens of Bliss" for the fore-runners and gave the right their whole paragraph only later, now inverts that generosity — the branch of the middle is nearly all hinge and no content — until verse 91 hands them a single greeting, which is, in this chapter's arithmetic of nearness (traced at 88 and 89), the correct dose: the nearer the class, the shorter the sentence, and the people of the right, not the nearest, receive exactly one line and a welcome inside it.

**"One of": The Partitive Repeated, the Mercy Insisted**

Verse 90 borrows the grammar of 88 — "one of the people of the right" — and the repetition at the two saved branches is itself a datum: the sūrah will not, anywhere in its final third, say "he is from the people of the right" in the indicative, only "if he was one of," and its commentators of the schools of conduct read the conditional as both pastoral warning (no one may die presuming) and pastoral permission (no one need despair), with the "min" softening even the assertion it makes: membership, not perfection, is the class's criterion — a reading this commentary anchored at 88's partitive and now finds confirmed by the middle branch's total silence about works: the panorama (28–34) mentioned the saved "because of what they used to do" (in the idiom of 24 and 34's "reward for what they used to do"), but at the dying the sūrah lists no deeds at all, and the reason is the sermon's last pastoral decision: at the throat, the saved are addressed as guests, not creditors, and a guest's identity — which house he belongs to — needs no résumé, which is how verse 91 can get away with its single word.

**The Largest Company, the Shortest Sentence**

One closing reckoning: the sūrah's first census said the multitudes were on the right's side ("a multitude from earlier generations and a multitude from later generations," 39–40, where the chapter itself took the right-hand census, against the near-rank's "a multitude from earlier generations and a few from later" at 13–14) — and the final third gives that majority a single verse and a single line of speech. The disproportion is al-Wāqiʿah's last joke on human organizations, which grade honor by length of citation: the many are saved by a word, the few by three nouns, and the deniers by two verses of drink and fire, and the sūrah, recited in rooms where the saved will outnumber everyone, says plainly that the Day is not a performance review — the greeting at 91 is the whole reward the middle class is given to hear, and every mourner who has stood at a deathbed knows the verse is true in the way sermons rarely are: what matters at the end is not what was said about the dead, how long, or with what honors, but that someone with authority says to them, at the moment they can no longer pretend, "welcome — you belong to us," and the sūrah, at 90–91, tells its market-town that the only such sentence that counts is the one that comes from the people God has already named, from the right side of every ledger they ever kept.
verses.91:
> then ˹they will be told,˺ “Greetings to you from the people of the right.”

**The Whole Reward, in One Sentence of Speech**

The brackets matter for the grammar: the sūrah's own text says "fa-salāmul-lakum" — peace/greetings to you — without naming the speaker, and the present translation's ˹they will be told˺ supplies the passive that Arabic conceals, which the sūrahs' readers mostly filled with the angels ("the angels will enter upon them from every gate, 'peace upon you'"), while others took the verse's own phrase — "from the people of the right" — literally: the saved greeting the saved, mutual welcome at the throat, and the commentary records both without choosing, because the verse's design tolerates either and the second is the sūrah's plain surface.

**"From the People of the Right": Salvation as Being Greeted by One's Own**

The genitive "from the people of the right" makes the greeting's sender the same class as its receiver — the saved welcome the saved — and that circularity is al-Wāqiʿah's quietest doctrine of the afterlife: the middle company's reward is to be recognized, at the last moment, by the community they spent their lives being; the sūrah's whole census-rhetoric (8, 27, 39, 90) was building toward the moment a person hears their own class's voice say "to you," and there is no divine speech-act at 91 at all (unlike the near-rank's wordless three nouns at 89 and the left's impersonal accommodation at 93), only the company — which is to say, in this chapter's anthropology of rizq and gratitude, that for the many-saved the final gift is the fellowship they were given the whole way, returned to them as a greeting. Commentators who noticed the absence of God's direct address at 91 explained it from the chapter's own economy: the near-rank were brought near to the Giver ("to Us," 88), the people of the right were kept in the company of the given, and the two modes of welcome — nearness and fellowship — correspond, in the sūrah's scale, to the two lives it knows: the rare, burning, few (13–14) and the wide, ordinary, many (39–40), each ending at its own register of joy.

**What 91 Withholds, and Why That Is the Praise**

One final negative observation belongs to the entry: the verse promises nothing — no garden re-listed, no spouses, no fruits — and that withholding, at the chapter's end, is not a lacuna but a judgment about the value of the greeting: having described Paradise's furniture for its panorama, the sūrah decides, for the bedside, that the saved dying one needs to hear only that they belong — that the company exists, that it greets, and that its welcome is the reward in its executable form. The commentary has argued (at 64–74, 77–82) that this sūrah's whole middle is an instruction in receiving — the world as gift, the Book as gift, gratitude as the only rational response — and 91 completes the instruction: the class of the many is received, at the end, by a greeting they neither earned nor arranged, only kept being part of, and the sūrah, whose mockers had "asked mockingly" (47) at their dinners and whose farmers would "lament" (66) in their fields, gives its saved, for their eternal audition, a single sentence whose content is that someone said "to you." Every embellishment the panorama could supply is, at the throat, unnecessary — the sūrah's last word about the saved is not what they will get but who will welcome them — and the doxology that follows two verses later (96) is therefore, in this architecture, not an addition but the only possible response: if the end of the saved is a greeting from the saved, the end of the sermon is "glorify the Name," because the God who arranges welcomes has, at last, nothing left to say about the welcome itself.
verses.92:
> But if such person is one of the misguided deniers

**They Become What They Did: The Verb Named Back at Its Owners**

"Fa-ammā in kāna min al-mukadhdhibīn" — "the deniers-of-lie" — and the participle is the chapter's final receipt: at 82 the audience was charged with making denial (takdhīb) their livelihood — "you repay your provisions with denial" — and at 92, at the throat, the doing has become the name: the one who called the Book a lie is, eternally, "of the deniers," his act fossilized into his class. The sūrah's whole anthropology has been this morphology in motion — you are what you repeatedly do to the given world — and the near-rank branch, by contrast, was named by what was done to them ("the brought-near," 88, passive, divine verb), while the middle branch was named by position ("the people of the right"), and only the lost are named by their own transitive verb, active, unrelieved: the three branches' three nominal forms are the chapter's last, silent sermon on how names are acquired on this side of dying, and the denier's, alone, is self-made.

**"The Misguided Deniers": Two Roots in One Title**

The present translation's "misguided deniers" packs the Arabic's double epithet — al-muḍallalīn, the "made-to-grope-in-error and deny" — the root ḍ-l-l (astray, lost) folded into the root k-dh-b (called a lie), and the combination is the sūrah's judgment on the relation between them: they did not stumble into denial; their error was itself an agency, a misguidance they enacted (the intensive-passive morphology reads, in the sūrahs' glosses, "led on and left to wander"), and their denial was itself an error, a falsehood committed against evidence the chapter has just spent seventeen verses supplying. The verse therefore closes the chapter's long argument with a definition of the audience's condition: from 47's mocking dinner-question to 81's trivializing, the Makkān posture toward the ḥadīth has been described as manner, then commerce, and here at 92, in two fused roots, as epistemology — a man who denied the Book and, in denying, lost the right order of knowing, so that the verdict names not a punishment's recipient but a knowledge's squanderer, which is exactly what a sūrah that kept asking its hearers to "consider," "remember," and "know" (57, 62, 76) must finally call them: those who knew the right hand of their own ledgers and did not know the right hand of God.

**The Left's Last Census, at the Scale of One Man**

The "min" of "one of," which at 88 and 90 carried mercy's partitive softness (membership, not perfection), carries here the plain arithmetic of the census — and readers of the sūrahs' pastoral literature have drawn the obvious conclusion, that the sūrah's final third is built so the reciter at every bedside hears all three branches as possibilities for the person before him and none as certainties, the "if" doing its last work of reverent suspension, while the chapter's whole preceding argument has already, of course, told the room which "if" the denier is fulfilling — and the tension between the conditional's humility and the sermon's confidence is, in this verse, the sound of late Makkān preaching refusing, even at 92, to damn a man it has not heard die.
verses.93:
> then their accommodation will be boiling water ˹to drink˺

**The Bracket's Verb: "˹To Drink˺" and the Gift That Is Not Taken**

The translators' ˹to drink˺ marks a verb the Arabic scene has already supplied at 54 ("then upon that, you will drink") and which 93 leaves to the noun — and the small bracket is the key to the verse's theology of shukr: the water of 68–70 was drinkable, sweet, unearned, and had to be received with gratitude to be received at all ("will you not then give thanks?" — 70, argued above at length); the water of 93 is drinkable only in the physical sense, ingested without reception, a rizq that cannot be thanked because it cannot be refused or enjoyed. Al-Wāqiʿah's entire hydrology, from "is it you who bring it down" (69) to this cup, says that the difference between the two waters is not chemistry but the drinker's history — and verse 93, placed one verse after the class was named "misguided deniers" (92), spells the class out as the condition of being handed a gift in a form that registers only as weight, the final drink as the final answer to a life of not-thanking: the sūrah's last hydrological word is that the ungrateful, at the end, still drink, and that is exactly what they made of all the water they were given — a universe in which everything is poured and nothing is received.

**"Min ḥamīm": The Partitive Some Readers Counted Twice**

The note earns its space in a chapter whose whole argument has turned on what a thing is — the fluid that was not made (58–59), the growth that was not grown (63–64), the fire that was assigned its jobs (73) — and if the cup of 93 is ḥamīm "as such," the verse has, in one preposition, completed the sūrah's doctrine of essences: the lost receive things in their bareness, drink without refreshment, shade without cool (44, the sūrah's negated pair), fire without provision, every created good present as a substance and absent as a gift, which is the most exact description this book offers of hell and the least embellished.

**The Repeated Rhyme: 93–94 as 42's Echo**

Finally, the sound: "in ḥamīmin wa-ḥamīm" (42) and the closing line's "min ḥamīm" — the same word, in the same slot at the line's end — and the bedside pair 93–94 rhymes ḥamīm against ṣalīr (94's "burning in Hellfire"), an assonance the panorama's left-passages had already tuned the ear for, so that the chapter's last word on the lost is delivered in the phonetics of its first: the sūrah's structure, read aloud, closes the left in the same sounds it opened them, and the audience at the dying man's side hears, in the rhyme, the whole interval of the chapter compress into a single couplet — accommodation and burning, water and fire, the two elements between which the left have been circling since verse 42 — and the sūrah's final device is that the verdict is not argued in these last lines but rhymed, because at the throat, al-Wāqiʿah has decided, the only arguments that carry are the ones the heart already knows by heart, and the chapter has made its hearers know even hell by heart, by sound, before it permits them to hear it named one last time, one verse short of its end.
verses.94:
> and burning in Hellfire

**Ṣalīr: The Noun of Roasting, the Chapter's One Occurrence**

The word "burning" (ṣalīr) belongs, in the Arabic's idiom, to the roasting of what is exposed — the sūrahs' lexica gloss it as the blazing fire's heat upon the surface, the searing, and it occurs in this chapter only here, in the present translation's rendering (73's bracketed "of the Hellfire" being supplied for the reminder-verse, as noted above). Its rarity is worth the note: the Book's commonst nouns for the abode — the "Jahannam" of the Medinan detail-passages and much of the Meccan, the "blazing" of the neighbors — are, in al-Wāqiʿah, absent or bracketed, and the chapter reaches its final word about the lost with a rare, searing concrete noun: not a place-name but a happening, "a burning," the sūrah's last grammatical judgment that hell, in this book's telling, is an event the self is inside of, not a geography one travels to. Commentators of the sūrahs, who counted such things, read the choice against the near-rank's three nouns — welcome, scent, garden, two states and a place — and found the left's two: a drink and a state, no place at all: "burning in," with the "in" hanging loose, the sūrah declining even to let the lost own a habitation, which is the whole poetics of verse 94 in one preposition's ellipsis.

**The Final Possessive: "In Hellfire," the Fire Owned by Its Name**

The construct — burning of the blazing-fire, ṣalīra l-jaḥīm — closes the chapter's long use of its fire-vocabulary (the kindled hearth of 71, the reminder-fire of 73, the column of smoke of 43) in a single iḍāfa, an attributive link, and the sūrah's last three noun-phrases are, in this translation, all iḍāfāt: "a Garden of Bliss" (89), "burning in Hellfire" (94), "the Name of your Lord, the Greatest" (96). That is the chapter's final theology in its syntax: al-Wāqiʿah ends by stacking possessions — the saved own a garden qualified by bliss, the lost a burning qualified by the Fire, and between them the Prophet is told to glorify a Name qualified by his Lord's greatest — and the sūrah's entire argument, that nothing in the world belongs to those who use it, resolves, grammatically, into a world where everything belongs: everything has its possessor, and the possessors are names of God, and the only fitting human act at the end of sorting is doxology. No commentary should pass verse 94 without noting that its four words place the reader between two genitives and one command, the lost "in" the burning as the saved are "in" the garden: the chapter's last word about both is not duration but possession, and the sūrah, whose middle argued that its audience owned every process wrongly, ends by telling the whole room whose the fire is — and whose, in fact, the praise.

**"And Burning": The Conjunction That Refuses Escalation**

The conjunction reads, in context, as the sūrah's settled judgment that the lost require no more words than they have had: the panorama said all there is to say, the deathbed re-said it at human scale, and 94's flat "and" is the end of the chapter's willingness to spend language on the subject — the reciter who has watched the sermon's long pity for the dying realize itself in these last clauses should hear, in the wa, something like the sūrah's own exhaustion of the theme, and its decision (which is also a mercy to the mourners in the room) to stop describing and say what is. Al-Wāqiʿah's restraint at 94 is not severity's coyness; it is preaching's respect for the scene it stands inside, in which the corpse does not need, and the family cannot bear, more than four words about the fire.
verses.95:
> Indeed, this is the absolute truth

**"This": The Demonstrative That Certifies the Whole Chapter**

The present translation's "this" (hādhā) is, at 95, the most contested finger in the sūrah — pointing back at the two verses of burning and drink, at the whole three-branch sorting, or at the entire chapter from the Event's first fall — and the sūrahs' exegetes preserved the range without closing it, most settling on the broadest: the sūrah ends its verdicts by swearing that everything just said is true, the near-rank's welcome and the left's cup alike. The formula has an exact twin elsewhere in the Book: "And indeed, this ˹Quran˺ is the absolute truth" (69:51, the Haqqah's line, in the present translation's wording) — a late-Makkān sūrah that also opens with its Day's name (al-Ḥāqqah, "The Reality") and also ends its description by certifying the Book itself, and the pair shows what 95 does: the demonstrative at the end of al-Wāqiʿah's last verdict behaves exactly as the Haqqah's behaves at its close — the chapter about the Day says, of itself, this is the truth — which is to say that in this register of sūrah, the final sentence about the doctrine of the Last Day is always also the final sentence about the book that speaks it, and no reader should be surprised that the chapter whose hinge-oath swore the recitation noble (75–77) ends by calling its contents the truth that certainty deserves.

**The Indicative After the Conditionals: How 95 Ends the Triptych**

Structurally, the last ten verses run on "if" — "if he was of the brought-near" (88), "if of the people of the right" (90), "if of the misguided deniers" (92) — and 95 breaks the grammar with a bare assertion: "this is the truth," no condition, no suspended verdict, the indicative mood returning to a chapter that began in the indicative ("when the Event befalls, its falsity no soul will deny," 1–2, in the plain sense of the opening lines' present translation). The movement is the sūrah's final lesson in modality: human knowledge sorts with "if," divine speech states with "is," and the whole late-Makkān device of the conditional triptych exists to make the hearer live, for three branches, in the "if" that his own position really occupies — the dying man's class is certain above and conditional below — so that verse 95's indicative lands as the lifting of a lid: the sūrah has said what it can say about the sorting (all of it, conditionally), and now says, flatly, what the sorting is: true, and true in the high grade.

**The Sūrah's Self-Referral, Read Against Its Bedside History**

The classical readers of the verse's taʿlīq — "this," they said, "is the certainty no doubt survives" — kept the line in their etiquette-books precisely for the rooms where consolation risks sounding like rhetoric, and a modern commentary, which has watched this chapter build its epistemology of seeing (84–85, "you look on… you cannot see"), should mark the arc complete: from the room that sees too little to the sentence that says too much, the sūrah has kept one promise — it never asked anyone to believe a thing it was willing to leave uncertified — and 95, four words of nominal clause at the edge of the last, is that promise's keeping, the chapter's final "is," spoken into a room whose every verb had, for ninety-four verses, been God's.

The phrase — truth of certainty, ḥaqq al-yaqīn — is a genitive of kind, and the sūrah's audience had heard its family before: "if you had known with knowing-certainty (bi-ʿilmi l-yaqīn)," the Rivalry chapter warns, "you would have seen the blazing-fire, then you would have seen it with the eye of certainty (ʿayni l-yaqīn)" (102:5–7, the sūrahs' plain account), and the tradition of this vocabulary grades knowledge into levels — know it, see it, be there at it — which is the ladder the commentary has been tracing in this chapter since its certainty-lam at 49–50, "most certainly… will surely be gathered," where certainty first entered as God's own register.
verses.96:
> So glorify the Name of your Lord, the Greatest

**The Repeat, and What the 22 Verses Between Did**

Verse 96 is verse 74 — "So glorify the Name of your Lord, the Greatest" — the present translation prints the two lines identically, and the sūrah's whole design turns on what the interval did to them: at 74 the command closed an argument about the world's making (57–73), and the hearer praised what he had been shown — seed, rain, fire, all of it unowned; at 96 the command closes the bedside sorting (88–95), and the same words now fall on a hearer who has been walked through the Book's four predicates (77–80), his own triviality indicted (81–82), a soul at its throat (83–87), and three final doors (88–94) — the second doxology is the first one, priced. This is the sūrah's last lesson in the difference between the two acts of praise the chapter has trained: you can glorify the Maker of crops, which the argument-half could reach, or glorify the Lord whose name is Greatest because He is the one whose welcome at 89 and greeting at 91 you intend to arrive inside — and al-Wāqiʿah, which has been educating its audience's vocabulary all along (the rayḥān re-weighted at 18–19 and 89, the shade at 30 and 43, the certainty-lam at 50, 52, 54, and 95), ends by handing the reciter back the sentence he heard at the hinge and letting him find, in it, all the chapter between.

**"The Greatest": The Superlative's Final Audit**

The chapter's ʿ-a-ẓ-m thread — the ˹great˺ loss of the keening farmers (66), the great oath at the hinge (76), the Greatest of both doxologies (74, 96) — closes here, and its audit is exact: in al-Wāqiʿah's economy, the word "great" was earned, before it was bestowed: the loss the farmers suffer is great, the oath God swears is great, and the Name alone is Greatest, the sūrah's adjectives sorted by their owners, human grief keeping the human scale and the divine name taking the superlative that nothing in the created list can share — an arrangement that answers, at the chapter's very last line, the mockers' whole register of magnitude (47's "when we are dust, will we really be raised?" is a complaint that God is being too small about resurrection; the sūrah's final word is that He is being too great for the complaint to have a subject). And the sūrah's own subject, at 96, is "your Lord" once more: the rabb which the four considerations spent their verses claiming for God (57–73) is, at the end, personalized to the Prophet and, through him, to every reciter — "your" Lord — which is the smallest, largest word in the last verse, and the sūrah's final claim: that the greatest God of the stars' positions and the soul's throat is, in the sentence that ends His chapter, addressed with a possessive pronoun that belongs to a man.

**The End, and the Next Beginning**

Finally — the canon's quiet grace: in the received sequence this chapter's last word, "the Greatest," stands immediately before the opening of Sūrah al-Ḥadīd: "Whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies Allah, for He is the Almighty, All-Wise" (57:1, the present translation verbatim) — the imperative al-Wāqiʿah gave the Prophet becoming, in the next sūrah's first word, the indicative of all creation: you are told to glorify; the heavens and the earth already do.
